text: Genesis places seed-bearing vegetation on day three (1:11–13) and the heavenly lights on day four (1:14–19). Reading these as the first physical appearance of plants and the Sun reverses the order in the accepted solar-system formation model.
scope: The strongest disagreement is the Sun–Earth–plants sequence under a literal first-creation reading. A literary arrangement, later visibility of an existing Sun, or miraculous light changes the claim being evaluated; these readings are not established by the scientific sources. Science models natural processes and cannot independently test an unspecified miracle.

title: Complete conquest and continuing inhabitants
summary: Broad victory summaries in Joshua sit alongside explicit reports that many inhabitants remained.
text: Broad victory summaries in Joshua sit alongside explicit reports that many inhabitants remained. Exodus 23:29–30 explicitly promises gradual removal rather than completion in one year, adding context to later conquest summaries. Numbers 33 commands dispossession and anticipates failure to remove inhabitants. A command or conditional warning is not itself a report that complete removal occurred. Deuteronomy 7 also pairs commands of complete destruction with gradual removal to prevent wild animals increasing. This reinforces the distinction between a stated goal and the pace or extent of a reported historical occupation. Deuteronomy 20 distinguishes distant-city rules from a destruction command concerning named local nations. This is a prescribed policy and rationale, not a report establishing its completion. Joshua 2:12–21 makes a conditional protection agreement for Rahab’s household: secrecy and remaining in the marked house are specified. Joshua 6:17,22–25 explicitly preserves that household as an exception, linking it to protection of the spies and their oath. Joshua 3:10 presents the coming crossing as assurance of displacement of seven named peoples. It is a promise within the narrative, not a census showing that displacement was completed. Joshua 6:21 describes destruction encompassing people of both sexes and ages and livestock; 6:24 describes burning the city with designated metals preserved for the treasury. The same account orders Rahab and her household brought out alive. These are explicitly differentiated outcomes, so the totalizing statement should be read together with the exceptions rather than quoted in isolation. Joshua 8:24–26 reports destruction of Ai’s inhabitants, while verses 2 and 27 explicitly permit cattle and spoil to be kept. This permission differs from Jericho’s disposal rule and is stated as an exception to treating the cities alike; it is not a claim that all campaigns used one uniform spoil policy. Joshua 10:20 explicitly mentions survivors entering fortified cities after a totalizing battle description. Verses 1 and 6–7 also retain Gibeon as a protected ally. The southern-city destruction reports in 28–40 should therefore be assessed with their stated targets and these exceptions, rather than expanded into an exhaustive population census. Joshua 11 combines a prolonged war (18), a protected Gibeon (19), and Anakim remaining in three named cities (22) with a whole-land summary (23). It also distinguishes killing inhabitants from burning every city: Hazor is singled out for burning, while cattle and spoil are retained (13–14). Neither totalizing victory language nor an absence of a burn layer alone establishes the fate of every settlement. Joshua 12 lists defeated kings associated with Jerusalem, Gezer, Taanach, Megiddo, and Dor. Later inhabitant reports at those places create tension with an exhaustive reading of territorial possession, but defeating a king does not itself assert permanent occupation or extinction of the population. Joshua 13:1 explicitly says much land remains to be possessed, and 13:6 orders allocation while removal of inhabitants is still promised. Verse 13 names peoples not expelled even in the eastern inheritance. Thus assigning land and occupying it are distinguished within Joshua itself. Caleb’s request at 14:12 anticipates his ability to dislodge the Anakim with divine help; 15:14–17 reports local conquests by Caleb and Othniel. These particulars sit beside the earlier Hebron and Anakim victory summaries in 10:37 and 11:21. Their order and scope require interpretation; the future-looking request alone does not prove the same people survived the earlier battle. Joshua 16:10 explicitly retains Gezer’s Canaanites under tribute, while 10:33 describes defeat of Gezer’s king and his assisting force. The earlier military action is not expressly a report that Gezer’s city population was eliminated; applying its no-survivor wording to every later inhabitant would broaden its stated target. Joshua 17:11–13 names towns whose Canaanite inhabitants remain and become tributaries rather than being expelled; the king-list victories therefore do not by themselves establish their permanent depopulation. The Joseph tribes describe iron chariots as an obstacle (16), but Joshua promises successful displacement despite them (18). This is not a statement that God is physically unable to defeat iron chariots. Joshua 18 calls the land subdued while seven tribes still lack their allotments and are urged to take possession (1–3). Survey and lot allocation follow (9–10). The difference between military subjection, administrative allocation and settled possession is explicit; treating these as identical makes the conquest summaries more exhaustive than these particulars support. Jerusalem’s inclusion in Benjamin’s city list (28) is an allotment statement, not a separate report that its remaining Jebusites had been expelled. Joshua 21:43-45 says Israel possessed the entire promised land, received rest, and saw all the good promises fulfilled; 22:4 invokes that rest when releasing the eastern tribes. These statements must be compared with the land still awaiting possession in 13:1-6 and the inhabitants retained in 16:10 and 17:12-13. An exhaustive claim that every promised district was settled and every enemy population removed conflicts with those particulars. A summary of the decisive victory and provision of inheritance has a narrower scope; the distinction is an interpretation of the statements, not proof that every geographical promise was already physically completed. Joshua 23 places remaining nations and future dispossession (4-7) alongside rest, undefeated victory, and fulfilled promises (1,9,14). It warns that future expulsion can cease if Israel abandons the covenant (12-13). Thus even the farewell speech distinguishes present success from future occupation. The congregation in 24:18 again uses a broad removal summary; its scope should not erase the earlier remaining-nation statements. Judges 1:8 reports Judah taking and burning Jerusalem, yet 1:21 reports Benjamin leaving its Jebusites in residence. A raid or capture need not establish permanent expulsion; the passage does not separately narrate a later return. Verse 19 places Judah’s failure against iron-equipped opponents alongside divine assistance: this does not independently establish that God was physically unable to overcome iron. Verses 24-25 explicitly protect the Bethel informant and his family; 27-35 repeatedly describe continued inhabitants and tribute rather than removal. Judges 2:20-23 attributes retained nations to covenant breach and testing, and expressly says they were not delivered into Joshua’s hand. This is a close verbal tension with the universal delivery summary at Joshua 21:44 if both describe every enemy without qualification. A restricted victory-summary reading and the conditional warnings in Joshua 23 give possible distinctions of scope; they do not independently establish how complete the historical occupation was. Judges 3:1-6 retains nations for testing obedience and teaching warfare. These purposes need not exclude the earlier gradual-removal or covenant-judgment explanations; the restrictive wording about teaching war should not be treated as an independently established exclusive cause. Judges 4 again presents a Jabin ruling at Hazor after Joshua 11 names Jabin and reports the king’s death and the city’s burning. The narratives do not identify this as the same individual or say Hazor could never be resettled. Assuming one king creates a chronological conflict; distinct rulers and renewed occupation are possible but their relationship is not narrated. A burn layer alone cannot identify either ruler or date both accounts.
reasoning: Joshua itself preserves an exception at Jerusalem, and Judges lists additional unconquered places. Totalizing military language need not mean every settlement was occupied or every person killed. This explicit exception qualifies an unqualified reading of destruction language; it does not by itself establish the historical extent of conquest or resolve the moral assessment of the killings.
scope: A literal exhaustive reading creates tension; a rhetorical summary of victory allows the stated exceptions. This does not independently date the conquest. Later presence can be explained by incomplete occupation or subsequent return, but these alternatives are not independently demonstrated here. The king list is not a population census or an archaeological chronology. These local accounts may narrate different stages or recap earlier events; their placement alone does not establish a dated sequence.

title: Seven or three years of famine?
summary: Gad offers David seven years of famine in 2 Samuel and three in 1 Chronicles. The Hebrew has the same two numbers. The Greek of 2 Samuel has three, as Chronicles does.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 24:13: “Shall seven years of famine come unto thee in thy land?” Hebrew (WLC): שֶֽׁבַע שָׁנִ֣ים ׀ רָעָ֣ב [seven years of famine]. KJV 1 Chronicles 21:12: “Either three years' famine”. Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 21:12: שָׁלֹ֨ושׁ שָׁנִ֜ים רָעָ֗ב [three years of famine]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 24:13: εἰ ἔλθῃ σοι τρία ἔτη λιμὸς ἐν τῇ γῇ σου [whether three years of famine shall come to you in your land]. Brenton Greek 1 Chronicles 21:12: ἢ τρία ἔτη λιμοῦ [either three years of famine]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/24/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/21/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA24.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1CH21.htm.
reasoning: Both passages give Gad’s three alternatives after the census, so the numbers are directly comparable. The KJV follows the Hebrew in each book: seven in Samuel, three in Chronicles. Brenton’s Greek has three years in both books, so in Samuel it differs from the KJV.
scope: This extends the published record of the same ID with the Hebrew and Greek wording; the finding between the two KJV verses is unchanged. No claim is made about which number is original. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

title: Seventy or seventy-five family members?
summary: Exodus and Genesis give a family total of seventy; Stephen’s speech in Acts gives seventy-five. The Septuagint also reads seventy-five in Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5.
text: Exodus 1:5 gives seventy descendants and notes Joseph was already in Egypt. Genesis 46:26–27 distinguishes sixty-six traveling descendants from a total household of seventy. Acts 7:14 gives seventy-five for the relatives Joseph summoned. Original-language wording: the Hebrew (WLC) has שִׁבְעִֽים [seventy] at Genesis 46:27 and שִׁבְעִ֣ים נָ֑פֶשׁ [seventy souls] at Exodus 1:5, which the KJV follows (“threescore and ten”; “seventy souls”). The Brenton Greek of Genesis 46:27 gives Joseph nine sons, not two, and a total of seventy-five: ψυχαὶ ἐννέα … ψυχαὶ ἑβδομηκονταπέντε; its Exodus 1:5 has πέντε καὶ ἑβδομήκοντα [seventy-five]. Acts 7:14 (KJV “threescore and fifteen souls”) reads ἐν ψυχαῖς ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε in the SBL and Tischendorf editions, and the same words in the Textus Receptus. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/46/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN46.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO01.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/SBLGNT/44/7/.
reasoning: The totals differ in all three packaged translations. The passages do not describe their counting categories in identical terms, so the numerical difference is directly visible while its explanation needs further evidence.
scope: This records an apparent textual discrepancy. Counting scope and textual transmission are questions for further research; these citations alone do not establish a particular reconciliation or manuscript history. Stephen’s seventy-five agrees with the Septuagint of Genesis and Exodus and disagrees with the Hebrew those KJV chapters translate. This shows where the two figures sit in the named editions; it does not show which figure is earlier or how either was counted. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier.

title: Achan’s household and individual punishment
summary: Achan’s children are included in the judgment scene, while Deuteronomy forbids executing children for a parent’s sin. The narrative does not state their individual guilt.
text: Joshua 7 begins with one named man taking prohibited spoil but attributes a trespass to Israel and connects it to the army’s defeat. Achan confesses his own action. Verse 24 lists his sons and daughters among those brought to Achor; verse 25 first describes stoning him and then uses plural objects for burning and stoning. Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids putting children to death for fathers and assigns death to each person’s own sin. Joshua 22:20 recalls that Achan did not perish alone and that wrath affected the congregation. Joshua 7:5 has already reported roughly thirty-six soldiers killed in the defeat. The later recollection confirms wider fatal consequences; it does not name each additional person or separately describe the death or guilt of each child. Verse 15 announces destruction of the offender and all he has, without separately naming the children. Brenton’s Greek-based English translation of verse 25 retains the singular stoning action but lacks the additional plural burning/stoning clause used by the packaged translations. It still includes sons and daughters in the group brought to the valley in verse 24. Original-language wording of 7:25: the KJV has “burned them with fire, after they had stoned them with stones”; the Hebrew (WLC) has וַיִּרְגְּמ֨וּ אֹתֹ֤ו כָל־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֶ֔בֶן וַיִּשְׂרְפ֤וּ אֹתָם֙ בָּאֵ֔שׁ וַיִּסְקְל֥וּ אֹתָ֖ם בָּאֲבָנִֽים [all Israel stoned him … burned them … stoned them]. In the Brenton Greek, verse 25 ends with Joshua’s words and the next verse has only the singular: Καὶ ἐλιθοβόλησαν αὐτὸν λίθοις πᾶς Ἰσραὴλ [and all Israel stoned him with stones]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/7/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS07.htm.
reasoning: Reading the plural action as extending to the listed family creates tension with the individual-punishment rule. The passage does not explicitly accuse the children of sharing Achan’s theft. Assuming their complicity supplies a fact not stated in this scene. Distinguishing exceptional divine judgment from ordinary legal proceedings is a proposed difference of scope, not an explicit explanation of each family member’s responsibility here. The retrospective statement therefore cannot settle the household question by itself: the earlier military deaths are also part of the narrative consequences.
scope: The final actions do not itemize each victim, so do not claim the text separately describes every child’s execution. The household-inclusive reading is a qualified interpretation of the listed group and plural wording. The collective military consequences and the execution rule are related but not identical kinds of responsibility. No independent historical occurrence or geological mechanism is established. The plural-action argument depends on the longer wording in the packaged editions; Brenton illustrates a different textual tradition without settling priority or the fate of every family member. title: Town lists and their stated totals
summary: Counting compound names together, Judah’s southern list has 36 towns against a total of 29; Naphtali’s fortified-city list has 16 against 19. Some other totals depend on alternative names.
text: Verses 21–32 give 38 comma-separated name entries in the packaged KJV, excluding the explicit Hazor alias. WEB joins the four names in verse 25 into two compound names, yielding 36 towns; both editions state 29. Verses 33–36 give 15 separately named entries in KJV but state 14; WEB treats Gederah/Gederothaim as alternative names, yielding 14. In Joshua 19:2–6 the packaged KJV separately lists Beersheba and Sheba, giving 14 names against 13. WEB treats Sheba as an alternative name, giving 13. The publisher’s eBible KJV page also uses an alternative-name wording here, unlike this packaged KJV dataset. At 19:35–38 both packaged KJV and WEB list 16 fortified-city names, while the stated total is 19; adjacent verses describe boundary locations separately.

The NET translator note likewise counts 36 against 29 and proposes alternative names or later additions as explanations. These are proposals, not a verified restoration. The second subtotal illustrates why punctuation alone cannot establish how many distinct places a list identifies. The Naphtali subtotal therefore requires an explanation of which places its total includes or how the list was transmitted. Boundary points should not automatically be counted as additional fortified cities. The differing Sheba wording demonstrates why counts must specify the edition being assessed.
scope: This compares the displayed lists with their subtotals; it does not identify the original manuscript reading or establish ancient administrative boundaries. title: Hornets and victory without sword or bow
summary: Joshua credits displacement to a hornet rather than Israel’s weapons, while the same speech mentions fighting. The tension depends on whether the weapon denial excludes combat or emphasizes divine agency.
text: Joshua 24:12 attributes displacement to a hornet rather than Israel’s sword or bow, referring to two Amorite kings without naming them. The same speech says the eastern Amorites and Jericho’s people fought Israel (24:8,11). Identifying the two kings as Sihon and Og follows the usage in Deuteronomy 3:8, but is an inference; verse 12 follows the western-Jordan events in verse 11. Deuteronomy 2:32-34 and 3:1-8 describes Israel striking Sihon and Og in battle while crediting divine delivery. Exodus 23:28 promises hornets. Brenton’s Greek-based English translation instead reads twelve kings at Joshua 24:12. KJV 24:12 reads “the two kings of the Amorites”, as does the Hebrew (WLC): שְׁנֵ֖י מַלְכֵ֣י הָאֱמֹרִ֑י. title: Who purchased the burial property?
summary: Joshua and Genesis name Jacob as purchaser of the Shechem land; Acts names Abraham as purchaser of a Shechem tomb. The texts do not explicitly explain the different purchaser.
text: Joshua 24:32 places Joseph’s bones in land at Shechem purchased by Jacob from Hamor’s sons; Genesis 33:19 also names Jacob. Acts 7:15-16 describes a tomb at Shechem purchased by Abraham from Hamor’s sons. Genesis 23 instead narrates Abraham purchasing the Machpelah property from Ephron near Hebron, where Genesis 50:12-13 places Jacob’s burial. In Acts 7:16, the location comes from the statement that the remains were carried to Shechem; the packaged KJV’s closing father-of-Sychem wording can refer to the person rather than the town. If the plural burial subject includes Jacob, Acts’ Shechem location also differs from Genesis 50’s Machpelah burial. If it resumes only the fathers, that particular burial-location conflict does not follow. Original-language wording: Joshua 24:32 (KJV) has “of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for an hundred pieces of silver”; the Hebrew (WLC) has מֵאֵ֛ת בְּנֵֽי־חֲמֹ֥ור אֲבִֽי־שְׁכֶ֖ם בְּמֵאָ֣ה קְשִׂיטָ֑ה [from the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem, for a hundred qesitah]. The Brenton Greek has other sellers and a price in animals: παρὰ τῶν Ἀμοῤῥαίων τῶν κατοικούντων ἐν Σικίμοις ἀμνάδων ἑκατὸν [from the Amorites living in Shechem, for a hundred ewe-lambs]. At Acts 7:16 the KJV ends “of the sons of Emmor the father of Sychem”. The Elzevir Textus Receptus has παρα των υιων εμμορ του συχεμ [from the sons of Emmor of Sychem; no word for “father”]. The SBL and Tischendorf editions have παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἑμμὼρ ἐν Συχέμ [from the sons of Hamor in Shechem]. All three Greek editions name Abraham as the buyer. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/24/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/44/7/, https://bolls.life/get-text/SBLGNT/44/7/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/44/7/.
reasoning: The named purchaser and transaction differ. Treating Abraham and Jacob as interchangeable erases the explicit names. A separate earlier purchase or compressed family history is a possible explanation, but the compared passages do not narrate a second Abraham purchase at Shechem. Acts’ plural burial statement also needs care about which persons it includes.
scope: This establishes a textual comparison, not an archaeological identification of the tombs. Do not claim Joseph was buried at Machpelah or that every patriarch’s burial is separately documented. Original wording, narrative compression and the scope of Acts’ plural subjects require further textual study. The purchaser difference between Acts and Joshua is in the Greek New Testament editions checked, so it is not a product of English translation. Three printed Greek New Testament editions are not a manuscript apparatus; no codex is named. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier. See also the separate record “Jacob buried at Machpelah, or carried to Sychem?” (jacob-buried-at-machpelah-or-at-sychem) for the burial-subject question.

title: Moses’ relatives and the in-law label

Numbers 10:29 introduces Hobab son of Raguel the Midianite, followed by the in-law label. Judges 4:11 calls Hobab father-in-law in the packaged KJV but brother-in-law in the packaged ASV and WEB. Judges 1:16 associates Moses’ in-law family with the Kenites. title: Seventy brothers, with a survivor?
summary: Judges reports seventy brothers killed while explicitly saying Jotham survived. A precise death count conflicts with that exception; seventy may instead describe the household group.
text: Judges 8:30 gives Gideon seventy sons, then 8:31 adds Abimelech. Judges 9:5 combines the seventy-person killing report with Jotham escaping. Jotham later repeats the number, and the narrator does so at 9:56.

scope: The text itself identifies the exception. It does not explain its counting convention, so neither sixty-nine nor sixty-eight is established as the actual death toll. This comparison concerns narrative arithmetic, not independent verification of the event.

title: Midian after the campaign in Numbers
summary: Numbers describes killing all Midianite males in its campaign; Judges later has Midian fighting Israel. The tension depends on whether “all” means the entire people or the campaign’s targets.
text: Numbers 31 reports male combat deaths, five kings killed and settlements burned; it then orders the captive boys killed. Its stated grievance concerns Peor. Judges 6–8 portrays Midian participating in a later invasion with Amalekites and eastern peoples.
reasoning: An extinction reading leaves no Midianite males for the later narrative. A campaign-specific reading permits other Midianite groups to remain. The large army figures in Judges 8:10 describe the eastern coalition, not a separately counted wholly Midianite army; the multitude language is not literal infinity.

text: KJV 2 Kings 13:1: “In the three and twentieth year of Joash the son of Ahaziah king of Judah Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned seventeen years.” Hebrew (WLC) 13:1: בִּשְׁנַ֨ת עֶשְׂרִ֤ים וְשָׁלֹשׁ֙ שָׁנָ֔ה לְיֹואָ֥שׁ [in the twenty-third year of Joash] … שְׁבַ֥ע עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה שָׁנָֽה [seventeen years]. KJV 13:10: “In the thirty and seventh year of Joash king of Judah began Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz to reign over Israel in Samaria”. Hebrew (WLC) 13:10: בִּשְׁנַ֨ת שְׁלֹשִׁ֤ים וָשֶׁ֙בַע֙ שָׁנָ֔ה לְיֹואָ֖שׁ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה [in the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah]. Brenton Greek 13:10: Ἐν ἔτει τριακοστῷ καὶ ἑβδόμῳ ἔτει τῷ Ἰωὰς [in the thirty-seventh year of Joas]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/13/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI13.htm.

title: Azariah: king from Jeroboam’s twenty-seventh year, when his father died about Jeroboam’s fifteenth?

title: Hoshea: king in “the twentieth year of Jotham”, who reigned sixteen years — or in the twelfth year of Ahaz?
summary: 2 Kings 15:30 has Hoshea take the throne in the twentieth year of Jotham. Three verses later Jotham reigns sixteen years. 17:1 has Hoshea begin in the twelfth year of Jotham’s son Ahaz.

Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 15:30: ἐν ἔτει εἰκοστῷ Ἰωάθαμ [in the twentieth year of Joatham]. title: Ahaz and Assyria: the king “hearkened unto him”, or “helped him not”?
summary: In 2 Kings Ahaz pays the king of Assyria to save him, and the king hearkens, takes Damascus and kills Rezin. In 2 Chronicles the king of Assyria comes, distresses Ahaz, and does not help him.
text: KJV 2 Kings 16:7: “come up, and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria, and out of the hand of the king of Israel”. KJV 16:8: “and sent it for a present to the king of Assyria”. KJV 16:9: “And the king of Assyria hearkened unto him: for the king of Assyria went up against Damascus, and took it, and carried the people of it captive to Kir, and slew Rezin.” Hebrew (WLC) 16:9: וַיִּשְׁמַ֤ע אֵלָיו֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר [and the king of Assyria listened to him]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 16:9: Καὶ ἤκουσεν αὐτοῦ βασιλεὺς Ἀσσυρίων [and the king of the Assyrians listened to him]. KJV 2 Chronicles 28:16: “At that time did king Ahaz send unto the kings of Assyria to help him.” KJV 28:20: “And Tilgathpilneser king of Assyria came unto him, and distressed him, but strengthened him not.” Hebrew (WLC) 28:20: וַיָּ֥צַר לֹ֖ו וְלֹ֥א חֲזָקֹֽו [and he distressed him and did not strengthen him]. Brenton Greek 28:20, end of the verse: καὶ ἔθλιψεν αὐτόν [and he afflicted him]. KJV 28:21: “and gave it unto the king of Assyria: but he helped him not”. Hebrew (WLC) 28:21: וְלֹ֥א לְעֶזְרָ֖ה לֹֽו [and not for a help to him]. Brenton Greek 28:21: καὶ οὐκ εἰς βοήθειαν αὐτῷ ἦν [and it was not for a help to him]. reasoning: Both books tell of Ahaz sending temple and palace treasure to the king of Assyria for help. Kings reports that the request was granted and Ahaz’s enemy was killed. Chronicles reports that the Assyrian king brought trouble and no help.

title: Ahaz’s age at his accession: twenty, or twenty-five?

title: What was the light of the first three days, before the lights of the fourth?

title: Whom does God address as “us”?
summary: Three times in Genesis God speaks in the plural: “Let us make man”, “as one of us”, “let us go down”. The narrative on either side speaks of God acting in the singular. The passages do not say who is addressed.

Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:26: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατʼ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθʼ ὁμοίωσιν [let us make man according to our image and according to likeness]. KJV 1:27: “So God created man in his own image”. KJV 3:22: “And the Lord God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil”. Hebrew (WLC) 3:22: הֵ֤ן הָֽאָדָם֙ הָיָה֙ כְּאַחַ֣ד מִמֶּ֔נּוּ [behold, the man has become like one of us]. Brenton Greek 3:22: ἰδοὺ Ἀδὰμ γέγονεν ὡς εἷς ἐξ ἡμῶν [behold, Adam has become as one of us]. KJV 11:5: “And the Lord came down to see the city and the tower”. KJV 11:7: “Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language”. Hebrew (WLC) 11:7: הָ֚בָה נֵֽרְדָ֔ה וְנָבְלָ֥ה שָׁ֖ם שְׂפָתָ֑ם [come, let us go down and confuse their language there]. Brenton Greek 11:7: Δεῦτε, καὶ καταβάντες συγχέωμεν αὐτῶν ἐκεῖ τὴν γλῶσσαν [come, and having gone down let us confound their tongue there]. KJV 11:8: “So the Lord scattered them abroad”. KJV Isaiah 6:8: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” KJV 1 Kings 22:19: “I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him”. KJV Job 38:7: “and all the sons of God shouted for joy”. KJV Isaiah 40:14: “With whom took he counsel”. title: Who was Melchizedek, and how did he come to be priest of the most high God?
summary: Melchizedek appears for three verses as king of Salem and priest of the most high God, blesses Abram and receives a tenth, and is not mentioned again in Genesis. His people, his descent and how he came to be a priest are not stated.
text: KJV Genesis 14:18: “And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.” Hebrew (WLC) 14:18: וּמַלְכִּי־צֶ֙דֶק֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ שָׁלֵ֔ם הֹוצִ֖יא לֶ֣חֶם וָיָ֑יִן וְה֥וּא כֹהֵ֖ן לְאֵ֥ל עֶלְיֹֽון [and Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine; and he was priest to God Most High]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 14:18: ἦν δὲ ἱερεὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου [and he was priest of God the Most High]. KJV 14:19: “Blessed be Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth”. KJV 14:20: “And he gave him tithes of all.” KJV 14:22: “I have lift up mine hand unto the Lord, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth”. KJV Psalms 110:4: “Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.” KJV Psalms 76:2: “In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Zion.” KJV Hebrews 7:1: “For this Melchisedec, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him”. KJV Hebrews 7:3: “Without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life; but made like unto the Son of God; abideth a priest continually.” Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/14/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN14.htm.
reasoning: Genesis 14:18 is the first verse in the packaged KJV that contains the word “priest”. Melchizedek is introduced without parents, people or history; he is a king of a city in the land where Abram is a stranger, and he is priest of the God whom Abram in verse 22 names as the Lord. Abram accepts his blessing and a tenth is given. The passage does not say how a king of Salem came to serve that God, who made him a priest, or what became of him.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is taken up elsewhere but, on the check made, not answered. title: Is the angel of the Lord a messenger, or the Lord himself?
summary: In Genesis the angel of the Lord speaks in the first person as God: “I will multiply thy seed”, “thou hast not withheld thy son … from me”, “I am the God of Bethel”. Hagar names “the Lord that spake unto her”. The passages do not say whether the angel is someone other than God or God himself appearing.

Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 16:10: Καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῇ ὁ ἄγγελος Κυρίου, πληθύνων πληθυνῶ τὸ σπέρμα σου [and the angel of the Lord said to her, multiplying I will multiply your seed]. KJV 16:11: “because the Lord hath heard thy affliction”. KJV 16:13: “And she called the name of the Lord that spake unto her, Thou God seest me”. Hebrew (WLC) 16:13: וַתִּקְרָ֤א שֵׁם־יְהוָה֙ הַדֹּבֵ֣ר אֵלֶ֔יהָ [and she called the name of YHWH who was speaking to her]. Brenton Greek 16:13: Καὶ ἐκάλεσε τὸ ὄνομα Κυρίου τοῦ λαλοῦντος πρὸς αὐτὴν [and she called the name of the Lord who was speaking to her]. KJV 22:11: “And the angel of the Lord called unto him out of heaven”. KJV 22:12: “for now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me”. Hebrew (WLC) 22:12: וְלֹ֥א חָשַׂ֛כְתָּ אֶת־בִּנְךָ֥ אֶת־יְחִידְךָ֖ מִמֶּֽנִּי [and you have not withheld your son, your only one, from me]. KJV 22:15: “And the angel of the Lord called unto Abraham out of heaven the second time,” KJV 22:16: “And said, By myself have I sworn, saith the Lord”. KJV 31:11: “And the angel of God spake unto me in a dream”. Hebrew (WLC) 31:11: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלַ֜י מַלְאַ֧ךְ הָאֱלֹהִ֛ים בַּחֲלֹ֖ום [and the angel of God said to me in the dream]. KJV 31:13: “I am the God of Bethel, where thou anointedst the pillar, and where thou vowedst a vow unto me”. Hebrew (WLC) 31:13: אָנֹכִ֤י הָאֵל֙ בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל [I am the God of Bethel]. Brenton Greek 31:13: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ὀφθείς σοι ἐν τόπῳ Θεοῦ [I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God]. KJV Exodus 3:2: “And the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush”. KJV Exodus 3:4: “God called unto him out of the midst of the bush”. KJV Judges 13:21: “Then Manoah knew that he was an angel of the Lord.” KJV Judges 13:22: “We shall surely die, because we have seen God.” KJV Zechariah 1:12: “Then the angel of the Lord answered and said, O Lord of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem”. reasoning: The narrator calls the speaker “the angel of the Lord” or “the angel of God”. The speaker then says things in the first person that belong to God: he will multiply Hagar’s seed; Abraham has not withheld his son “from me”; “I am the God of Bethel”. The same alternation is found outside Genesis: at the bush the angel of the Lord appears and God calls (Exodus 3:2, 3:4), and Manoah, knowing he had seen an angel of the Lord, says they have seen God (Judges 13:21–22). title: Who were the three men at Mamre, and was the Lord one of them?
summary: The Lord appears to Abraham; Abraham looks up and sees three men. Later “the men” leave for Sodom while Abraham still stands before the Lord, and two angels arrive at Sodom. The passage does not say how the Lord and the three men are related, or why three become two.
text: KJV Genesis 18:1: “And the Lord appeared unto him in the plains of Mamre”. Hebrew (WLC) 18:1: וַיֵּרָ֤א אֵלָיו֙ יְהוָ֔ה [and YHWH appeared to him]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 18:1: Ὤφθη δὲ αὐτῷ ὁ Θεὸς [and God appeared to him]. KJV 18:2: “And he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him”. Hebrew (WLC) 18:2: וְהִנֵּה֙ שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה אֲנָשִׁ֔ים נִצָּבִ֖ים עָלָ֑יו [and behold, three men standing by him]. Brenton Greek 18:2: καὶ ἰδοὺ τρεῖς ἄνδρες εἱστήκεισαν ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ [and behold, three men stood over him]. KJV 18:3: “My Lord, if now I have found favour in thy sight”. KJV 18:9: “And they said unto him, Where is Sarah thy wife?” KJV 18:10: “And he said, I will certainly return unto thee”. KJV 18:13: “And the Lord said unto Abraham, Wherefore did Sarah laugh”. KJV 18:22: “And the men turned their faces from thence, and went toward Sodom: but Abraham stood yet before the Lord.” Hebrew (WLC) 18:22: וַיִּפְנ֤וּ מִשָּׁם֙ הָֽאֲנָשִׁ֔ים וַיֵּלְכ֖וּ סְדֹ֑מָה וְאַ֨בְרָהָ֔ם עֹודֶ֥נּוּ עֹמֵ֖ד לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה [and the men turned from there and went toward Sodom, and Abraham was still standing before YHWH]. Brenton Greek 18:22: Καὶ ἀποστρέψαντες ἐκεῖθεν οἱ ἄνδρες, ἦλθον εἰς Σόδομα· Ἁβραὰμ δὲ ἔτι ἦν ἑστηκὼς ἐναντίον Κυρίου [and the men, having turned away from there, came to Sodom; and Abraham was still standing before the Lord]. KJV 18:33: “And the Lord went his way, as soon as he had left communing with Abraham”. KJV 19:1: “And there came two angels to Sodom at even”. Hebrew (WLC) 19:1: וַ֠יָּבֹאוּ שְׁנֵ֨י הַמַּלְאָכִ֤ים סְדֹ֙מָה֙ בָּעֶ֔רֶב [and the two angels came to Sodom in the evening]. Brenton Greek 19:1: οἱ δύο ἄγγελοι εἰς Σόδομα ἑσπέρας [the two angels, to Sodom, at evening]. KJV 19:13: “and the Lord hath sent us to destroy it”. KJV Hebrews 13:2: “for thereby some have entertained angels unawares”. reasoning: Verse 1 says the Lord appeared; verse 2 says that what Abraham saw was three men. Through the meal and the promise the speaker changes without comment: “they said” (18:9), “he said” (18:10), “the Lord said” (18:13). title: Beasts and fowl: made before man, or formed after him?
summary: Genesis 1 has the fowl made on the fifth day and the beasts on the sixth, and then man. Genesis 2, as worded, has man formed, then the beasts and fowl formed and brought to him. Brenton’s Greek of 2:19 has a word the KJV lacks: God formed them “further”.
text: KJV Genesis 1:21: “and every winged fowl after his kind”. KJV 1:25: “And God made the beast of the earth after his kind”. KJV 1:27: “So God created man in his own image”. KJV 2:7: “And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground”. KJV 2:18: “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him”. KJV 2:19: “And out of the ground the Lord God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them”. Hebrew (WLC) 2:19: וַיִּצֶר֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהִ֜ים מִן־הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה כָּל־חַיַּ֤ת הַשָּׂדֶה֙ [and the LORD God formed from the ground every beast of the field]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2:19: Καὶ ἔπλασεν ὁ Θεὸς ἔτι ἐκ τῆς γῆς πάντα τὰ θηρία τοῦ ἀγροῦ [and God formed further, out of the earth, all the beasts of the field]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/2/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN02.htm.
reasoning: In chapter 1 the order is fowl, then beasts, then man. summary: Terah is seventy when he begets Abram, Nahor and Haran, and dies at two hundred and five. Abram leaves Haran at seventy-five, and Acts says he left after his father died. Seventy and seventy-five make a hundred and forty-five, sixty years short.

title: Ishmael sent away: a youth past fourteen, or a child set on Hagar’s shoulder?

title: Two treasure cities, or three? The Greek adds On

text: KJV Exodus 1:11: “And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses.” Hebrew (WLC) 1:11: וַיִּ֜בֶן עָרֵ֤י מִסְכְּנֹות֙ לְפַרְעֹ֔ה אֶת־פִּתֹ֖ם וְאֶת־רַעַמְסֵֽס [and they built store cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Raamses]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:11: Καὶ ᾠκοδόμησαν πόλεις ὀχυρὰς τῷ Φαραῷ, τήν τε Πειθὼ, καὶ Ῥαμεσσῆ, καὶ Ὢν, ἥ ἐστιν Ἡλιού πολις [and they built strong cities for Pharaoh, both Pitho and Ramesses, and On, which is Heliopolis]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/1/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO01.htm.
reasoning: The KJV and the Hebrew quoted list two cities. Brenton’s Greek lists three, and the third is a city the KJV of Exodus never says the Israelites built. The Greek also calls the cities “strong” where the KJV has “treasure”.
scope: G applies at Exodus 1:11. This is a difference between two published texts; the KJV does not say that only two cities were built, so the two statements can both stand. title: “I AM THAT I AM” — or “I am the one who is”?
summary: In the KJV, with the Hebrew, God answers Moses with a first-person verb repeated: “I Am That I Am”, and “I Am hath sent me”. Brenton’s Greek has a different construction: “I am the one who is”, and “the one who is has sent me”.
text: KJV Exodus 3:13: “What is his name? what shall I say unto them?” KJV 3:14: “And God said unto Moses, I Am That I Am: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I Am hath sent me unto you.” Hebrew (WLC) 3:14: אֶֽהְיֶ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר אֶֽהְיֶ֑ה [I am that I am, or I will be what I will be: the same first-person verb twice]; אֶֽהְיֶ֖ה שְׁלָחַ֥נִי אֲלֵיכֶֽם [“I am” has sent me to you: the same first-person verb]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 3:14: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ Ὤν [I am the one who is]; ὁ Ὢν ἀπέσταλκέ με πρὸς ὑμᾶς [the one who is has sent me to you]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/3/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO03.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew quoted uses one first-person verb form three times, and the KJV keeps that: “I Am … I Am … I Am”. Brenton’s Greek uses “I am” once, and then a participle with the article, “the one who is”, both in the answer and as the name of the sender. In the Greek the sender is spoken of in the third person; in the KJV the name sent to Israel is itself the first-person “I Am”.
scope: G applies at Exodus 3:14. This compares two published wordings and is not a contradiction: both give an answer built on the verb “to be”. No H is proposed; the KJV follows the Hebrew form, and the Hebrew verb form can be read as present or future, which this record does not decide. title: Who sought to kill him at the inn: the Lord, or an angel of the Lord?
summary: The KJV, with the Hebrew, says the Lord met him and sought to kill him, and that Zipporah said “a bloody husband art thou to me”. Brenton’s Greek says an angel of the Lord met him, and gives Zipporah different words: “the blood of the circumcision of my child has stopped”.
text: KJV Exodus 4:24: “And it came to pass by the way in the inn, that the Lord met him, and sought to kill him.” KJV 4:25: “Then Zipporah took a sharp stone, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and cast it at his feet, and said, Surely a bloody husband art thou to me.” KJV 4:26: “So he let him go: then she said, A bloody husband thou art, because of the circumcision.” Hebrew (WLC) 4:24: וַיִּפְגְּשֵׁ֣הוּ יְהוָ֔ה וַיְבַקֵּ֖שׁ הֲמִיתֹֽו [and the LORD met him and sought to put him to death]. 4:25: וַתַּגַּ֖ע לְרַגְלָ֑יו וַתֹּ֕אמֶר כִּ֧י חֲתַן־דָּמִ֛ים אַתָּ֖ה לִֽי [and she made it touch his feet and said, Surely a bridegroom of blood you are to me]. 4:26: חֲתַ֥ן דָּמִ֖ים לַמּוּלֹֽת [a bridegroom of blood, for the circumcision]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 4:24: συνήντησεν αὐτῷ Ἄγγελος Κυρίου, καὶ ἐζήτει αὐτὸν ἀποκτεῖναι [an angel of the Lord met him, and sought to kill him]. 4:25: καὶ προσέπεσε πρὸς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ, καὶ εἶπεν, ἔστη τὸ αἷμα τῆς περιτομῆς τοῦ παιδίου μου [and she fell at his feet and said, The blood of the circumcision of my child has stopped]. 4:26: Καὶ ἀπῆλθεν ἀπʼ αὐτοῦ, διότι εἶπεν, ἔστη τὸ αἷμα τῆς περιτομῆς τοῦ παιδίου μου [and he went away from him, because she said, The blood of the circumcision of my child has stopped]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/4/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO04.htm.

In 4:25 the KJV has Zipporah cast the foreskin at his feet; the Greek has her fall at his feet. In 4:25 and 4:26 the KJV has her call someone “a bloody husband”; the Greek has no husband in her words at all, and says the attacker left because of what she said.

title: Did Amram marry his father’s sister, or his father’s brother’s daughter?
summary: The KJV, with the Hebrew, says Amram married Jochebed his father’s sister and lived 137 years. Brenton’s Greek says she was the daughter of his father’s brother, and gives him 132 years.
text: KJV Exodus 6:20: “And Amram took him Jochebed his father's sister to wife; and she bare him Aaron and Moses: and the years of the life of Amram were an hundred and thirty and seven years.” Hebrew (WLC) 6:20: וַיִּקַּ֨ח עַמְרָ֜ם אֶת־יֹוכֶ֤בֶד דֹּֽדָתֹו֙ לֹ֣ו לְאִשָּׁ֔ה [and Amram took Jochebed his aunt to himself for a wife]; שֶׁ֧בַע וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֛ים וּמְאַ֖ת שָׁנָֽה [a hundred and thirty-seven years]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 6:20: Καὶ ἔλαβεν Ἀμβρὰν τὴν Ἰωχαβὲδ, θυγατέρα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ, ἑαυτῷ εἰς γυναῖκα [and Ambran took Jochabed, daughter of the brother of his father, to himself for a wife]; τὰ δὲ ἔτη τῆς ζωῆς Ἀμβρὰμ, ἑκατὸν τριάκοντα δύο ἔτη [and the years of the life of Ambram were a hundred and thirty-two years]. KJV Numbers 26:59: “And the name of Amram's wife was Jochebed, the daughter of Levi, whom her mother bare to Levi in Egypt”. KJV Leviticus 18:12: “Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's sister”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/6/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO06.htm.
reasoning: In the KJV Jochebed is the sister of Amram’s father Kohath, and Numbers 26:59 agrees by calling her the daughter of Levi. In Brenton’s Greek of Exodus she is one generation lower: a daughter of Kohath’s brother, and so Amram’s cousin. The difference matters because the law later given in Leviticus forbids a man his father’s sister. The Greek also gives Amram’s age as 132 where the KJV and the Hebrew quoted have 137.
scope: G applies at Exodus 6:20 only, for the kinship and for the age. Numbers 26:59 and Leviticus 18:12 are context and were quoted from the KJV alone; the Greek of those verses was not compared. The marriage is before the law at Sinai, so no breach of law is claimed. The Hebrew word rendered “father’s sister” is the ordinary word for an aunt; this record does not claim it can mean a cousin. title: Four hundred and thirty years in Egypt — or in Egypt and Canaan? And 400, or 430?
summary: Exodus says the sojourning of Israel, who dwelt in Egypt, was 430 years. Genesis and Acts say 400 years. Galatians counts 430 years from the promise to Abraham to the law. Brenton’s Greek of Exodus makes the 430 years cover Egypt and Canaan together.
text: KJV Exodus 12:40: “Now the sojourning of the children of Israel, who dwelt in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years.” KJV 12:41: “And it came to pass at the end of the four hundred and thirty years, even the selfsame day it came to pass, that all the hosts of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt.” Hebrew (WLC) 12:40: וּמֹושַׁב֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָשְׁב֖וּ בְּמִצְרָ֑יִם שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה וְאַרְבַּ֥ע מֵאֹ֖ות שָׁנָֽה [and the dwelling of the children of Israel, which they dwelt in Egypt, was thirty years and four hundred years]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 12:40: Ἡ δὲ κατοίκησις τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, ἣν κατῴκησαν ἐν γῇ Αἰγύπτῳ καὶ ἐν γῇ Χαναὰν, ἔτη τετρακόσια τριάκοντα [and the dwelling of the children of Israel, which they dwelt in the land of Egypt and in the land of Chanaan, was four hundred and thirty years]. KJV Genesis 15:13: “thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years”. Hebrew (WLC) 15:13: אַרְבַּ֥ע מֵאֹ֖ות שָׁנָֽה [four hundred years]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 15:13: τετρακόσια ἔτη [four hundred years]. KJV Acts 7:6: “that they should bring them into bondage, and entreat them evil four hundred years”. Greek New Testament (TISCH; TR has the same words) Acts 7:6: ἔτη τετρακόσια [four hundred years]. KJV Galatians 3:17: “the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after”. Greek New Testament (TISCH) 3:17: ὁ μετὰ τετρακόσια καὶ τριάκοντα ἔτη γεγονὼς νόμος; (TR, unaccented as served) ο μετα ετη τετρακοσια και τριακοντα γεγονως νομος [the law, which came four hundred and thirty years after: the same number in both, in a different word order]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/12/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/15/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO12.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN15.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/44/7/, https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/44/7/, https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/48/3/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/48/3/.
reasoning: Two things differ. First, the number: Exodus has 430 years; Genesis 15:13 and Acts 7:6 have 400. Second, what the 430 years cover. In the KJV and the Hebrew quoted they are the dwelling in Egypt. In Galatians 3:17 the 430 years run from the covenant with Abraham to the law, a span that begins long before Jacob’s family went into Egypt. Brenton’s Greek of Exodus 12:40 has words the KJV lacks, “and in the land of Chanaan”, which make the 430 years cover both lands, as the count in Galatians does.

title: 430 years in Egypt, yet Kohath, Amram and Moses span at most 350
summary: Kohath is named among those who came into Egypt. He lived 133 years, his son Amram 137, and Amram’s son Moses was 80 at the exodus. Those three figures add up to 350 years at the very most, yet Exodus says Israel dwelt in Egypt 430 years.
text: KJV Genesis 46:8: “And these are the names of the children of Israel, which came into Egypt”. KJV 46:11: “And the sons of Levi; Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.” KJV Exodus 6:16: “the sons of Levi according to their generations; Gershon, and Kohath, and Merari”. KJV 6:18: “And the sons of Kohath; Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel: and the years of the life of Kohath were an hundred thirty and three years.” KJV 6:20: “and she bare him Aaron and Moses: and the years of the life of Amram were an hundred and thirty and seven years”. KJV 7:7: “And Moses was fourscore years old”. KJV Exodus 12:40: “Now the sojourning of the children of Israel, who dwelt in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years.” Hebrew (WLC) 6:18: וּשְׁנֵי֙ חַיֵּ֣י קְהָ֔ת שָׁלֹ֧שׁ וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֛ים וּמְאַ֖ת שָׁנָֽה [and the years of the life of Kohath were a hundred and thirty-three years]. 6:20: וּשְׁנֵי֙ חַיֵּ֣י עַמְרָ֔ם שֶׁ֧בַע וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֛ים וּמְאַ֖ת שָׁנָֽה [and the years of the life of Amram were a hundred and thirty-seven years]. 7:7: וּמֹשֶׁה֙ בֶּן־שְׁמֹנִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה [and Moses was eighty years old]. 12:40: שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה וְאַרְבַּ֥ע מֵאֹ֖ות שָׁנָֽה [thirty years and four hundred years]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 6:18: καὶ τὰ ἔτη τῆς ζωῆς Καὰθ ἑκατὸν τριάκοντα τρία ἔτη [a hundred and thirty-three years]. 6:20: ἑκατὸν τριάκοντα δύο ἔτη [a hundred and thirty-two years]. 7:7: Μωυσῆς δὲ ἦν ἐτῶν ὀγδοήκοντα [and Moses was eighty years old]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/6/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/7/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/12/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO06.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO07.htm.
reasoning: Kohath is listed among those who came into Egypt, so he was already born when the 430 years began. Suppose Amram was born in the last year of Kohath’s 133 years, and Moses in the last year of Amram’s 137. Moses was 80 when he spoke to Pharaoh. 133 + 137 + 80 = 350. That is the greatest span the three figures allow, and it is 80 years short of 430. With any earlier births the gap is wider.
scope: No tag is proposed: the Hebrew agrees with the KJV in all four verses. Brenton’s Greek gives Amram 132 years, which makes the greatest span 345; and at 12:40 it has the 430 years cover Egypt and Canaan, which is treated in a separate record. The figures can be reconciled if the line Levi, Kohath, Amram, Moses leaves out generations; Exodus 6 does not say that it does, and 6:20 says Jochebed “bare him Aaron and Moses”. They can also be reconciled if the 430 years begin before the family entered Egypt; the KJV of 12:40 says “who dwelt in Egypt”. No claim is made about the actual length of the stay. title: Silver from 603,550 men numbered — a month before the numbering that gives that total
summary: The silver for the sockets of the tabernacle came from 603,550 men who were numbered, and the tabernacle was reared on the first day of the first month of the second year. The numbering that yields 603,550 is commanded on the first day of the second month of that year.
text: KJV Exodus 38:25: “And the silver of them that were numbered of the congregation was an hundred talents”. KJV 38:26: “for every one that went to be numbered, from twenty years old and upward, for six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty men”. KJV 38:27: “And of the hundred talents of silver were cast the sockets of the sanctuary”. KJV Exodus 40:17: “And it came to pass in the first month in the second year, on the first day of the month, that the tabernacle was reared up.” KJV Numbers 1:1: “on the first day of the second month, in the second year after they were come out of the land of Egypt”. KJV 1:46: “Even all they that were numbered were six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty.” Hebrew (WLC) Exodus 38:26: לְשֵׁשׁ־מֵאֹ֥ות אֶ֙לֶף֙ וּשְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֔ים וַחֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵאֹ֖ות וַחֲמִשִּֽׁים [for six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty]. Numbers 1:1: בְּאֶחָד֩ לַחֹ֨דֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִ֜י בַּשָּׁנָ֣ה הַשֵּׁנִ֗ית [on the first of the second month, in the second year]. Numbers 1:46: שֵׁשׁ־מֵאֹ֥ות אֶ֖לֶף וּשְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֑ים וַחֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵאֹ֖ות וַחֲמִשִּֽׁים [six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek), where the passage is printed as Exodus 39:3: εἰς τὰς ἑξήκοντα μυριάδας, καὶ τρισχίλιοι πεντακόσιοι καὶ πεντήκοντα [for the sixty ten-thousands, and three thousand five hundred and fifty]. Numbers 1:46: ἑξακόσιαι χιλιάδες καὶ τρισχίλιοι καὶ πεντακόσιοι καὶ πεντήκοντα [six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/38/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/4/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO39.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/NUM01.htm.

The numbering in Numbers is commanded a month later, on the first day of the second month, and its total is the same figure to the last man: 603,550. KJV 1 Kings 11:40: “unto Shishak king of Egypt”. KJV 2 Kings 23:29: “Pharaohnechoh king of Egypt”. KJV Jeremiah 44:30: “Pharaohhophra king of Egypt”. summary: Where the KJV has “the Red sea”, the Hebrew has “sea of suph”. The KJV renders the same word suph as “flags” at Exodus 2:3 and “weeds” at Jonah 2:5. The Hebrew has no word for “red” in these verses. Brenton’s Greek has “Red sea”, as the KJV does.

title: “The morrow after the sabbath”: which sabbath starts the count of fifty days?

title: Seven sevens make forty-nine years; the jubile is the fiftieth. Where does the fiftieth year stand in the count?
summary: Every seventh year the land is not sown. Seven such sevens are forty-nine years, and then the fiftieth year is hallowed and not sown either. The chapter does not say whether the fiftieth year stands outside the sevens or is counted as the first year of the next seven. Under either reading that keeps it distinct from the forty-ninth, the two consecutive years are unsown.

Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/3/25/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/LEV25.htm.
reasoning: The forty-ninth year is a seventh year, so it is not sown. The fiftieth is the jubile and is not sown. If the fiftieth is a distinct year after the forty-ninth, two years pass without sowing whether the next seven starts at year fifty or year fifty-one; the quoted instructions do not specify that starting point. The quoted provision does not explicitly explain how the seventh-year sowing timetable applies at the jubile. The length of the cycle, forty-nine years or fifty, depends on the answer, and land prices and the release of servants in the same chapter are reckoned by years to the jubile.

title: Thirty-two persons were the tribute given to Eleazar the priest: what was done with them?

title: The passover: “thou shalt roast and eat it” — the Greek says “boil and roast”, and the Hebrew verb is the one Exodus forbids with water
summary: Exodus forbids eating the passover “sodden at all with water” and requires it “roast with fire”. The KJV of Deuteronomy 16:7 says “roast”. The Hebrew verb there is the one rendered “sodden” in Exodus, not the Exodus word for roast, and Brenton’s Greek has two verbs: “thou shalt boil and roast”.

Exodus 12:9: וּבָשֵׁ֥ל מְבֻשָּׁ֖ל בַּמָּ֑יִם כִּ֣י אִם־צְלִי־אֵ֔שׁ [nor cooked, cooked in water, but roast of fire]. 2 Chronicles 35:13: וַֽיְבַשְּׁל֥וּ הַפֶּ֛סַח בָּאֵ֖שׁ [and they cooked the passover in the fire]; וְהַקֳּדָשִׁ֣ים בִּשְּׁל֗וּ בַּסִּירֹ֤ות [and the holy things they cooked in the pots]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Deuteronomy 16:7: Καὶ ἑψήσεις καὶ ὀπτήσεις καὶ φαγῇ [and thou shalt boil and thou shalt roast and thou shalt eat]. Exodus 12:9: οὐδὲ ἡψημένον ἐν ὕδατι, ἀλλʼ ἢ ὀπτὰ πυρὶ [nor boiled in water, but only roast with fire]. 2 Chronicles 35:13: Καὶ ὤπτησαν τὸ φασὲκ ἐν πυρὶ [and they roasted the passover in fire]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/16/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/12/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/35/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/DEU16.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO12.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH35.htm.
reasoning: In Exodus 12:9 the Hebrew sets two words against each other: a verb of cooking, said there to be “in water”, which the KJV renders “sodden”, and a word for roasting. title: Who buried Moses?
summary: Deuteronomy says of Moses “he buried him” and that no man knows the grave. The verse does not name the one who buried him. Jude speaks of a dispute between Michael and the devil “about the body of Moses” and does not say what the dispute was or who buried the body.

title: The sun, moon and stars “divided unto all nations” — divided to them for what?
summary: Israel is warned not to worship the sun, moon and stars, “which the Lord thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven”. The verse does not say for what purpose they were divided to the nations. The next verse sets Israel apart: “But the Lord hath taken you”.
text: KJV Deuteronomy 4:19: “shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them, which the Lord thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven” KJV 4:20: “But the Lord hath taken you, and brought you forth out of the iron furnace, even out of Egypt, to be unto him a people of inheritance” KJV 17:3: “either the sun, or moon, or any of the host of heaven, which I have not commanded” KJV 29:26: “For they went and served other gods, and worshipped them, gods whom they knew not, and whom he had not given unto them:” KJV Genesis 1:17: “And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth,” Hebrew (WLC) Deuteronomy 4:19: אֲשֶׁ֨ר חָלַ֜ק יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֙יךָ֙ אֹתָ֔ם לְכֹל֙ הָֽעַמִּ֔ים תַּ֖חַת כָּל־הַשָּׁמָֽיִם [which the LORD thy God has apportioned, them, to all the peoples under all the heavens]. WLC 29:25, which is KJV 29:26: אֱלֹהִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא־יְדָע֔וּם וְלֹ֥א חָלַ֖ק לָהֶֽם [gods whom they did not know and he had not apportioned to them]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 4:19: ἃ ἀπένειμε Κύριος ὁ Θεός σου αὐτὰ πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσι τοῖς ὑποκάτω τοῦ οὐρανοῦ [which the Lord thy God has assigned, them, to all the nations under heaven]. 29:26: οὐδὲ διένειμεν αὐτοῖς [nor did he distribute to them]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/4/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/29/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/DEU04.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/DEU29.htm.
reasoning: The clause stands inside a warning against worshipping the heavenly bodies, and gives as a fact about them that God divided them to all nations. What was given to the nations — the use of their light, or the bodies as what those nations serve — changes what the passage says about the worship of other peoples. The same Hebrew verb is used at 29:26 (WLC 29:25) of gods “whom he had not given unto them”, said of Israel.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verse states: that the heavenly bodies were given to every nation alike for light and for marking time, as Genesis 1:17 says they were set “to give light upon the earth”, so that the clause is a reason not to worship what serves everyone; that they were allotted to the other nations as what those nations worship, while Israel was taken as the Lord’s own people (4:20), which is how the shared verb at 29:26 can be taken. The second reading does not by itself mean that such worship is approved. Check made: Deuteronomy 4:15–20, 17:2–5 and 29:24–28 were read in the KJV, and the Hebrew and Greek of the clauses quoted were compared; no other passage was searched, so a statement of the purpose elsewhere is not excluded. These checked passages do not explicitly settle for what the host of heaven was divided to the nations. The Hebrew of chapter 29 is numbered one verse lower than the KJV. No H or G is proposed. title: Moses blesses “the children of Israel” tribe by tribe — why is Simeon not named?
summary: Deuteronomy 33 is introduced as the blessing with which Moses blessed the children of Israel, and it names the tribes one after another. Simeon is not named in the chapter. The chapter gives no reason, though Simeon is named among the tribes six chapters earlier.
text: KJV Deuteronomy 33:1: “And this is the blessing, wherewith Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death.” KJV 33:6: “Let Reuben live, and not die; and let not his men be few.” KJV 33:7: “And this is the blessing of Judah” KJV 27:12: “These shall stand upon mount Gerizim to bless the people, when ye are come over Jordan; Simeon, and Levi, and Judah” KJV Genesis 49:5: “Simeon and Levi are brethren” KJV Genesis 49:7: “I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel” KJV Joshua 19:1: “their inheritance was within the inheritance of the children of Judah” KJV Numbers 1:23: “of the tribe of Simeon, were fifty and nine thousand and three hundred” KJV Numbers 26:14: “These are the families of the Simeonites, twenty and two thousand and two hundred” Hebrew (WLC) Deuteronomy 33:1: אֲשֶׁ֨ר בֵּרַ֥ךְ מֹשֶׁ֛ה אִ֥ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים אֶת־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל [with which Moses the man of God blessed the sons of Israel]. 33:6: יְחִ֥י רְאוּבֵ֖ן וְאַל־יָמֹ֑ת [let Reuben live and not die]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 33:6: Ζήτω Ῥουβὴν, καὶ μὴ ἀποθανέτω, καὶ ἔστω πολὺς ἐν ἀριθμῷ [let Reuben live and not die, and let him be many in number]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/33/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/DEU33.htm.
reasoning: The heading says the blessing is of the children of Israel, and the chapter then speaks of Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph with Ephraim and Manasseh, Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali and Asher. One of the tribes numbered in the wilderness and placed on mount Gerizim in chapter 27 has no saying. Whether that is a judgement on the tribe, a statement about its standing at the time, or an accident of the text changes how the chapter is read, and the chapter does not say.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the chapter states: that Simeon is passed over because of what Jacob says of Simeon and Levi in Genesis 49:5–7, though Levi is blessed here; that Simeon is counted within Judah, in whose land the tribe later has its inheritance (Joshua 19:1); that the tribe had become small, as the two numberings quoted may suggest; that a saying for Simeon has dropped out of the text. Check made: a whole-word search of the 29 verses of Deuteronomy 33 in the packaged KJV finds each of the other names listed above and does not find “Simeon”; the same search of all Deuteronomy finds “Simeon” at 27:12 only; the 29 verses printed on the cited page of Brenton’s Greek for chapter 33 were searched for the name and it was not found. That is a word search of the editions named, not a survey of manuscripts. These checked passages do not explicitly settle why Simeon is not named. title: Who is the “captain of the host of the Lord” that Joshua meets by Jericho?
summary: By Jericho Joshua sees “a man” with a drawn sword who calls himself “captain of the host of the Lord”. Joshua falls on his face and is told to take off his shoe because the place is holy. The passage does not say who or what this figure is, and his command about the holy ground does not explicitly identify him.
text: KJV Joshua 5:13: “behold, there stood a man over against him with his sword drawn in his hand: and Joshua went unto him, and said unto him, Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?” KJV 5:14: “And he said, Nay; but as captain of the host of the Lord am I now come. And Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and did worship, and said unto him, What saith my Lord unto his servant?” KJV 5:15: “And the captain of the Lord's host said unto Joshua, Loose thy shoe from off thy foot; for the place whereon thou standest is holy. And Joshua did so.” KJV 6:1: “Now Jericho was straitly shut up because of the children of Israel” KJV 6:2: “And the Lord said unto Joshua, See, I have given into thine hand Jericho” KJV Exodus 3:5: “put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground” KJV Genesis 23:7: “And Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land” KJV Revelation 22:8: “I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which shewed me these things” KJV Revelation 22:9: “Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant” Hebrew (WLC) Joshua 5:13: וְהִנֵּה־אִישׁ֙ עֹמֵ֣ד לְנֶגְדֹּ֔ו [and behold a man standing over against him]. 5:14: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ׀ לֹ֗א כִּ֛י אֲנִ֥י שַׂר־צְבָֽא־יְהוָ֖ה עַתָּ֣ה בָ֑אתִי [and he said, No; for I am the captain of the host of the LORD; now I have come]; וַיִּשְׁתָּ֔חוּ [and he bowed down]. 5:15: שַׁל־נַֽעַלְךָ֙ מֵעַ֣ל רַגְלֶ֔ךָ [loose thy sandal from off thy foot]. Exodus 3:5: שַׁל־נְעָלֶ֙יךָ֙ מֵעַ֣ל רַגְלֶ֔יךָ [loose thy sandals from off thy feet]. Genesis 23:7: וַיִּשְׁתַּ֥חוּ לְעַם־הָאָ֖רֶץ [and he bowed down to the people of the land]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Joshua 5:14: ἐγὼ ἀρχιστράτηγος δυνάμεως Κυρίου, νυνὶ παραγέγονα. Καὶ Ἰησοῦς ἔπεσεν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ, δέσποτα, τί προστάσσεις τῷ σῷ οἰκέτῃ; [I, chief captain of the force of the Lord, have now come. And Joshua fell on his face upon the earth and said to him, Master, what dost thou command thy servant?]. Greek New Testament (TISCH) Revelation 22:9: τῷ θεῷ προσκύνησον [worship God]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/5/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/3/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/23/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS05.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/66/22/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/66/22/.
reasoning: The figure is first called “a man”, then gives himself a title found in the KJV only in these two verses, and Joshua answers by falling on his face and calling him “my Lord”. Whether Joshua is meeting a human officer, an angel or God bears on what Joshua’s act is and on who speaks next: the three verses give no message from the captain beyond the command about the shoe, and the next words of instruction are introduced with “And the Lord said unto Joshua” after a verse about Jericho being shut up.

title: Rahab’s house was “upon the town wall” — how were the spies sent into it after “the wall fell down flat”?
summary: Rahab’s house is said to be upon the wall of Jericho, and her family is to be kept safe by staying inside it. The account then says the wall “fell down flat”, and the narrative next reports Joshua’s instruction and the spies going in to bring the family out. The verses compared do not say how the house was still there to be entered.
text: KJV Joshua 2:15: “Then she let them down by a cord through the window: for her house was upon the town wall, and she dwelt upon the wall.” KJV 2:18: “thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by” KJV 2:19: “whosoever shall be with thee in the house, his blood shall be on our head, if any hand be upon him” KJV 6:5: “the wall of the city shall fall down flat, and the people shall ascend up every man straight before him” KJV 6:17: “only Rahab the harlot shall live, she and all that are with her in the house” KJV 6:20: “the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city” KJV 6:22: “But Joshua had said unto the two men that had spied out the country, Go into the harlot's house, and bring out thence the woman, and all that she hath, as ye sware unto her.” KJV 6:23: “And the young men that were spies went in, and brought out Rahab” Hebrew (WLC) Joshua 2:15: כִּ֤י בֵיתָהּ֙ בְּקִ֣יר הַֽחֹומָ֔ה וּבַֽחֹומָ֖ה הִ֥יא יֹושָֽׁבֶת [for her house was in the side of the wall, and in the wall she was dwelling]. 6:20: וַתִּפֹּ֨ל הַֽחֹומָ֜ה תַּחְתֶּ֗יהָ [and the wall fell in its place]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Joshua 2:15, the whole verse as printed: Καὶ κατεχάλασεν αὐτοὺς διὰ τῆς θυρίδος [and she let them down through the window]. 6:20: καὶ ἔπεσεν ἅπαν τὸ τεῖχος κύκλῳ [and all the wall fell round about]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/6/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS02.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS06.htm.
reasoning: The agreement with Rahab depends on the house: her family must be inside it, and the window in the wall is to be marked. The fall of the wall is then told without any exception, and the next thing said of the house is Joshua’s reported instruction and the spies going in and bringing the family out. The KJV “had said” does not fix the instruction itself as later than the collapse. Whether the house stood, and so whether the whole wall fell or a part of it, changes how “the wall fell down flat” is to be read, and the verses compared do not say.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses state: that the stretch of wall with her house was left standing; that the wall fell where the people stood and went up “every man straight before him”, and not on every side; that the house was built against the side of the wall, as the Hebrew wording quoted can be taken, and was not brought down with it; that the account is brief and passes over how the family came through. The record does not say the two statements cannot both be true. In Brenton’s Greek the wording differs at both ends: 2:15 as printed has no clause about the house or the wall, and the 24 verses printed on the cited page for chapter 2 were searched for the Greek word for wall and it was not found; 6:20 says “all the wall fell round about”. Those differences are noted and no G is proposed here. Check made: Joshua 2:15–21, 6:1, 6:5, 6:15–17 and 6:20–25 were read in the KJV; a search of the packaged KJV for “Rahab” and “Rachab” finds, outside Joshua, Matthew 1:5, Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25 of this woman and three verses of the Psalms and Isaiah that use the name otherwise, and none of those speaks of her house or the wall. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle how the house was standing. title: What was “the book of Jasher”, and how much of the sun-and-moon passage is taken from it?
summary: In the middle of the account of the sun standing still the text asks, “Is not this written in the book of Jasher?” The same book is named once more, at David’s lament. Neither place says what the book was, and Joshua does not mark which of the words around the question are quoted from it.
text: KJV Joshua 10:12: “and he said in the sight of Israel, Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon.” KJV 10:13: “And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. Is not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day.” KJV 10:14: “And there was no day like that before it or after it” KJV 2 Samuel 1:17: “And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son:” KJV 2 Samuel 1:18: “(Also he bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow: behold, it is written in the book of Jasher.)” Hebrew (WLC) Joshua 10:13: הֲלֹא־הִ֥יא כְתוּבָ֖ה עַל־סֵ֣פֶר הַיָּשָׁ֑ר [is it not written upon the book of the upright]. 2 Samuel 1:18: הִנֵּ֥ה כְתוּבָ֖ה עַל־סֵ֥פֶר הַיָּשָֽׁר [behold, it is written upon the book of the upright]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Joshua 10:13: Καὶ ἔστη ὁ ἥλιος καὶ ἡ σελήνη ἐν στάσει, ἕως ἠμύνατο ὁ Θεὸς τοὺς ἐχθροὺς αὐτῶν· καὶ ἔστη ὁ ἥλιος κατὰ μέσον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ [and the sun stood and the moon in their station until God avenged himself on their enemies; and the sun stood in the middle of heaven]. 2 Samuel 1:18: ἰδοὺ γέγραπται ἐπὶ βιβλίου τοῦ εὐθοῦς [behold, it is written upon the book of the upright]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/10/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS10.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA01.htm.
reasoning: The question about the book stands between two statements that the sun stood still. If the words before it, or the words on both sides of it, are taken from a book of songs, the standing of the sun is being reported in that book’s words; if only the narrator is speaking, the words are attributed to that narrator. Neither attribution alone settles whether the language is literal or figurative. The passage names the book and does not say what kind of book it was, who wrote it, or where the words taken from it begin and end.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that the book was a collection of songs, since the other thing said to be written in it is David’s lament; that “Jasher” is not a person’s name and the title means “the book of the upright”, as the Hebrew and the Greek of 2 Samuel 1:18 can be rendered; that only the address to the sun and moon and the lines before the question are from the book, with the words after it being the narrator’s own; that the words after the question are from the book as well. None of these readings by itself decides whether the event is told as literal or as figure. Brenton’s Greek of Joshua 10:13 as quoted runs from the first statement to the second with no sentence about a book between them, and the 41 verses printed on the cited page for chapter 10 were searched for the Greek word for book and it was not found; that difference is noted and no G is proposed here. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV for “Jasher” finds Joshua 10:13 and 2 Samuel 1:18 only; Joshua 10:12–14 and 2 Samuel 1:17–18 were read in the KJV. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what the book was or how much is quoted from it. A published record sets a literal reading of the long day beside astronomy, and another asks about a different book named at Numbers 21:14; this record asks only about the book named here. title: “Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God” — which words, and in which book?
summary: After the covenant at Shechem, Joshua is said to have written “these words in the book of the law of God”. The verse does not say which words he wrote, or whether the book is the book of the law that Moses wrote and had placed beside the ark, which the book of Joshua elsewhere calls “the book of the law of Moses”.

Deuteronomy 31:24: לִכְתֹּ֛ב אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֥י הַתֹּורָֽה־הַזֹּ֖את עַל־סֵ֑פֶר עַ֖ד תֻּמָּֽם [to write the words of this law upon a book until they were finished]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Joshua 24:26: Καὶ ἔγραψε τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα εἰς βιβλίον νόμων τοῦ Θεοῦ [and he wrote these words in a book of laws of God]. title: Judges opens “after the death of Joshua”, then tells of Joshua sending the people away and dying — in what order did these things happen?
summary: The first verse of Judges dates what follows “after the death of Joshua”. A chapter later Joshua lets the people go and his death is reported. One event of chapter 1, the taking of Kirjathsepher by Othniel, is also told in Joshua 15 in almost the same words. The verses compared do not say which of these events came before Joshua’s death and which after.

title: What was the ephod Gideon made of the gold, and what did Israel do when it “went thither a whoring after it”?
summary: Gideon asks for the golden earrings of the spoil, makes “an ephod thereof” and puts it in his city, and all Israel goes “a whoring after it”. In the other verses compared an ephod is a thing a priest wears or brings. The passage does not say what Gideon’s ephod was, what it was for, or what the people did with it.
text: KJV Judges 8:23: “I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the Lord shall rule over you” KJV 8:24: “I would desire a request of you, that ye would give me every man the earrings of his prey” KJV 8:26: “And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold” KJV 8:27: “And Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.” KJV 8:33: “as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim” KJV 17:5: “And the man Micah had an house of gods, and made an ephod, and teraphim” KJV Exodus 28:4: “And these are the garments which they shall make; a breastplate, and an ephod, and a robe” KJV Exodus 28:6: “And they shall make the ephod of gold, of blue, and of purple, of scarlet, and fine twined linen, with cunning work.” KJV 1 Samuel 2:18: “girded with a linen ephod” KJV 1 Samuel 23:9: “he said to Abiathar the priest, Bring hither the ephod” KJV Hosea 3:4: “without an image, and without an ephod, and without teraphim” Hebrew (WLC) Judges 8:27: וַיַּעַשׂ֩ אֹותֹ֨ו גִדְעֹ֜ון לְאֵפֹ֗וד וַיַּצֵּ֨ג אֹותֹ֤ו בְעִירֹו֙ בְּעָפְרָ֔ה וַיִּזְנ֧וּ כָֽל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל אַחֲרָ֖יו שָׁ֑ם [and Gideon made it into an ephod and set it in his city, in Ophrah, and all Israel went whoring after it there]. Exodus 28:6: וְעָשׂ֖וּ אֶת־הָאֵפֹ֑ד [and they shall make the ephod]. title: What was the “evil spirit” God sent between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and how did it work?
summary: After three years of Abimelech’s rule “God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem”, and the men of Shechem turn on him. The next verse gives the purpose: the blood of Gideon’s sons is to come upon both. The passage does not say what the evil spirit was or how it brought the treachery about.
text: KJV Judges 9:22: “When Abimelech had reigned three years over Israel,” KJV 9:23: “Then God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem; and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech:” KJV 9:24: “That the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother” KJV 9:25: “And the men of Shechem set liers in wait for him in the top of the mountains” KJV 9:56: “Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech” KJV 9:57: “And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads” KJV 1 Samuel 16:14: “But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.” KJV 1 Kings 22:21: “And there came forth a spirit, and stood before the Lord, and said, I will persuade him.” KJV 1 Kings 22:22: “I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” KJV Numbers 5:14: “the spirit of jealousy come upon him” Hebrew (WLC) Judges 9:23: וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח אֱלֹהִים֙ ר֣וּחַ רָעָ֔ה בֵּ֣ין אֲבִימֶ֔לֶךְ וּבֵ֖ין בַּעֲלֵ֣י שְׁכֶ֑ם [and God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the lords of Shechem]. 1 Samuel 16:14: רֽוּחַ־רָעָ֖ה מֵאֵ֥ת יְהוָֽה [an evil spirit from the LORD]. 1 Kings 22:22: ר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר [a spirit of falsehood]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Judges 9:23: Καὶ ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ Θεὸς πνεῦμα πονηρὸν ἀναμέσον Ἀβιμέλεχ καὶ ἀναμέσον τῶν ἀνδρῶν Σικίμων [and God sent out an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem]. 1 Samuel 16:14: πνεῦμα πονηρὸν παρὰ Κυρίου [an evil spirit from the Lord].
