title: Jephthah “did with her according to his vow” — what was done to his daughter?
summary: Jephthah vows that whatever comes out of his house to meet him “shall surely be the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering”. His only child comes out. After two months she returns and he “did with her according to his vow which he had vowed: and she knew no man”. Verse 39 reports fulfillment by reference to the vow, without separately describing the act.
text: KJV Judges 11:30: “And Jephthah vowed a vow unto the Lord” KJV 11:31: “Then it shall be, that whatsoever cometh forth of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, shall surely be the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering.” KJV 11:34: “his daughter came out to meet him with timbrels and with dances: and she was his only child” KJV 11:35: “for I have opened my mouth unto the Lord, and I cannot go back” KJV 11:37: “let me alone two months, that I may go up and down upon the mountains, and bewail my virginity” KJV 11:38: “and bewailed her virginity upon the mountains” KJV 11:39: “And it came to pass at the end of two months, that she returned unto her father, who did with her according to his vow which he had vowed: and she knew no man. And it was a custom in Israel,” KJV 11:40: “That the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year.” KJV Deuteronomy 12:31: “for even their sons and their daughters they have burnt in the fire to their gods” KJV 1 Samuel 12:11: “And the Lord sent Jerubbaal, and Bedan, and Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you” KJV Hebrews 11:32: “for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae” Hebrew (WLC) Judges 11:31: וְהָיָה֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה וְהַעֲלִיתִ֖הוּ עֹולָֽה [and it shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering]. 11:39: וַיַּ֣עַשׂ לָ֔הּ אֶת־נִדְרֹ֖ו אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָדָ֑ר וְהִיא֙ לֹא־יָדְעָ֣ה אִ֔ישׁ [and he did to her his vow which he had vowed; and she had not known a man]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Judges 11:31: καὶ ἔσται τῷ Κυρίῳ, ἀνοίσω αὐτὸν ὁλοκαύτωμα [and he shall be the Lord's; I will offer him up as a whole burnt offering]. 11:39: καὶ ἐποίησεν ἐν αὐτῇ τὴν εὐχὴν αὐτοῦ ἣν ηὔξατο· καὶ αὕτη οὐκ ἔγνω ἄνδρα [and he performed on her his vow which he had vowed; and she knew no man]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/11/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG11.htm.
reasoning: The vow names a burnt offering, and the fulfilment is told in seven English words that point back to the vow without repeating it. What the passage dwells on instead is her virginity: she asks two months to bewail it, and the report of the fulfilment is followed at once by “and she knew no man”. The reference back to a vow naming a burnt offering provides textual support for the reading that Jephthah sacrificed his daughter. Other readings depend on interpreting the vow or its fulfillment differently. title: Naomi “selleth a parcel of land, which was our brother Elimelech's” — how did the land come to be hers to sell?

title: Boaz took Ruth “to raise up the name of the dead”, and “Boaz begat Obed” — how was the dead man’s name raised, and was the child also counted legally in his house?

The verses compared give Obed as the son of Boaz and do not name Mahlon or Elimelech in the line; they do not say how the name of the dead was raised up.

And Saul perceived that it was Samuel” KJV 28:15: “And Samuel said to Saul, Why hast thou disquieted me, to bring me up?” KJV 28:16: “Then said Samuel, Wherefore then dost thou ask of me, seeing the Lord is departed from thee, and is become thine enemy?” KJV 28:19: “to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me” KJV 28:20: “and was sore afraid, because of the words of Samuel” KJV 1 Chronicles 10:13: “and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it” KJV Leviticus 20:27: “A man also or woman that hath a familiar spirit, or that is a wizard, shall surely be put to death” KJV Deuteronomy 18:11: “Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer.” KJV Isaiah 8:19: “should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Samuel 28:7: אֵ֣שֶׁת בַּעֲלַת־אֹ֔וב [a woman, mistress of an ob]. 28:12: וַתֵּ֤רֶא הָֽאִשָּׁה֙ אֶת־שְׁמוּאֵ֔ל וַתִּזְעַ֖ק בְּקֹ֣ול גָּדֹ֑ול [and the woman saw Samuel and cried with a great voice]. 28:13: אֱלֹהִ֥ים רָאִ֖יתִי עֹלִ֥ים מִן־הָאָֽרֶץ [elohim I saw coming up from the earth; the participle is plural]. 28:14: וַיֵּ֤דַע שָׁאוּל֙ כִּֽי־שְׁמוּאֵ֣ל ה֔וּא [and Saul knew that it was Samuel]. 28:15: לָ֥מָּה הִרְגַּזְתַּ֖נִי לְהַעֲלֹ֣ות אֹתִ֑י [why have you disturbed me, to bring me up]. 28:19: וּמָחָ֕ר אַתָּ֥ה וּבָנֶ֖יךָ עִמִּ֑י [and tomorrow you and your sons with me]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Samuel 28:12: Καὶ εἶδεν ἡ γυνὴ τὸν Σαμουὴλ, καὶ ἀνεβόησε φωνῇ μεγάλῃ [and the woman saw Samuel, and cried out with a loud voice]. 28:14: ἄνδρα ὄρθιον ἀναβαίνοντα ἐκ τῆς γῆς [an upright man coming up out of the earth]. 28:19: αὔριον σὺ καὶ οἱ υἱοί σου μετὰ σοῦ πεσοῦνται [tomorrow you and your sons with you shall fall]. 1 Chronicles 10:13: ὅτι ἐπηρώτησε Σαοὺλ ἐν τῷ ἐγγαστριμύθῳ τοῦ ζητῆσαι, καὶ ἀπεκρίνατο αὐτῷ Σαμουὴλ ὁ προφήτης [because Saul enquired by the one with a divining spirit, to seek, and Samuel the prophet answered him]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/9/28/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1SA28.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1CH10.htm.
reasoning: The passage sets two things side by side. The laws quoted forbid consulting one “that hath a familiar spirit”, and 28:6 says the Lord would not answer Saul by the three means it names. Yet from 28:12 the narrative itself uses the name Samuel for what the woman sees and for the speaker (“the woman saw Samuel”, “Samuel said to Saul”), and the words spoken name the Lord and say what will happen the next day. Between the request at 28:11 and the sight at 28:12 no act of the woman is told. So the verses quoted leave unstated whether Samuel came up through the woman’s practice, apart from it, or in some other way, and they give no reason for her cry or for how she then knew her visitor was Saul. Which of these is taken decides how the passage bears on the laws quoted and on the statement that the Lord did not answer.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the woman’s practice brought Samuel up; that Samuel was sent apart from anything she did, which is offered as the reason for her cry; that what appeared was not Samuel, although the narrative uses his name. Limits: the narrative calls the one seen and the speaker “Samuel” at 28:12, 28:15, 28:16 and 28:20, and nothing in these verses says the appearance was false; only the woman is said to see, Saul asks her what she saw, and “Saul perceived that it was Samuel” follows her description; the woman’s words at 28:13 are her report, and the KJV’s “gods” there stands for a Hebrew word that the KJV elsewhere renders “God”, with a plural participle; 28:15 has Samuel say “to bring me up”, which states that he was brought up and does not say by whom; 1 Chronicles 10:13 in the KJV says Saul asked counsel of one that had a familiar spirit and does not say what answered, while Brenton’s Greek of that verse adds that “Samuel the prophet answered him”, a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding; Brenton’s Greek of 28:14 has “an upright man” where the KJV has “An old man”, and of 28:19 “with you shall fall” where the KJV has “be with me”, both also stated as wording only. Check made: 1 Samuel 28:3 and 28:6–25 were read in the KJV, verses 3 and 6–20 also in the Hebrew and the Greek; a search of the packaged KJV for “familiar spirit” finds Leviticus 19:31, 20:6, 20:27, Deuteronomy 18:11, 1 Samuel 28:3, 28:7, 28:8, 28:9, 2 Kings 21:6, 23:24, 1 Chronicles 10:13, 2 Chronicles 33:6, Isaiah 8:19, 19:3 and 29:4, and a whole-word search for “Endor” finds Joshua 17:11, 1 Samuel 28:7 and Psalms 83:10. Those are word searches and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle by what means Samuel came up. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

title: What became of Shiloh, and of the house of the Lord there, after “the ark of God was taken”?
summary: In 1 Samuel 1–4 the yearly worship, Eli’s priesthood and the ark are at Shiloh. The ark is taken in battle and a runner brings the news to Shiloh. The compared passages do not narrate what happened to the sanctuary at Shiloh: the returned ark goes to Kirjathjearim, and priests with the shewbread are later described at Nob. Jeremiah says “see what I did to it” and a psalm says God “forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh”. The verses compared do not say what was done to Shiloh, when, or by whom.
text: KJV Joshua 18:1: “assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there” KJV 1 Samuel 1:3: “went up out of his city yearly to worship and to sacrifice unto the Lord of hosts in Shiloh” KJV 1:9: “Eli the priest sat upon a seat by a post of the temple of the Lord” KJV 2:22: “the women that assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation” KJV 4:4: “So the people sent to Shiloh, that they might bring from thence the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts” KJV 4:11: “And the ark of God was taken; and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were slain.” KJV 4:12: “came to Shiloh the same day with his clothes rent” KJV 7:1: “And the men of Kirjathjearim came, and fetched up the ark of the Lord, and brought it into the house of Abinadab in the hill” KJV 14:3: “the son of Eli, the Lord's priest in Shiloh, wearing an ephod” KJV 21:1: “Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest” KJV 21:6: “there was no bread there but the shewbread, that was taken from before the Lord” KJV 22:19: “And Nob, the city of the priests, smote he with the edge of the sword” KJV 1 Kings 14:2: “get thee to Shiloh: behold, there is Ahijah the prophet” KJV Psalms 78:60: “So that he forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent which he placed among men;” KJV 78:61: “And delivered his strength into captivity, and his glory into the enemy's hand.” KJV Jeremiah 7:12: “But go ye now unto my place which was in Shiloh, where I set my name at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel.” KJV 7:14: “Therefore will I do unto this house, which is called by my name”; “as I have done to Shiloh” KJV 26:6: “Then will I make this house like Shiloh” KJV 41:5: “there came certain from Shechem, from Shiloh, and from Samaria” KJV 2 Chronicles 1:3: “the high place that was at Gibeon; for there was the tabernacle of the congregation of God, which Moses the servant of the Lord had made in the wilderness” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Samuel 2:22: פֶּ֖תַח אֹ֥הֶל מֹועֵֽד [the door of the tent of meeting]. 14:3: כֹּהֵ֧ן ׀ יְהוָ֛ה בְּשִׁלֹ֖ו נֹשֵׂ֣א אֵפֹ֑וד [priest of the LORD in Shiloh, bearing an ephod]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Samuel 14:3: ἱερεὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν Σηλὼμ αἴρων ἐφούδ [priest of God in Selom, bearing an ephod]. Brenton’s Greek of 2:22 reads in full: Καὶ Ἡλὶ πρεσβύτης σφόδρα· καὶ ἤκουσεν ἃ ἐποίουν οἱ υἱοὶ αὐτοῦ τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραήλ· [And Eli was very old, and he heard what his sons did to the children of Israel]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/9/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/9/14/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1SA14.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1SA02.htm.
reasoning: Shiloh is where the tabernacle was set up (Joshua 18:1) and where the first chapters of 1 Samuel place the sacrifices, the priests and the ark. The cited scene at Shiloh reports the arrival of news that the ark was taken (4:12 and the verses after it). When the ark comes back it is not brought to Shiloh, and priests with the shewbread are later at Nob. Jeremiah points to Shiloh as a place where something was done that his hearers could go and see, and makes it the pattern for what will be done to the house in Jerusalem; Psalm 78 says God forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh. None of the verses compared narrates that event. What it was, and whether it followed the battle of 1 Samuel 4 or came later, bears on how the later priestly setting at Nob, the separate resting place of the ark and Jeremiah’s warning are read; these verses do not directly narrate a move of the priesthood from Shiloh to Nob.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the Philistines destroyed Shiloh after the battle; that the place was left by the priests without being destroyed, and that what Jeremiah speaks of happened at a later time; that the forsaking in Psalm 78 is the loss of the ark and nothing more. Limits: Jeremiah 7:12 says something was done to “my place which was in Shiloh” because of wickedness and does not say what, when, or by whose hand; Psalms 78:60–61 joins the forsaking of the tabernacle of Shiloh to the delivering of “his strength into captivity” and does not describe the place afterwards; 1 Kings 14:2 and Jeremiah 41:5 speak of people at or from Shiloh in later times, so the verses quoted do not show the place empty for ever; at 1 Samuel 14:3 the words “the Lord's priest in Shiloh” may describe Eli and not Ahiah, and the verse does not say the priesthood was still at Shiloh in Saul’s time; 1 Samuel calls the house at Shiloh “the temple of the Lord” (1:9) and “the tabernacle of the congregation” (2:22), and whether the tabernacle later said to be at Gibeon (2 Chronicles 1:3) was moved from Shiloh, and when, is not told in the verses quoted; Brenton’s Greek of 2:22, quoted in full above, has no clause about the women or the tabernacle, a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “Shiloh” finds, in 1 Samuel, 1:3, 1:9, 1:24, 2:14, 3:21, 4:3, 4:4, 4:12 and 14:3, and after 1 Samuel, 1 Kings 2:27, 14:2 and 14:4, Psalms 78:60, and Jeremiah 7:12, 7:14, 26:6, 26:9 and 41:5; each of those verses was read in the KJV, with 1 Samuel 4:3–4, 4:10–22, 7:1–2, 21:1–6 and 22:9–19; 1 Samuel 2:22 and 14:3 were also read in the Hebrew and the Greek. That is a word search and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible, and a passage that tells of Shiloh without naming it would not be found by it. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what was done to Shiloh or when. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. title: “Michal took an image, and laid it in the bed” — what was it, and how did it come to be in David's house?
summary: To cover David’s escape Michal puts “an image” in his bed, and Saul’s messengers find it there. The Hebrew word is the one the KJV prints as “teraphim” in Judges, renders “images” where Rachel steals her father’s and Laban calls them “my gods”, and renders “idolatry” in Samuel’s rebuke of Saul. The verses compared do not say what the object was, whose it was, or what it was kept for.
text: KJV 1 Samuel 19:11: “Saul also sent messengers unto David's house, to watch him, and to slay him in the morning” KJV 19:13: “And Michal took an image, and laid it in the bed, and put a pillow of goats' hair for his bolster, and covered it with a cloth.” KJV 19:14: “And when Saul sent messengers to take David, she said, He is sick.” KJV 19:16: “And when the messengers were come in, behold, there was an image in the bed, with a pillow of goats' hair for his bolster.” KJV 15:23: “For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry” KJV Genesis 31:19: “Rachel had stolen the images that were her father's” KJV 31:30: “yet wherefore hast thou stolen my gods?” KJV 31:34: “Now Rachel had taken the images, and put them in the camel's furniture, and sat upon them” KJV Judges 17:5: “And the man Micah had an house of gods, and made an ephod, and teraphim” KJV 2 Kings 23:24: “the workers with familiar spirits, and the wizards, and the images, and the idols, and all the abominations that were spied in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem, did Josiah put away” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Samuel 19:13: וַתִּקַּ֨ח מִיכַ֜ל אֶת־הַתְּרָפִ֗ים [and Michal took the teraphim]. 19:16: וְהִנֵּ֥ה הַתְּרָפִ֖ים אֶל־הַמִּטָּ֑ה [and behold, the teraphim at the bed]. 15:23: וְאָ֥וֶן וּתְרָפִ֖ים הַפְצַ֑ר [and iniquity and teraphim is stubbornness]. Genesis 31:19: וַתִּגְנֹ֣ב רָחֵ֔ל אֶת־הַתְּרָפִ֖ים [and Rachel stole the teraphim]. 31:34: וְרָחֵ֞ל לָקְחָ֣ה אֶת־הַתְּרָפִ֗ים [and Rachel had taken the teraphim]. Judges 17:5: אֵפֹוד֙ וּתְרָפִ֔ים [an ephod and teraphim]. 2 Kings 23:24: וְאֶת־הַתְּרָפִ֨ים וְאֶת־הַגִּלֻּלִ֜ים [and the teraphim and the idols]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Samuel 19:13: Καὶ ἔλαβεν ἡ Μελχὸλ τὰ κενοτάφια [and Melchol took the kenotaphia]. 15:23: θεραφὶν [theraphin, the Hebrew word in Greek letters]. Genesis 31:19: ἔκλεψε δὲ Ῥαχὴλ τὰ εἴδωλα τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῆς [and Rachel stole her father's idols]. 2 Kings 23:24: καὶ τὰ θεραφὶν, καὶ τὰ εἴδωλα [and the theraphin, and the idols]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/9/19/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/9/15/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/31/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/17/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/23/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1SA19.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1SA15.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN31.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI23.htm.
reasoning: The object is the means of the escape, and the Hebrew gives it the definite article: “the teraphim”. The article alone does not establish its ownership or prior use in the household. In the other verses quoted the same Hebrew word names things a man calls “my gods” (Genesis 31:30), things made with an ephod for “an house of gods” (Judges 17:5), things Josiah put away with the idols (2 Kings 23:24), and the thing to which Samuel likens Saul’s stubbornness (1 Samuel 15:23). Here it lies in David’s bed, and the verses quoted pass no remark on it. What it was and whose it was decides whether the passage shows an object of worship kept in David’s house, something of Michal’s own, or a thing with another use.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that it was a household figure of the kind Laban calls his gods; that it belonged to Michal and not to David; that it was a figure kept for some use other than worship; that it was large enough to pass for a man in a bed. Limits: a shared Hebrew word does not show that the object in David’s house was the same kind of thing as Laban’s or Micah’s, or that it was used as theirs were; the Hebrew word is plural in form in every verse quoted, and the KJV renders it “an image” here and “images” in Genesis, so its form does not settle whether one object or several is meant; the verses quoted do not say the object had a human shape or size — they say it was laid in the bed and covered, and that Michal said “He is sick”; Rachel sits upon hers (Genesis 31:34), which says something of the size of those and nothing of this one; the passage does not say David knew of the object, and it records no word of blame or of approval; no finding of a broken law is proposed, because the verses quoted do not describe any act of worship. The KJV’s “an image” for the Hebrew “the teraphim”, the KJV’s “idolatry” at 15:23, and Brenton’s Greek word at 19:13 are stated here as wording and are not proposed as separate findings. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “teraphim” finds Judges 17:5, 18:14, 18:17, 18:18, 18:20 and Hosea 3:4 only, so the English word does not lead to this passage; the Hebrew word was confirmed by script in the Westminster Leningrad text of 1 Samuel 19:13, 19:16 and 15:23, Genesis 31:19 and 31:34, Judges 17:5 and 2 Kings 23:24, and the Hebrew Bible was not searched for its other occurrences; 1 Samuel 19:8–18 was read in the KJV. That is a word search and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what the image was or whose it was. No H, G or V is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. title: Samuel “told the people the manner of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book” — what did the book say?
summary: When Saul is made king, Samuel tells the people “the manner of the kingdom”, writes it in a book and lays it up “before the Lord”. Two chapters earlier Samuel has told them “the manner of the king”: what a king will take from them. Deuteronomy has a law for a king, with limits on him and a book he is to copy. The verses compared do not say what Samuel wrote, or whether it was either of these.
text: KJV 1 Samuel 8:9: “protest solemnly unto them, and shew them the manner of the king that shall reign over them” KJV 8:11: “This will be the manner of the king that shall reign over you: He will take your sons, and appoint them for himself” KJV 8:17: “He will take the tenth of your sheep: and ye shall be his servants.” KJV 8:18: “And ye shall cry out in that day because of your king which ye shall have chosen you” KJV 10:24: “And all the people shouted, and said, God save the king” KJV 10:25: “Then Samuel told the people the manner of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book, and laid it up before the Lord. And Samuel sent all the people away, every man to his house.” KJV Deuteronomy 17:14: “and shalt say, I will set a king over me, like as all the nations that are about me” KJV 17:16: “But he shall not multiply horses to himself” KJV 17:18: “And it shall be, when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites:” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Samuel 10:25: מִשְׁפַּ֣ט הַמְּלֻכָ֔ה וַיִּכְתֹּ֣ב בַּסֵּ֔פֶר וַיַּנַּ֖ח לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה [the mishpat of the kingdom, and he wrote in the book, or in a book, and laid it before the LORD]. 8:9: מִשְׁפַּ֣ט הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִמְלֹ֖ךְ עֲלֵיהֶֽם [the mishpat of the king who shall reign over them]. 8:11: זֶ֗ה יִֽהְיֶה֙ מִשְׁפַּ֣ט הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ [this shall be the mishpat of the king]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Samuel 10:25: τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ βασιλέως, καὶ ἔγραψεν ἐν βιβλίῳ, καὶ ἔθηκεν ἐνώπιον Κυρίου [the dikaioma of the king, and he wrote in a book, and set it before the Lord]. 8:9: τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ βασιλέως ὃς βασιλεύσει ἐπʼ αὐτούς [the dikaioma of the king who shall reign over them]. 8:11: τοῦτο ἔσται τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ βασιλέως [this shall be the dikaioma of the king]. title: “Because he slew the Gibeonites” — when and how did Saul slay them?
summary: A three-year famine is said to be “for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites”, and seven of Saul’s descendants are put to death for it. The chapter says that Saul “sought to slay them” and that he “consumed” them, but the verses compared do not give the time, place, extent or circumstances of the killing; and a word search finds no Gibeonite named in 1 Samuel, the book that tells Saul’s reign.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 21:1: “Then there was a famine in the days of David three years, year after year; and David enquired of the Lord. And the Lord answered, It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites.” KJV 21:2: “now the Gibeonites were not of the children of Israel, but of the remnant of the Amorites; and the children of Israel had sworn unto them: and Saul sought to slay them in his zeal to the children of Israel and Judah.” KJV 21:5: “And they answered the king, The man that consumed us, and that devised against us that we should be destroyed from remaining in any of the coasts of Israel,” KJV 21:6: “Let seven men of his sons be delivered unto us, and we will hang them up unto the Lord in Gibeah of Saul” KJV 21:9: “And he delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them in the hill before the Lord” KJV 21:14: “And after that God was intreated for the land.” KJV Joshua 9:15: “And Joshua made peace with them, and made a league with them, to let them live: and the princes of the congregation sware unto them.” KJV Joshua 9:17: “Now their cities were Gibeon, and Chephirah, and Beeroth, and Kirjathjearim.” KJV Joshua 9:27: “hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the Lord” KJV 2 Samuel 4:2: “for Beeroth also was reckoned to Benjamin” KJV 2 Samuel 4:3: “And the Beerothites fled to Gittaim, and were sojourners there until this day.” KJV 1 Samuel 22:19: “And Nob, the city of the priests, smote he with the edge of the sword” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 21:1: עַל־אֲשֶׁר־הֵמִ֖ית אֶת־הַגִּבְעֹנִֽים [because he put the Gibeonites to death]. 21:2: וַיְבַקֵּ֤שׁ שָׁאוּל֙ לְהַכֹּתָ֔ם בְּקַנֹּאתֹ֥ו לִבְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִיהוּדָֽה [and Saul sought to strike them in his zeal for the children of Israel and Judah]. 21:5: הָאִישׁ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר כִּלָּ֔נוּ [the man who made an end of us]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 21:1: περὶ οὗ ἐθανάτωσε τοὺς Γαβαωνίτας [because he put the Gibeonites to death]. 21:2: καὶ ἐζήτησε Σαοὺλ πατάξαι αὐτοὺς [and Saul sought to smite them]. 21:5: ὁ ἀνὴρ ὃς συνετέλεσεν ἐφʼ ἡμᾶς καὶ ἐδίωξεν ἡμᾶς [the man who made an end upon us and pursued us]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/21/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA21.htm.
reasoning: The chapter does state the charge and its ground. The Lord’s answer names the act (“he slew the Gibeonites”), 21:2 names the oath Israel had sworn and Saul’s motive (“in his zeal to the children of Israel and Judah”), and the Gibeonites describe a man who “consumed us” and planned that they should not remain “in any of the coasts of Israel”. The verses compared state that killing occurred but do not give its time in Saul’s reign, place, number killed or detailed circumstances; 21:1 says “slew”, while 21:2 says “sought to slay”. The charge is laid on “his bloody house” as well as on Saul, and no act of the house is told here. The gap matters to the passage, because a famine and the death of seven men, who are not said in these verses to have taken part, rest on an act that the chapter mentions only by reference.

title: “After forty years” — forty years counted from what, before Absalom asked to go to Hebron?
summary: Absalom’s request to go to Hebron, which opens his revolt, is dated “after forty years”. The verse does not say from what the forty years are counted. The time notes just before it are three years and two years, David’s whole reign is given as forty years, and Absalom is listed among the sons born to David in Hebron.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 15:7: “And it came to pass after forty years, that Absalom said unto the king, I pray thee, let me go and pay my vow, which I have vowed unto the Lord, in Hebron.” KJV 15:8: “For thy servant vowed a vow while I abode at Geshur in Syria” KJV 15:1: “And it came to pass after this, that Absalom prepared him chariots and horses” KJV 13:38: “So Absalom fled, and went to Geshur, and was there three years.” KJV 14:28: “So Absalom dwelt two full years in Jerusalem, and saw not the king's face.” KJV 3:2: “And unto David were sons born in Hebron” KJV 3:3: “and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur” KJV 5:4: “David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years.” KJV 5:5: “In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months” KJV 1 Kings 2:11: “And the days that David reigned over Israel were forty years” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 15:7: וַיְהִ֕י מִקֵּ֖ץ אַרְבָּעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֑ה [and it came to pass at the end of forty years]. 5:4: אַרְבָּעִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה מָלָֽךְ [forty years he reigned]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 15:7: Καὶ ἐγένετο ἀπὸ τέλους τεσσαράκοντα ἐτῶν, καὶ εἶπεν Ἀβεσσαλὼμ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ [and it came to pass from the end of forty years, and Abessalom said to his father]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/15/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA15.htm.
reasoning: The verse gives a number and no starting point. The periods the narrative has just named are short: three years at Geshur (13:38) and “two full years” in Jerusalem (14:28), followed by “after this” (15:1). The larger figures stated elsewhere do not supply an evident starting point either. David “reigned forty years” in all (5:4; 1 Kings 2:11), and at 15:7 he is still king, with the revolt and what follows it still to come. Absalom is listed among the sons born to David in Hebron (3:2–3), where David reigned seven years and six months (5:5); if he was born during that Hebron reign, forty years counted from his birth would reach the very end of David’s forty years or pass it. So the passage dates the opening of the revolt by a figure whose reference the verses compared leave unstated, and the order and length of the events of David’s reign depend on how it is taken.

Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the forty years run from an earlier event that the verse does not name, such as David’s anointing or the beginning of the kingdom; that the number was once a smaller one. Limits: both editions quoted have “forty” at 15:7, and no text with another number was examined in this session; the statement about Absalom’s birth rests on the condition that he was born while David reigned in Hebron, which 3:2–5 places there without giving a year; the chapters after 15 are not shown to stand in order of time, so the figure is not set here against the length of David’s reign as a contradiction; the vow of 15:8 is dated to the stay at Geshur, which 13:38 gives as three years, and that does not give the forty years a starting point. Brenton’s Greek of 15:7 has “to his father” where the KJV has “unto the king”, a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. title: Ziba or Mephibosheth — whose account of the day David fled was true?
summary: When David flees Jerusalem, Ziba tells him that Mephibosheth has stayed behind expecting to be given “the kingdom of my father”, and David gives Ziba all that was Mephibosheth’s. When David returns, Mephibosheth says “my servant deceived me” and that Ziba “hath slandered thy servant”. David answers, “Thou and Ziba divide the land.” The verses compared do not say which of the two accounts was true.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 9:9: “I have given unto thy master's son all that pertained to Saul and to all his house.” KJV 9:10: “Thou therefore, and thy sons, and thy servants, shall till the land for him” KJV 9:13: “So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem”; “and was lame on both his feet” KJV 4:4: “that he fell, and became lame” KJV 16:1: “behold, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of asses saddled” KJV 16:2: “The asses be for the king's household to ride on” KJV 16:3: “And the king said, And where is thy master's son? And Ziba said unto the king, Behold, he abideth at Jerusalem: for he said, To day shall the house of Israel restore me the kingdom of my father.” KJV 16:4: “Then said the king to Ziba, Behold, thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth.” KJV 19:17: “and Ziba the servant of the house of Saul, and his fifteen sons and his twenty servants with him; and they went over Jordan before the king” KJV 19:24: “And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king, and had neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace.” KJV 19:25: “Wherefore wentest not thou with me, Mephibosheth?” KJV 19:26: “And he answered, My lord, O king, my servant deceived me: for thy servant said, I will saddle me an ass, that I may ride thereon, and go to the king; because thy servant is lame.” KJV 19:27: “And he hath slandered thy servant unto my lord the king; but my lord the king is as an angel of God: do therefore what is good in thine eyes.” KJV 19:29: “And the king said unto him, Why speakest thou any more of thy matters? I have said, Thou and Ziba divide the land.” KJV 19:30: “And Mephibosheth said unto the king, Yea, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace unto his own house.” Hebrew (WLC), where chapter 19 is numbered one verse ahead of the KJV. 2 Samuel 16:3: הַיֹּ֗ום יָשִׁ֤יבוּ לִי֙ בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֵ֖ת מַמְלְכ֥וּת אָבִֽי [today the house of Israel will give back to me the kingdom of my father]. 19:25 (KJV 19:24): וְלֹא־עָשָׂ֨ה רַגְלָ֜יו וְלֹא־עָשָׂ֣ה שְׂפָמֹ֗ו וְאֶת־בְּגָדָיו֙ לֹ֣א כִבֵּ֔ס [and he had not done his feet, and had not done his moustache, and his clothes he had not washed]. 19:27 (KJV 19:26): עַבְדִּ֣י רִמָּ֑נִי כִּֽי־אָמַ֨ר עַבְדְּךָ֜ אֶחְבְּשָׁה־לִּי֩ הַחֲמֹ֨ור [my servant deceived me, for your servant said, I will saddle the ass for myself]. 19:28 (KJV 19:27): וַיְרַגֵּ֣ל בְּעַבְדְּךָ֔ אֶל־אֲדֹנִ֖י הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ [and he slandered your servant to my lord the king]. 19:30 (KJV 19:29): אַתָּ֣ה וְצִיבָ֔א תַּחְלְק֖וּ אֶת־הַשָּׂדֶֽה [you and Ziba shall divide the field]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek), numbered as the Hebrew in chapter 19. 2 Samuel 16:3: σήμερον ἐπιστρέψουσί μοι οἶκος Ἰσραὴλ τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ πατρός μου [today the house of Israel will return to me the kingdom of my father]. 19:27 (KJV 19:26): ὁ δοῦλός μου παρελογίσατό με, ὅτι εἶπεν ὁ παῖς σου αὐτῷ, ἐπίσαξόν μοι τὴν ὄνον [my servant deceived me, for your servant said to him, Saddle the ass for me]. 19:28 (KJV 19:27): Καὶ μεθώδευσεν ἐν τῷ δούλῳ σου πρὸς τὸν κύριόν μου τὸν βασιλέα [and he dealt craftily with your servant before my lord the king]. 19:30 (KJV 19:29): σὺ καὶ Σιβὰ διελεῖσθε τὸν ἀγρόν [you and Siba shall divide the field]. The narrator does add one statement in its own voice: Mephibosheth “had neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace” (19:24). title: “again the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel” — for what, before David numbered the people?
summary: The chapter opens with the Lord’s anger already kindled “against Israel”, before describing David being moved to number the people. Seventy thousand die. David says the sin is his and asks of the people, “these sheep, what have they done?” The verses compared name no act of Israel that the anger was for, and do not say to what earlier anger “again” looks back.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 24:1: “And again the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them to say, Go, number Israel and Judah.” KJV 24:3: “but why doth my lord the king delight in this thing?” KJV 24:10: “I have sinned greatly in that I have done” KJV 24:15: “and there died of the people from Dan even to Beersheba seventy thousand men” KJV 24:17: “Lo, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly: but these sheep, what have they done?” KJV 21:1: “Then there was a famine in the days of David three years, year after year” KJV 6:7: “And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah” KJV 1 Chronicles 21:1: “And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel.” KJV 1 Chronicles 21:3: “why will he be a cause of trespass to Israel?” KJV 1 Chronicles 21:7: “And God was displeased with this thing; therefore he smote Israel.” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 24:1: וַיֹּ֙סֶף֙ אַף־יְהוָ֔ה לַחֲרֹ֖ות בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיָּ֨סֶת אֶת־דָּוִ֤ד בָּהֶם֙ [and the anger of the LORD burned again against Israel, and he incited David against them]. 24:17: וְאֵ֥לֶּה הַצֹּ֖אן מֶ֣ה עָשׂ֑וּ [and these, the flock, what have they done]. 1 Chronicles 21:1: וַיַּֽעֲמֹ֥ד שָׂטָ֖ן עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל [and an adversary, or Satan, stood against Israel]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 24:1: Καὶ προσέθετο ὀργὴν Κύριος ἐκκαῆναι ἐν Ἰσραήλ, καὶ ἐπέσεισε τὸν Δαυὶδ ἐν αὐτοῖς [and the Lord added wrath to burn in Israel, and stirred up David among them]. 1 Chronicles 21:1: Καὶ ἔστη διάβολος ἐν τῷ Ἰσραήλ [and a slanderer, or the devil, stood in Israel]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/24/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/21/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA24.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1CH21.htm.
reasoning: In the order of 24:1 the anger comes first and the numbering second: the anger is “against Israel”, and David is moved “against them”. In that presentation, the numbering is not identified as the cause of the opening anger; the sentence’s order alone does not establish an independently dated sequence. The sin the chapter does name is David’s (“I have sinned greatly in that I have done”), and David himself separates the people from it (“these sheep, what have they done?”), yet it is the people who die. “Again” says that this anger follows an earlier one, and the verse does not name it. The parallel at 1 Chronicles 21:1 opens without any statement of anger, and 1 Chronicles 21:7 places God’s displeasure after the numbering, “with this thing”. This record does not take up who moved David, on which 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1 are the subject of a separate record; the two verses are quoted here only for what they say of the anger. title: “But he lied unto him” — why did the old prophet of Bethel lie to the man of God?
summary: An old prophet of Bethel tells the man of God from Judah that an angel has ordered him to bring him home to eat, and the narrator adds “But he lied unto him.” The man of God eats, is sentenced by the word of the Lord spoken through the same old prophet, and is killed by a lion. The verses read state the lie and its result; they do not state why the old prophet told it.
text: KJV 1 Kings 13:9: “For so was it charged me by the word of the Lord, saying, Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest.” KJV 13:11: “Now there dwelt an old prophet in Bethel; and his sons came and told him all the works that the man of God had done that day in Bethel” KJV 13:15: “Then he said unto him, Come home with me, and eat bread.” KJV 13:18: “He said unto him, I am a prophet also as thou art; and an angel spake unto me by the word of the Lord, saying, Bring him back with thee into thine house, that he may eat bread and drink water. But he lied unto him.” KJV 13:19: “So he went back with him, and did eat bread in his house, and drank water.” KJV 13:20: “And it came to pass, as they sat at the table, that the word of the Lord came unto the prophet that brought him back:” KJV 13:21: “Forasmuch as thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the Lord” KJV 13:22: “thy carcase shall not come unto the sepulchre of thy fathers.” KJV 13:24: “And when he was gone, a lion met him by the way, and slew him” KJV 13:26: “It is the man of God, who was disobedient unto the word of the Lord” KJV 13:30: “And he laid his carcase in his own grave; and they mourned over him, saying, Alas, my brother!” KJV 13:31: “When I am dead, then bury me in the sepulchre wherein the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones” KJV 13:32: “For the saying which he cried by the word of the Lord against the altar in Bethel” … “shall surely come to pass.” KJV 2 Kings 23:18: “And he said, Let him alone; let no man move his bones. So they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet that came out of Samaria.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 13:18: וּמַלְאָ֡ךְ דִּבֶּ֣ר אֵלַי֩ בִּדְבַ֨ר יְהוָ֜ה [and an angel spoke to me by the word of the Lord] … כִּחֵ֖שׁ לֹֽו [he lied to him]. 13:31: אֵ֚צֶל עַצְמֹתָ֔יו הַנִּ֖יחוּ אֶת־עַצְמֹתָֽי [beside his bones lay my bones]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 13:18: καὶ ἐψεύσατο αὐτῷ [and he lied to him]. 13:31: παρὰ τὰ ὀστᾶ αὐτοῦ θέτε με, ἵνα σωθῶσι τὰ ὀστᾶ μου μετὰ τῶν ὀστῶν αὐτοῦ [lay me beside his bones, that my bones may be preserved with his bones]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/13/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI13.htm.
reasoning: The chapter states a good deal about the old prophet. His sons told him what the man of God had done and said (13:11); he rode after him and invited him home (13:15); when refused, he claimed an angel’s command, and the narrator says in the same verse that this was a lie (13:18). The word of the Lord then came to that same prophet at the table, and he spoke the sentence (13:20–22). After the death he said the man “was disobedient unto the word of the Lord” (13:26), buried him in his own grave, mourned “Alas, my brother!”, asked to be buried beside him, and affirmed that the saying against the altar “shall surely come to pass” (13:30–32). What none of these verses gives is the reason for the lie. The gap matters to the passage: the man of God had been charged to eat no bread there (13:9), he had refused the same invitation once (13:16–17), the lie is the stated means by which he was brought back, and his death follows from it.

Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the old prophet wished to test whether the man of God would keep his charge; that he wanted the company or the honour of a man whose word had just been confirmed by a sign; that he acted for Bethel and its altar, to undo or discredit the message; that he sought a tie with the man of God for his own sake, in the light of his later request to lie in the same grave. It is a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. title: Elijah is told to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha — did Elijah anoint any of them?
summary: At Horeb the Lord tells Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Syria, Jehu king over Israel and Elisha prophet in his place. In the verses read, Elijah casts his mantle on Elisha; it is Elisha who tells Hazael he will be king; and a young prophet sent by Elisha pours oil on Jehu. The verses read report no anointing done by Elijah, and they do not say how the command given to him was carried out.
text: KJV 1 Kings 19:15: “And the Lord said unto him, Go, return on thy way to the wilderness of Damascus: and when thou comest, anoint Hazael to be king over Syria:” KJV 19:16: “And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel: and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abelmeholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room.” KJV 19:19: “and Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.” KJV 19:21: “Then he arose, and went after Elijah, and ministered unto him.” KJV 2 Kings 2:13: “He took up also the mantle of Elijah that fell from him” KJV 2 Kings 8:13: “And Elisha answered, The Lord hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria.” KJV 2 Kings 8:15: “and Hazael reigned in his stead.” KJV 2 Kings 9:1: “And Elisha the prophet called one of the children of the prophets, and said unto him, Gird up thy loins, and take this box of oil in thine hand, and go to Ramothgilead” KJV 2 Kings 9:3: “Then take the box of oil, and pour it on his head, and say, Thus saith the Lord, I have anointed thee king over Israel.” KJV 2 Kings 9:6: “and he poured the oil on his head, and said unto him, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, I have anointed thee king over the people of the Lord, even over Israel.” KJV 2 Chronicles 22:7: “Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom the Lord had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 19:15: וּבָ֗אתָ וּמָשַׁחְתָּ֧ אֶת־חֲזָאֵ֛ל לְמֶ֖לֶךְ עַל־אֲרָֽם [and you shall come and anoint Hazael as king over Aram]. 19:16: תִּמְשַׁ֥ח לְמֶ֖לֶךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל [you shall anoint as king over Israel] … תִּמְשַׁ֥ח לְנָבִ֖יא תַּחְתֶּֽיךָ [you shall anoint as prophet in your place]. 19:19: וַיַּשְׁלֵ֥ךְ אַדַּרְתֹּ֖ו אֵלָֽיו [and he cast his mantle to him]. 2 Kings 9:6: וַיִּצֹ֥ק הַשֶּׁ֖מֶן אֶל־רֹאשֹׁ֑ו [and he poured the oil on his head]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 19:15: καὶ ἥξεις καὶ χρίσεις τὸν Ἀζαὴλ εἰς βασιλέα τῆς Συρίας [and you shall come and anoint Azael to be king of Syria]. 19:16: χρίσεις εἰς προφήτην ἀντὶ σοῦ [you shall anoint to be prophet in your place]. 19:19: καὶ ἐπέῥῥιψε τὴν μηλωτὴν αὐτοῦ ἐπʼ αὐτόν [and he cast his mantle upon him]. 2 Kings 8:13: ἔδειξέ μοι Κύριός σε βασιλεύοντα ἐπὶ Συρίαν [the Lord has shown me you reigning over Syria]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/19/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/9/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI19.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI08.htm.
reasoning: The command is in the second person and names three acts for Elijah: “anoint Hazael”, Jehu “shalt thou anoint”, Elisha “shalt thou anoint”. The verses read report something for each of the three men. Elijah finds Elisha and casts his mantle on him, and Elisha follows and serves him (19:19–21); the verse names a mantle and does not name oil or use the word “anoint”. With Hazael it is Elisha who speaks, at Damascus, and his words are that the Lord has shown him that Hazael will be king (2 Kings 8:13); no oil and no word “anoint” stands in 8:7–15. Jehu is anointed with oil, by “one of the children of the prophets” whom Elisha sends (2 Kings 9:1–6). The command lists Hazael, Jehu and Elisha, while the account presents Elisha, Hazael and Jehu. The list does not explicitly require that the acts occur in its stated order. The gap matters because the command is the Lord’s answer to Elijah at Horeb and sets out what is to follow; the verses read do not say whether Elijah did any of the three acts himself, or by what step the task passed to Elisha.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that Elijah carried out the command through his successor, so that what Elisha did or ordered counts as done by Elijah; that “anoint” is used here for appointing or designating, so that the mantle and the spoken word answer to it; that Elijah did anoint one or more of the three in acts the books do not report; that the command was left in part undone by Elijah. Limits: the command sets no time and does not say that Elijah must act in person at each step; that an act is not reported does not show that it was not done; 2 Chronicles 22:7 says the Lord had anointed Jehu and names no human hand; the casting of the mantle is not called an anointing in the verses read, and it is not said there to be anything else. Those are word searches and a reading of the verses listed, not a reading of 1 and 2 Kings in full; an account that uses other words would not be found by them. title: Twelve pieces, ten tribes and “one tribe” — which tribe is the twelfth?
summary: Ahijah tears a garment into twelve pieces, gives Jeroboam ten for “ten tribes”, and says Solomon’s son shall have “one tribe”. Ten and one make eleven. In the KJV and the Hebrew, the verses read do not say whose the twelfth piece is or which tribe it stands for; Brenton’s Greek reads “two tribes” at 11:32 and 11:36.
text: KJV 1 Kings 11:13: “Howbeit I will not rend away all the kingdom; but will give one tribe to thy son” KJV 11:30: “And Ahijah caught the new garment that was on him, and rent it in twelve pieces:” KJV 11:31: “And he said to Jeroboam, Take thee ten pieces: for thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel, Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee:” KJV 11:32: “But he shall have one tribe for my servant” KJV 11:35: “But I will take the kingdom out of his son's hand, and will give it unto thee, even ten tribes.” KJV 11:36: “And unto his son will I give one tribe” KJV 12:20: “there was none that followed the house of David, but the tribe of Judah only.” KJV 12:21: “he assembled all the house of Judah, with the tribe of Benjamin” KJV 12:23: “unto all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the remnant of the people” KJV 2 Chronicles 11:12: “having Judah and Benjamin on his side.” KJV Joshua 19:1: “and their inheritance was within the inheritance of the children of Judah.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 11:30: שְׁנֵ֥ים עָשָׂ֖ר קְרָעִֽים [twelve pieces]. 11:31: וְנָתַתִּ֣י לְךָ֔ אֵ֖ת עֲשָׂרָ֥ה הַשְּׁבָטִֽים [and I will give you the ten tribes]. 11:32: וְהַשֵּׁ֥בֶט הָאֶחָ֖ד יִֽהְיֶה־לֹּ֑ו [and the one tribe shall be his]. 11:36: וְלִבְנֹ֖ו אֶתֵּ֣ן שֵֽׁבֶט־אֶחָ֑ד [and to his son I will give one tribe]. 12:20: זוּלָתִ֥י שֵֽׁבֶט־יְהוּדָ֖ה לְבַדֹּֽו [except the tribe of Judah alone]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 11:13: σκῆπτρον ἓν δώσω τῷ υἱῷ σου [one tribe I will give to your son]. 11:30: δώδεκα ῥήγματα [twelve pieces]. 11:31: καὶ δώσω σοι δέκα σκῆπτρα [and I will give you ten tribes]. 11:32: Καὶ δύο σκῆπτρα ἔσονται αὐτῷ [and two tribes shall be his]. 11:36: Τῷ δὲ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ δώσω τὰ δύο σκῆπτρα [and to his son I will give the two tribes]. 12:20: πάρεξ σκήπτρου Ἰούδα καὶ Βενιαμὶν μόνοι [except the tribe of Judah and Benjamin alone]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/11/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/12/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI11.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI12.htm.
reasoning: The sign gives the numbers itself: twelve pieces (11:30), ten to Jeroboam for “ten tribes” (11:31, 11:35), and “one tribe” for Solomon’s line (11:13, 11:32, 11:36). The prophet does not say what becomes of the two remaining pieces, and the sum of the tribes named is eleven. The account that follows says first that none followed the house of David “but the tribe of Judah only” (12:20) and in the next verse that Rehoboam gathered “all the house of Judah, with the tribe of Benjamin” (12:21). So in the KJV and the Hebrew quoted, the verses read leave open which tribe the twelfth piece stands for and on which side it is counted. The gap matters because the sign is the stated ground of the division of the kingdom, and the count is its content. The Greek quoted does give a count that reaches twelve at two of the verses: it has “two tribes” at 11:32 and 11:36 and “Judah and Benjamin” at 12:20, while at 11:13 it has “one tribe”, as the Hebrew does.

title: “The book of the acts of Solomon” — what was this book, and is it the source Chronicles names?
summary: For the rest of Solomon’s acts and his wisdom, 1 Kings sends the reader to “the book of the acts of Solomon”. A phrase search of the packaged KJV finds that title in this verse only. At the same point 2 Chronicles names three other writings. The verses read do not say who wrote the book, what it held beyond the words quoted, or whether it is the same as any of the three.
text: KJV 1 Kings 11:41: “And the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the book of the acts of Solomon?” KJV 1 Kings 14:19: “behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.” KJV 1 Kings 14:29: “are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?” KJV 2 Chronicles 9:29: “Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, are they not written in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam the son of Nebat?” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 11:41: הֲלֹֽוא־הֵ֣ם כְּתֻבִ֔ים עַל־סֵ֖פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י שְׁלֹמֹֽה [are they not written on the book of the words (or acts) of Solomon?]. 2 Chronicles 9:29: הֲלֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ נָתָ֣ן הַנָּבִ֔יא [are they not written on the words of Nathan the prophet]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 11:41: οὐκ ἰδοὺ ταῦτα γέγραπται ἐν βιβλίῳ ῥημάτων Σαλωμών; [behold, are not these written in a book of the words of Solomon?]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/11/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/9/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI11.htm.
reasoning: The verse names the book by a title and says what is in it: “the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom”. That much is stated. The verses read do not say who wrote it, when, or where it was kept, and the account of Solomon closes by pointing to it for what the account itself leaves out. From the next reign onward the same formula points to differently named books, “the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel” (14:19) and “of the kings of Judah” (14:29). At the matching place 2 Chronicles 9:29 points instead to “the book of Nathan the prophet”, “the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite” and “the visions of Iddo the seer”. The gap matters because the verse directs readers to another writing for additional information about Solomon, without explaining that writing’s identity or its relation to the sources named in Chronicles.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the book was a record of Solomon’s reign kept at court, distinct from the later “chronicles of the kings”; that it is the same body of writing that 2 Chronicles 9:29 cites under the names of Nathan, Ahijah and Iddo; that it was a collection that held sayings as well as deeds, in view of “and his wisdom”; that it has not survived. Limits: the two books may point to different writings for the same reign without conflict, and no conflict is asserted here; that a title is found in one verse by a phrase search does not show that the writing is not meant elsewhere under another name; whether any existing writing is this book is not something these verses settle; the Hebrew word in the title can mean “words” or “acts”, and the KJV has “acts” for it in both halves of the verse. Check made: 1 Kings 11:41–43, 14:19 and 14:29 and 2 Chronicles 9:29 were read in the KJV, and 1 Kings 11:41 and 2 Chronicles 9:29 also in the Hebrew and 1 Kings 11:41 in the Greek; a phrase search of the packaged KJV for “acts of Solomon” finds 1 Kings 11:41 and 2 Chronicles 9:29, and for “book of the acts” finds 1 Kings 11:41 only. Those are phrase searches, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not say who wrote the book of the acts of Solomon or whether it is one of the writings named at 2 Chronicles 9:29. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: “There was great indignation against Israel” — whose indignation, and why did Israel depart?
summary: Israel, Judah and Edom are winning the war against Moab when the king of Moab offers his eldest son as a burnt offering on the wall. The next sentence says “there was great indignation against Israel”, and the armies go home. The verses read do not say whose indignation it was, why it fell on Israel, or how it made the armies leave.
text: KJV 2 Kings 3:18: “And this is but a light thing in the sight of the Lord: he will deliver the Moabites also into your hand.” KJV 3:24: “And when they came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose up and smote the Moabites, so that they fled before them: but they went forward smiting the Moabites, even in their country.” KJV 3:26: “And when the king of Moab saw that the battle was too sore for him, he took with him seven hundred men that drew swords, to break through even unto the king of Edom: but they could not.” KJV 3:27: “Then he took his eldest son that should have reigned in his stead, and offered him for a burnt offering upon the wall. And there was great indignation against Israel: and they departed from him, and returned to their own land.” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Kings 3:27: וַיְהִ֥י קֶצֶף־גָּדֹ֖ול עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיִּסְעוּ֙ מֵֽעָלָ֔יו וַיָּשֻׁ֖בוּ לָאָֽרֶץ [and there was great wrath upon Israel, and they set out from him and returned to the land]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Kings 3:27: καὶ ἐγένετο μετάμελος μέγας ἐπὶ Ἰσραήλ. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/3/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI03.htm.
reasoning: Elisha had said of the Lord, “he will deliver the Moabites also into your hand” (3:18), and the chapter reports the Moabites beaten and driven back into their own country (3:24) and their king unable to break out (3:26). Then one verse reports the offering of the king’s son and, straight after it, “great indignation against Israel”, followed by the withdrawal. The sentence names no one who was indignant. It does not say that the offering caused the indignation, although it is told directly before it, and it does not say what the indignation did. The gap matters to the passage because it is the stated turning point of the campaign: the armies that were winning “departed from him, and returned to their own land”.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the wrath was the Lord’s, against Israel; that the passage speaks of the wrath of the god of Moab, to whom the son is taken to have been offered; that it was the fury of the Moabites, roused by the act; that it was horror or anger felt by the besiegers themselves, or by Judah and Edom against Israel. Limits: the verse does not name the god to whom the son was offered, and does not say the offering had any effect; no failure of the words at 3:18 is asserted here, since 3:24 reports the Moabites smitten; the Hebrew noun and the Greek noun are quoted as printed and neither names whose feeling is meant; a use of the same Hebrew or Greek noun in another passage would not settle the sense here. Check made: 2 Kings 3:18–19 and 3:24–27 were read in the KJV, and 3:27 also in the Hebrew and the Greek; a phrase search of the packaged KJV for “great indignation” finds Deuteronomy 29:28, 2 Kings 3:27 and Nehemiah 4:1, and a whole-word search for “indignation” in 2 Kings finds 3:27 only. Those are word searches and a reading of the verses listed, not a reading of the whole book. These checked verses do not say whose indignation is meant or why the armies departed. title: “The blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons” — what happened to Naboth's sons?
summary: When Jehu has Joram’s body thrown into Naboth’s field, he recalls a word of the Lord about “the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons”. The account of Naboth’s death in 1 Kings 21 reports that Naboth was stoned and does not mention any sons. The verses read do not say when, how or by whom Naboth’s sons were killed.
text: KJV 2 Kings 9:25: “Then said Jehu to Bidkar his captain, Take up, and cast him in the portion of the field of Naboth the Jezreelite: for remember how that, when I and thou rode together after Ahab his father, the Lord laid this burden upon him;” KJV 9:26: “Surely I have seen yesterday the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons, saith the Lord; and I will requite thee in this plat, saith the Lord. Now therefore take and cast him into the plat of ground, according to the word of the Lord.” KJV 1 Kings 21:13: “Then they carried him forth out of the city, and stoned him with stones, that he died.” KJV 21:14: “Then they sent to Jezebel, saying, Naboth is stoned, and is dead.” KJV 21:16: “And it came to pass, when Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, that Ahab rose up to go down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, to take possession of it.” KJV 21:19: “Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?” … “In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine.” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Kings 9:26: אֶת־דְּמֵ֣י נָבֹות֩ וְאֶת־דְּמֵ֨י בָנָ֜יו רָאִ֤יתִי אֶ֙מֶשׁ֙ [the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons I saw yesterday]. 1 Kings 21:13: וַיִּסְקְלֻ֥הוּ בָאֲבָנִ֖ים וַיָּמֹֽת [and they stoned him with stones and he died]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Kings 9:26: τὰ αἵματα Ναβουθαὶ καὶ τὰ αἵματα τῶν υἱῶν αὐτοῦ εἶδον ἐχθὲς [the blood of Nabuthai and the blood of his sons I saw yesterday]. Brenton’s Greek prints the Naboth chapter as chapter 20; there, at 20:13: καὶ ἐλιθοβόλησαν αὐτὸν ἐν λίθοις, καὶ ἀπέθανε [and they stoned him with stones, and he died]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/9/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/21/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI09.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI20.htm.
reasoning: 2 Kings 9:26 gives, as the Lord’s own words, that he had seen “the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons”. In 1 Kings 21 the verses read tell of one death: Naboth is accused, carried out of the city and stoned (21:13), the message to Jezebel is “Naboth is stoned, and is dead” (21:14), and Elijah’s charge to Ahab speaks of “the blood of Naboth” (21:19). A whole-word search of 1 Kings 21 in the packaged KJV for “son” or “sons” finds only 21:10, 21:22 and 21:29, and none of those is about Naboth’s children. So the later verse refers to bloodshed that the earlier account, in the verses read, does not report. The gap matters because the sons’ blood is part of the stated ground for what is done to Joram’s body, and because Ahab then goes down “to take possession” of the vineyard (21:16), which Naboth had called the inheritance of his fathers.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the sons were put to death with Naboth, at the same time, and 1 Kings 21 leaves it out; that they were killed afterwards so that no heir could claim the vineyard; that “the blood of his sons” speaks of the loss done to his descendants and not of a separate killing. Limits: no conflict between the two books is asserted, since an account that reports one death does not deny others; 2 Kings 9:26 does speak of the sons’ blood, so what is missing is any report of the event, not the fact of bloodshed; the words Jehu recalls are not found in those words in 1 Kings 21:19, and whether they are a second saying or another form of the same one is not settled by these verses; “yesterday” is quoted as printed and its reference is not fixed here. Brenton’s Greek of 9:26 has “him” where the KJV has “I will requite thee”; that wording was seen and not examined. Check made: 2 Kings 9:21–26 and 1 Kings 21:3, 21:13–16 and 21:19 were read in the KJV, 1 Kings 21:10, 21:21–22 and 21:29 were read for the word search, and 2 Kings 9:26 and 1 Kings 21:13 were also read in the Hebrew and the Greek; a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “Naboth” finds the name only in 1 Kings 21 (verses 1–4, 6–9, 12–16, 18 and 19) and 2 Kings 9:21, 9:25 and 9:26. Those are word searches and a reading of the verses listed, not a reading of the whole of either book. These checked verses do not say when, how or by whom Naboth’s sons were killed. title: “The Lord gave Israel a saviour” — who was the saviour?
summary: In the account of Jehoahaz the narrator says that “the Lord gave Israel a saviour, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians”. The verse does not name him, and the same chapter says that Hazael oppressed Israel “all the days of Jehoahaz”. The verses read do not say who the saviour was or when he came.
text: KJV 2 Kings 13:3: “And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria, and into the hand of Benhadad the son of Hazael, all their days.” KJV 13:4: “And Jehoahaz besought the Lord, and the Lord hearkened unto him: for he saw the oppression of Israel, because the king of Syria oppressed them.” KJV 13:5: “(And the Lord gave Israel a saviour, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians: and the children of Israel dwelt in their tents, as beforetime.” KJV 13:7: “Neither did he leave of the people to Jehoahaz but fifty horsemen, and ten chariots, and ten thousand footmen” KJV 13:22: “But Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.” KJV 13:25: “And Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again out of the hand of Benhadad the son of Hazael the cities, which he had taken out of the hand of Jehoahaz his father by war. Three times did Joash beat him, and recovered the cities of Israel.” KJV 14:27: “but he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash.” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Kings 13:5: וַיִּתֵּ֨ן יְהוָ֤ה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מֹושִׁ֔יעַ [and the Lord gave to Israel a deliverer]. 14:27: וַיֹּ֣ושִׁיעֵ֔ם בְּיַ֖ד יָרָבְעָ֥ם בֶּן־יֹואָֽשׁ [and he delivered them by the hand of Jeroboam son of Joash]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Kings 13:5: Καὶ ἔδωκε Κύριος σωτηρίαν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ [and the Lord gave deliverance to Israel]. 14:27: καὶ ἔσωσεν αὐτοὺς διὰ χειρὸς Ἱεροβοὰμ υἱοῦ Ἰωάς [and he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam son of Joas]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/13/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/14/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI13.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI14.htm.
reasoning: The KJV and the Hebrew of 13:5 speak of a person given to Israel, by whom Israel came out from under Syria. The verse stands inside the account of Jehoahaz, after his prayer (13:4), yet the chapter also says that the king of Syria left Jehoahaz almost no army (13:7) and that Hazael oppressed Israel “all the days of Jehoahaz” (13:22). Relief is then reported under two later kings: Jehoash took back the cities and beat Benhadad three times (13:25), and of Jeroboam the narrator says the Lord “saved them by the hand of Jeroboam” (14:27), with the verb that belongs to the noun at 13:5. None of the verses read says that either king is the saviour of 13:5, and the verse itself gives no name, people or office. The identity matters to the passage because it is the stated answer to the king’s prayer and the stated means of Israel’s release.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state as the meaning of 13:5: that the saviour is Jehoash, whose victories are told at 13:25; that he is Jeroboam the son of Joash, by whose hand the Lord “saved them” at 14:27; that he is Elisha, who foretells the victories in the same chapter; that he is a foreign king whose pressure on Syria relieved Israel, whom the book does not mention in these verses. Limits: 14:27 does name Jeroboam as one by whom the Lord saved Israel, so what is open is whether 13:5 looks ahead to him, to Jehoash, or to someone else, not whether the book names any deliverer at all; a shared Hebrew root between 13:5 and 14:27 does not settle that they speak of the same person; no conflict between 13:5 and 13:22 is asserted, since 13:5 may look past the reign in which it is told; a foreign king is not named in the verses read and no outside record was opened. Brenton’s Greek of 13:5 has an abstract noun, “deliverance”, where the Hebrew and the KJV have a person; that is a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. That is a word search and a reading of the verses listed, not a reading of the whole book. These checked verses do not say who the saviour of 13:5 was. title: “I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord” — which book was it, and how had it gone out of knowledge?
summary: In Josiah’s eighteenth year the high priest says he has “found the book of the law in the house of the Lord”. The king hears it, rends his clothes and reforms Judah by it. The verses read call it the book of the law and the book of the covenant, and Chronicles calls it a book of the law of the Lord given by Moses; they do not say how much writing it held, where it had been, or how it came to be found at that time.
text: KJV 2 Kings 22:8: “And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.” KJV 22:11: “And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes.” KJV 22:13: “because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us.” KJV 23:2: “and he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in the house of the Lord.” KJV 23:21: “And the king commanded all the people, saying, Keep the passover unto the Lord your God, as it is written in the book of this covenant.” KJV 23:24: “that he might perform the words of the law which were written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the Lord.” KJV 14:6: “according unto that which is written in the book of the law of Moses” KJV 2 Chronicles 34:14: “And when they brought out the money that was brought into the house of the Lord, Hilkiah the priest found a book of the law of the Lord given by Moses.” KJV Deuteronomy 31:26: “Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, that it may be there for a witness against thee.” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Kings 22:8: סֵ֧פֶר הַתֹּורָ֛ה מָצָ֖אתִי בְּבֵ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה [the book of the law I have found in the house of the Lord]. 23:2: סֵ֣פֶר הַבְּרִ֔ית הַנִּמְצָ֖א בְּבֵ֥ית יְהוָֽה [the book of the covenant that was found in the house of the Lord]. 2 Chronicles 34:14: סֵ֥פֶר תֹּֽורַת־יְהוָ֖ה בְּיַד־מֹשֶֽׁה [the book of the law of the Lord by the hand of Moses]. Deuteronomy 31:26: לָקֹ֗חַ אֵ֣ת סֵ֤פֶר הַתֹּורָה֙ הַזֶּ֔ה [take this book of the law]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Kings 22:8: βιβλίον τοῦ νόμου εὗρον ἐν οἴκῳ Κυρίου [a book of the law I have found in the house of the Lord]. 23:2: τοῦ βιβλίου τῆς διαθήκης τοῦ εὑρεθέντος ἐν οἴκῳ Κυρίου [of the book of the covenant that was found in the house of the Lord]. 2 Chronicles 34:14: βιβλίον νόμου Κυρίου διὰ χειρὸς Μωυσῆ [a book of the law of the Lord by the hand of Moses]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/22/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/23/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/34/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/31/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI22.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI23.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH34.htm.
reasoning: The verses read say several things about the book. It was found in the house of the Lord by Hilkiah (22:8; 23:24). It is called “the book of the law” (22:8, 22:11), “the book of the covenant” (23:2) and “the book of this covenant” (23:21), and Chronicles calls it “a book of the law of the Lord given by Moses” (2 Chronicles 34:14). Its words told of wrath because “our fathers have not hearkened” (22:13), it was read aloud to the people at one gathering (23:2), and a passover was kept “as it is written” in it (23:21). What the verses do not give is its extent, the place in the house where it lay, how long it had been unread, or what led to its discovery and the king’s response. Deuteronomy 31:26 tells of “this book of the law” being put beside the ark, and 2 Kings 14:6 has the narrator cite “the book of the law of Moses” for an act of an earlier king; neither verse says what became of that book between then and Josiah. The gap matters because the whole reform of chapters 22 and 23 is said to rest on this book.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the book was Deuteronomy or a part of it; that it was the whole of the five books of Moses; that it was the copy laid beside the ark, lost or hidden during earlier reigns; that it was a writing first made known at that time. Limits: 2 Chronicles 34:14 does state that it was a book of the law of the Lord by the hand of Moses, so what is open in these verses is which writing and how much of it, and the circumstances of its discovery, not whether the text ascribes it to Moses; the narrator’s citation at 14:6 shows that the book of Kings can refer to a book of the law of Moses for an earlier reign, and does not show who then had a copy or read it; that the book was read out at one gathering does not fix its length; that the king was alarmed does not show that no one in Judah knew the law. Brenton’s Greek prints no article before the word for “book” at 22:8, where the Hebrew and the KJV have “the book”; that is a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. title: Saul’s father Kish: son of Ner, or son of Abiel and brother of Ner?
summary: Chronicles says twice “Ner begat Kish, and Kish begat Saul”. Samuel calls Kish “the son of Abiel”, calls Ner “the son of Abiel”, with “Saul's uncle” in the description of Abner son of Ner. Chronicles 9:36 also lists a Kish and a Ner side by side as sons of one father.
text: KJV 1 Chronicles 8:33: “And Ner begat Kish, and Kish begat Saul” KJV 9:36: “And his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, and Kish, and Baal, and Ner, and Nadab.” KJV 9:39: “And Ner begat Kish; and Kish begat Saul” KJV 1 Samuel 9:1: “whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel” KJV 1 Samuel 14:50: “Abner, the son of Ner, Saul's uncle” KJV 1 Samuel 14:51: “And Kish was the father of Saul; and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 8:33: וְנֵר֙ הֹולִ֣יד אֶת־קִ֔ישׁ וְקִ֖ישׁ הֹולִ֣יד אֶת־שָׁא֑וּל [and Ner begat Kish, and Kish begat Saul]. 1 Samuel 9:1: וּ֠שְׁמֹו קִ֣ישׁ בֶּן־אֲבִיאֵ֞ל [and his name was Kish son of Abiel]. 1 Samuel 14:51: וְקִ֧ישׁ אֲבִֽי־שָׁא֛וּל וְנֵ֥ר אֲבִֽי־אַבְנֵ֖ר בֶּן־אֲבִיאֵֽל [and Kish the father of Saul, and Ner the father of Abner, son of Abiel]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Chronicles 8:33: Καὶ Νὴρ ἐγέννησε τὸν Κὶς [and Ner begat Kis]. 1 Samuel 14:51: Καὶ Κὶς πατὴρ Σαοὺλ, καὶ Νὴρ πατὴρ [and Kis the father of Saul, and Ner the father] followed by Abner’s name and υἱὸς Ἰαμὶν [son of Jamin] before Abiel’s name. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/8/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/9/9/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/9/14/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1CH08.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1SA14.htm.
reasoning: In Chronicles the line runs Ner, Kish, Saul: Ner is Saul’s grandfather. In Samuel Kish is the son of Abiel, Ner is the son of Abiel, and Abner is described as the son of Ner, “Saul's uncle”. If the uncle phrase describes Ner and both references to Abiel indicate immediate fatherhood, Ner is Kish’s brother; those assumptions are not independently established here. Chronicles 9:36 itself names a Kish and a Ner together among the sons of the father of Gibeon, three verses before it says “Ner begat Kish”.
scope: No tag is proposed: the KJV follows the Hebrew in both books and Brenton’s Greek of 1 Chronicles 8:33 agrees. Brenton’s Greek of 1 Samuel 14:51 has one more name, Jamin, between Ner and Abiel; that is noted as wording and not tagged. The statements can stand together if there were two men named Ner, a grandfather and an uncle, or if “son of Abiel” at 1 Samuel 9:1 means a later descendant; none of the quoted verses says so. In 1 Samuel 14:50 the words “Saul’s uncle” may describe Ner or Abner; the record does not decide which. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: “All his house died together” — yet Saul’s son Ishbosheth is made king
summary: Chronicles says that Saul, his three sons “and all his house died together”. The parallel verse in Samuel says “all his men”. Samuel then tells of Saul’s son Ishbosheth reigning two years, and of a living son of Jonathan.
text: KJV 1 Chronicles 10:6: “So Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house died together.” KJV 1 Samuel 31:6: “So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together.” KJV 2 Samuel 2:8: “took Ishbosheth the son of Saul, and brought him over to Mahanaim” KJV 2 Samuel 2:10: “Ishbosheth Saul's son was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and reigned two years.” KJV 2 Samuel 9:3: “Is there not yet any of the house of Saul” … “Jonathan hath yet a son” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 10:6: וַיָּ֤מָת שָׁאוּל֙ וּשְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת בָּנָ֔יו וְכָל־בֵּיתֹ֖ו יַחְדָּ֥ו מֵֽתוּ [and Saul died and his three sons, and all his house together died]. 1 Samuel 31:6: גַּ֧ם כָּל־אֲנָשָׁ֛יו בַּיֹּ֥ום הַה֖וּא יַחְדָּֽו [also all his men, on that day together]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Chronicles 10:6: καὶ πᾶς ὁ οἶκος αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ἀπέθανε [and all his house died together]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/10/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/9/31/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1CH10.htm.
reasoning: Where Samuel has “all his men”, Chronicles has “all his house”. If “all his house” includes every member of Saul’s family, the Chronicles sentence leaves none alive after the battle; its scope is the point at issue. Samuel goes on to name a son of Saul who reigns two years, and the king later asks for and finds one “of the house of Saul”.
scope: No tag is proposed: the KJV follows the Hebrew, and Brenton’s Greek of 1 Chronicles 10:6 also has “all his house”. The statements can stand together if “all his house” means those of his household who were with him in the battle, or the end of his house as a reigning line; the verse does not say so. Brenton’s Greek of 1 Samuel 31:6 was read and has no words for “and all his men”; that is noted and not tagged, since the tag would rest on a verse outside this book’s session. title: Hired by Ammon: thirty-two thousand chariots, or twenty thousand footmen and twelve thousand men?
summary: In Chronicles the children of Ammon hire “thirty and two thousand chariots”, besides the king of Maachah and his people. In Samuel they hire twenty thousand footmen, a thousand men of king Maacah and twelve thousand men of Ishtob; no chariots are named.

Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 10:6: εἴκοσι χιλιάδας πεζῶν [twenty thousand footmen] and δώδεκα χιλιάδας ἀνδρῶν [twelve thousand men]. 1 Chronicles 19:7: δύο καὶ τριάκοντα χιλιάδας ἁρμάτων [thirty-two thousand chariots]. Samuel names no payment and Chronicles names a thousand talents of silver; that is a detail in one book only and is not set out as a conflict. title: “Whom the men of Gath … slew … And Ephraim their father mourned” — when and where did this happen?

title: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying, Thou hast shed blood abundantly” — when, and by whom, was this word given?
summary: David twice says that God told him he might not build the house because he had shed blood. title: In the ark: nothing “save the two tables”, or also the pot of manna and Aaron’s rod?
