text: KJV 2 Chronicles 22:6: “And Azariah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Jehoram the son of Ahab at Jezreel, because he was sick” KJV 2 Kings 8:29: “And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was sick” KJV 2 Chronicles 22:1: “So Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah reigned” KJV 2 Chronicles 22:7: “And the destruction of Ahaziah was of God by coming to Joram” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Chronicles 22:6: וַעֲזַרְיָ֨הוּ בֶן־יְהֹורָ֜ם מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֗ה יָרַ֡ד [and Azariah son of Jehoram king of Judah went down]. 2 Kings 8:29: וַאֲחַזְיָ֨הוּ בֶן־יְהֹורָ֜ם מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֗ה יָרַ֡ד [and Ahaziah son of Jehoram king of Judah went down]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Chronicles 22:6: Καὶ Ὀχοζίας υἱὸς Ἰωρὰμ βασιλεὺς Ἰούδα κατέβη [and Ochozias son of Joram, king of Juda, went down]. 22:1: καὶ ἐβασίλευσεν Ὀχοζίας υἱὸς Ἰωρὰμ βασιλέως Ἰούδα [and Ochozias son of Joram king of Juda reigned]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/22/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/8/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH22.htm.
reasoning: The Chronicles and Kings verses are the same sentence with one name changed. In the KJV and the Hebrew of Chronicles the visitor is Azariah; everywhere else in the passage, and in Kings, he is Ahaziah. The Greek of Chronicles prints one name throughout.

title: The men who killed Joash: sons of an Ammonitess and a Moabitess, or an Ammanite and a Moabite?
summary: The KJV of Chronicles names the conspirators Zabad son of Shimeath “an Ammonitess” and Jehozabad son of Shimrith “a Moabitess”: the foreign parent is a woman in each case. In Brenton’s Greek the words are masculine and stand with the conspirators’ own names: “the Ammanite”, “the Moabite”. Kings names the two men Jozachar son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer and says nothing of Ammon or Moab.
text: KJV 2 Chronicles 24:26: “And these are they that conspired against him; Zabad the son of Shimeath an Ammonitess, and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith a Moabitess.” KJV 2 Kings 12:21: “For Jozachar the son of Shimeath, and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, smote him, and he died” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Chronicles 24:26: זָבָ֗ד בֶּן־שִׁמְעָת֙ הָֽעַמֹּונִ֔ית וִיהֹ֣וזָבָ֔ד בֶּן־שִׁמְרִ֖ית הַמֹּואָבִֽית [Zabad son of Shimeath the Ammonitess, and Jehozabad son of Shimrith the Moabitess]. Hebrew (WLC) 2 Kings, numbered 12:22: וִיהֹוזָבָ֨ד בֶּן־שֹׁמֵ֤ר ׀ עֲבָדָיו֙ הִכֻּ֣הוּ [and Jehozabad son of Shomer, his servants, struck him]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/24/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/12/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH24.htm.

By the Greek wording the killers are themselves called a man of Ammon and a man of Moab; by the KJV they are sons of women of those peoples.

title: Manasseh’s altars in the house of the Lord: taken away by Manasseh, or beaten down by Josiah?
summary: Both books say Manasseh built altars in the two courts of the house of the Lord. Chronicles says that Manasseh himself later took away all the altars he had built there and cast them out of the city. Kings says that Josiah, two reigns later, beat down “the altars which Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the Lord”.
text: KJV 2 Chronicles 33:5: “And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord.” KJV 2 Kings 21:5: “And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord.” KJV 2 Chronicles 33:15: “And he took away the strange gods, and the idol out of the house of the Lord, and all the altars that he had built in the mount of the house of the Lord, and in Jerusalem, and cast them out of the city.” KJV 2 Kings 23:12: “and the altars which Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the Lord, did the king beat down” KJV 2 Chronicles 33:22: “for Amon sacrificed unto all the carved images which Manasseh his father had made, and served them” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Chronicles 33:15: וְכָל־הַֽמִּזְבְּחֹ֗ות אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָ֛ה בְּהַ֥ר בֵּית־יְהוָ֖ה וּבִירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וַיַּשְׁלֵ֖ךְ ח֥וּצָה לָעִֽיר [and all the altars that he had built in the mount of the house of the LORD and in Jerusalem, and he cast them outside the city]. Hebrew (WLC) 2 Kings 23:12: וְאֶת־הַֽמִּזְבְּחֹות֙ אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֣ה מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה בִּשְׁתֵּ֛י חַצְרֹ֥ות בֵּית־יְהוָ֖ה נָתַ֣ץ הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ [and the altars that Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the LORD the king pulled down]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Chronicles 33:15: καὶ πάντα τὰ θυσιαστήρια, ἃ ᾠκοδόμησεν ἐν ὄρει οἴκου Κυρίου καὶ ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ, καὶ ἔξωθεν τῆς πόλεως [and all the altars which he built in the mount of the house of the Lord and in Jerusalem and outside the city]. 2 Kings 23:12: καὶ τὰ θυσιαστήρια ἃ ἐποίησε Μανασσῆς ἐν ταῖς δυσὶν αὐλαῖς οἴκου Κυρίου καθεῖλεν ὁ βασιλεὺς [and the altars which Manasses made in the two courts of the house of the Lord the king pulled down]. title: Jehoiakim’s end: bound “to carry him to Babylon” — the Greek says he was carried there, and was buried with his fathers
summary: The KJV of Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim “to carry him to Babylon” and the quoted Chronicles verses do not describe his death or burial. Brenton’s Greek says the king “carried him away to Babylon”, and two verses later adds that Jehoiakim slept with his fathers “and was buried in Ganozae with his fathers”. Jeremiah had said he would have “the burial of an ass”, cast out beyond the gates.
text: KJV 2 Chronicles 36:6: “Against him came up Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and bound him in fetters, to carry him to Babylon.” KJV 36:8: “Now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and his abominations which he did, and that which was found in him, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah: and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his stead.” KJV 2 Kings 24:6: “So Jehoiakim slept with his fathers: and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his stead.” KJV Jeremiah 22:19: “He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem.” KJV Jeremiah 36:30: “and his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Chronicles 36:6: וַיַּֽאַסְרֵ֙הוּ֙ בַּֽנְחֻשְׁתַּ֔יִם לְהֹלִיכֹ֖ו בָּבֶֽלָה [and he bound him in bronze fetters to take him to Babylon]. 36:8 ends: עַל־סֵ֛פֶר מַלְכֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִֽיהוּדָ֑ה וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְהֹויָכִ֥ין בְּנֹ֖ו תַּחְתָּֽיו [in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah; and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Chronicles 36:6: καὶ ἔδησεν αὐτὸν ἐν χαλκαῖς πέδαις, καὶ ἀπήγαγεν αὐτὸν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα [and bound him in bronze fetters, and carried him away to Babylon]. 36:8: καὶ ἐκοιμήθη Ἰωακὶμ μετὰ τῶν πατέρων αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐτάφη ἐν γανοζαὴ μετὰ τὼν πατέρων αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐβασίλευσεν Ἰεχονίας υἱὸς αὐτοῦ ἀντʼ αὐτοῦ [and Joakim slept with his fathers, and was buried in Ganozae with his fathers, and Jechonias his son reigned in his place]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Jeremiah 22:19: Ταφὴν ὄνου ταφήσεται [he shall be buried with the burial of an ass]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/36/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH36.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JER22.htm.
reasoning: At 36:6 the KJV and the Hebrew state a purpose; the Greek states that it was done. At 36:8 the Greek has a death notice and a burial that the KJV and the Hebrew of the verse lack. The burial matters beside Jeremiah’s two sayings about Jehoiakim’s body: a burial “with his fathers” and “the burial of an ass … beyond the gates of Jerusalem” are different ends.

The KJV states “slept with his fathers” in another book, at 2 Kings 24:6; it states no burial of Jehoiakim in any verse quoted here. title: “There came a writing to him from Elijah the prophet” — when was it written, and how did it reach Jehoram?
summary: Jehoram of Judah receives a writing from Elijah that condemns him for killing his brothers, an act Chronicles places after his father Jehoshaphat’s death. Kings tells of Elijah being taken up into heaven before it tells of a campaign in which Jehoshaphat is still alive. The verses do not say when the writing was made or who carried it.
text: KJV 2 Chronicles 21:12: “And there came a writing to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, Thus saith the Lord God of David thy father, Because thou hast not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat thy father, nor in the ways of Asa king of Judah,” KJV 21:13: “and also hast slain thy brethren of thy father's house, which were better than thyself” KJV 21:1: “Now Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers” KJV 21:4: “Now when Jehoram was risen up to the kingdom of his father, he strengthened himself, and slew all his brethren with the sword” KJV 2 Kings 2:11: “and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven” KJV 2 Kings 3:11: “But Jehoshaphat said, Is there not here a prophet of the Lord” … “Here is Elisha the son of Shaphat, which poured water on the hands of Elijah” KJV 2 Kings 1:17: “And Jehoram reigned in his stead in the second year of Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah” KJV 2 Kings 8:16: “Jehoshaphat being then king of Judah” Hebrew (WLC) 2 Chronicles 21:12: וַיָּבֹ֤א אֵלָיו֙ מִכְתָּ֔ב מֵֽאֵלִיָּ֥הוּ הַנָּבִ֖יא לֵאמֹ֑ר [and there came to him a writing from Elijah the prophet, saying]. Kings tells of Elijah’s going up in its second chapter, and in its third has Jehoshaphat alive and Elisha introduced as the man who “poured water on the hands of Elijah”. The timing affects how the event is read: the writing may have arrived during Elijah’s earthly life, or after his departure, including a writing composed beforehand and delivered later. The quoted verses do not settle these possibilities.

What the verses do state is that a writing came, that it was from Elijah the prophet, and what it said. title: “The words of Necho from the mouth of God” — how did a word of God come to the king of Egypt?
summary: Necho of Egypt tells Josiah that God has commanded him to make haste and warns him not to meddle with God. The verses do not say how the command reached Necho, or by what sign Josiah could have known whose word it was.

title: “Put the holy ark in the house which Solomon … did build” — where had the ark been?
summary: In Josiah’s eighteenth year the king tells the Levites to put the holy ark in the house Solomon built, and that it shall no longer be a burden on their shoulders. Chronicles had the priests bring the ark into that house at its dedication. The verses checked do not say that the ark had left the house, or where it was when Josiah spoke.

Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/35/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2CH35.htm.

The verses checked report its entry under Solomon and then this command, without describing its intervening movements in those quotations.

title: “The whole congregation together was forty and two thousand three hundred and threescore” — the counts given add up to far fewer
summary: Ezra and Nehemiah both give 42,360 as the whole congregation. The counts each book lists before that total add up to 29,818 in Ezra and 31,089 in Nehemiah. Neither list reaches the total, and the two sums differ from each other.
text: KJV Ezra 2:64: “The whole congregation together was forty and two thousand three hundred and threescore,” KJV Ezra 2:65: “Beside their servants and their maids, of whom there were seven thousand three hundred thirty and seven” KJV Nehemiah 7:66: “The whole congregation together was forty and two thousand three hundred and threescore,” KJV Nehemiah 7:5: “And I found a register of the genealogy of them which came up at the first, and found written therein”. The first and last of them: Ezra 2:3 “The children of Parosh, two thousand an hundred seventy and two.” Ezra 2:60 “six hundred fifty and two”. Nehemiah 7:8 “The children of Parosh, two thousand an hundred seventy and two.” Nehemiah 7:62 “six hundred forty and two”. Hebrew (WLC) Ezra 2:64: כָּל־הַקָּהָ֖ל כְּאֶחָ֑ד אַרְבַּ֣ע רִבֹּ֔וא אַלְפַּ֖יִם שְׁלֹשׁ־מֵאֹ֥ות שִׁשִּֽׁים [the whole assembly as one: four ten-thousands, two thousand, three hundred, sixty]. Nehemiah 7:66: כָּל־הַקָּהָ֖ל כְּאֶחָ֑ד אַרְבַּ֣ע רִבֹּ֔וא אַלְפַּ֖יִם שְׁלֹשׁ־מֵאֹ֥ות וְשִׁשִּֽׁים. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Ezra 2:64: Πᾶσα δὲ ἡ ἐκκλησία ὁμοῦ ὡσεὶ τέσσαρες μυριάδες δισχίλιοι τριακόσιοι ἑξήκοντα, [and all the assembly together, about four ten-thousands, two thousand, three hundred, sixty]. title: Gifts to the treasure of the work: 61,000 drams of gold, or 41,000?

title: Who laid the foundation of the house: Sheshbazzar, or Zerubbabel?
summary: The elders’ answer reported in Tatnai’s letter says that Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundation of the house of God. The narrative of Ezra 3 has Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin the work at which the foundation was laid, and Zechariah says “The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house”.

Ezra 3:10: וְיִסְּד֥וּ הַבֹּנִ֖ים אֶת־הֵיכַ֣ל יְהוָ֑ה [and the builders founded the temple of the Lord]. title: The foundation of the temple: laid in the second year of the return, or on the day Haggai names in the second year of Darius?
summary: Ezra says the builders laid the foundation of the temple in the second year after the return, and that the work then stopped until the second year of Darius. Haggai, speaking on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month in the second year of Darius, names that date and adds “even from the day that the foundation of the Lord’s temple was laid”, and looks back to the time “before a stone was laid upon a stone”.

So it ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.” KJV Haggai 2:10: “In the four and twentieth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius” KJV Haggai 2:15: “consider from this day and upward, from before a stone was laid upon a stone in the temple of the Lord” KJV Haggai 2:18: “Consider now from this day and upward, from the four and twentieth day of the ninth month, even from the day that the foundation of the Lord's temple was laid, consider it.” Hebrew (WLC) Haggai 2:18: מִיֹּום֩ עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְאַרְבָּעָ֜ה לַתְּשִׁיעִ֗י לְמִן־הַיֹּ֛ום אֲשֶׁר־יֻסַּ֥ד הֵֽיכַל־יְהוָ֖ה [from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth (month), from the day that the temple of the Lord was founded]. Ezra 3:10: וְיִסְּד֥וּ הַבֹּנִ֖ים אֶת־הֵיכַ֣ל יְהוָ֑ה [and the builders founded the temple of the Lord]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Haggai 2:18: ἀπὸ τῆς τετράδος καὶ εἰκάδος τοῦ ἐννάτου μηνὸς, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἡμέρας ἧς τεθεμελίωται ὁ ναὸς Κυρίου [from the twenty-fourth of the ninth month, and from the day on which the temple of the Lord has been founded]. Ezra 3:10: Καὶ ἐθεμελίωσαν τοῦ οἰκοδομῆσαι τὸν οἶκον Κυρίου [and they laid a foundation to build the house of the Lord]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/37/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/15/3/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/HAG02.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EZR03.htm.
reasoning: In Ezra the laying of the foundation falls in the second year of the coming to Jerusalem, in the days of Cyrus, and is celebrated as done; the stoppage that follows lasts until the second year of Darius. In the KJV of Haggai the words “even from the day that the foundation of the Lord’s temple was laid” can be read as describing the date in Darius’s second year, and the same speech speaks of a time before stone was laid on stone in the temple.

The two can also stand if the foundation was laid in the days of Cyrus and laid or begun again when the work was taken up under Darius; no verse quoted reports a second laying. title: Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes between Cyrus and Darius — which kings are meant, and is the order of telling the order of events?
summary: Ezra 4 tells of opposition from the days of Cyrus “until the reign of Darius”, then of an accusation under Ahasuerus and letters under Artaxerxes about the city and its walls, and then says the work on the house stopped until the second year of Darius. The verses do not say who these two kings are or whether their reigns fall before Darius.

So it ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.” KJV Ezra 6:14: “according to the commandment of Cyrus, and Darius, and Artaxerxes king of Persia” KJV Ezra 6:15: “in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king” KJV Ezra 7:1: “Now after these things, in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia” KJV Ezra 7:7: “in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king” KJV Nehemiah 2:1: “in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king” KJV Esther 1:1: “Now it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus” KJV Daniel 9:1: “In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes” Hebrew (WLC) Ezra 4:6: וּבְמַלְכוּת֙ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹ֔ושׁ בִּתְחִלַּ֖ת מַלְכוּתֹ֑ו [and in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign]. 4:7: וּבִימֵ֣י אַרְתַּחְשַׁ֗שְׂתָּא [and in the days of Artaxerxes]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Ezra 4:6: Καὶ ἐν βασιλείᾳ Ἀσσουήρου, καὶ ἐν ἀρχῇ βασιλείας αὐτοῦ [and in the reign of Assuerus, and in the beginning of his reign]. 4:7: Καὶ ἐν ἡμέραις Ἀρθασασθὰ [and in the days of Arthasastha]. title: “Some of them had wives by whom they had children” — what became of the wives and the children?
summary: The book proposes a covenant to put away the foreign wives “and such as are born of them”, reports an inquiry that finished on a stated day, records a pledge by the priests first named, lists the men, and ends by saying that some had children by these wives. title: “Their horses, seven hundred thirty and six: their mules, two hundred forty and five” — a verse the Hebrew edition and the Greek do not print in Nehemiah
summary: KJV Nehemiah 7:68 counts 736 horses and 245 mules. The Westminster Leningrad text of Nehemiah 7 goes straight from the singers to the camels and has no such sentence, and Brenton’s Greek page prints no verse 68. The same sentence stands in all three texts at Ezra 2:66.
text: KJV Nehemiah 7:67: “and they had two hundred forty and five singing men and singing women” KJV Nehemiah 7:68: “Their horses, seven hundred thirty and six: their mules, two hundred forty and five:” KJV Nehemiah 7:69: “Their camels, four hundred thirty and five: six thousand seven hundred and twenty asses.” Hebrew (WLC) Nehemiah 7:67 ends וְלָהֶ֗ם מְשֹֽׁרֲרִים֙ וּמְשֹׁ֣רֲרֹ֔ות מָאתַ֖יִם וְאַרְבָּעִ֥ים וַחֲמִשָּֽׁה [and they had singing men and singing women, two hundred and forty-five], and its next verse, numbered 7:68, reads in full גְּמַלִּ֕ים אַרְבַּ֥ע מֵאֹ֖ות שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים וַחֲמִשָּׁ֑ה ס חֲמֹרִ֕ים שֵׁ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֔ים שְׁבַ֥ע מֵאֹ֖ות וְעֶשְׂרִֽים [camels, four hundred and thirty-five; asses, six thousand seven hundred and twenty]. The edition has 72 verses in this chapter where the KJV has 73. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): verse 67 ends καὶ ᾄδοντες καὶ ᾄδουσαι, διακόσιοι τεσσαρακονταπέντε. and the next verse printed is numbered 69: Ὄνοι δισχίλιοι ἑπτακόσιοι. The page prints the verse numbers 1 to 67 and 69 to 73. title: The gifts to the work: 530 priests’ garments or 30, and different weights of silver, in the Greek of Nehemiah
summary: In the KJV the Tirshatha gives 530 priests’ garments, the chief of the fathers 2,200 pound of silver and the rest of the people 2,000. Brenton’s Greek has 30 garments, 2,300 and 2,200, and at 7:70 it does not say that the Tirshatha gave: the gift is given “to Nehemiah”.

title: Chisleu “in the twentieth year”, then Nisan “in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes” — how is the year counted, and whose year is the first?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Nehemiah hears the report from Jerusalem in the month Chisleu “in the twentieth year” and speaks to the king in the month Nisan “in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes”. Elsewhere the KJV calls Chisleu the ninth month and Nisan the first. The book does not say from what point its years are counted, or whose twentieth year 1:1 means.

title: “The wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned with fire” — which breaking and burning is reported to Nehemiah?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. title: “The wood offering … as it is written in the law” — what written law is meant?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The people cast lots for “the wood offering”, to be brought by families at appointed times each year “to burn upon the altar of the Lord our God, as it is written in the law”. title: “On that night could not the king sleep” — the Greek says “the Lord removed sleep from the king”, and names God in three more verses
summary: In four verses that the KJV and the Hebrew also have, Brenton’s Greek names God or the Lord where they do not: Mordecai charges Esther to fear God (2:20) and to call upon the Lord (4:8), the Lord takes away the king’s sleep (6:1), and Haman is told that a living God is with Mordecai (6:13). A whole-word search of the packaged KJV of Esther finds neither “God” nor “Lord” anywhere in the book.
text: KJV Esther 6:1: “On that night could not the king sleep” Hebrew (WLC): בַּלַּ֣יְלָה הַה֔וּא נָדְדָ֖ה שְׁנַ֣ת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ [in that night the sleep of the king fled]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): Ὁ δε Κύριος ἀπέστησε τὸν ὕπνον ἀπὸ τοὺ βασιλέως τὴν νύκτα ἐκείνην [but the Lord removed sleep from the king that night]. KJV Esther 2:20: “for Esther did the commandment of Mordecai, like as when she was brought up with him” Hebrew: וְאֶת־מַאֲמַ֤ר מָרְדֳּכַי֙ אֶסְתֵּ֣ר עֹשָׂ֔ה [and the command of Mordecai Esther did]. Greek: οὕτως γὰρ ἐνετείλατο αὐτῇ Μαρδοχαῖος, φοβεῖσθαι τὸν Θεὸν, καὶ ποιεῖν τὰ προστάγματα αὐτοῦ [for so Mardochaeus commanded her, to fear God and to do his commandments]. KJV Esther 4:8: “to make supplication unto him, and to make request before him for her people” Hebrew: וּלְבַקֵּ֥שׁ מִלְּפָנָ֖יו עַל־עַמָּֽהּ [and to make request before him for her people], the last words of the verse. Greek, continuing after the matching words: ἐπικάλεσαι τὸν Κύριον, καὶ λάλησον τῷ βασιλεῖ περὶ ἡμῶν, ῥύσαι ἡμᾶς ἐκ θανάτου. [call upon the Lord, and speak to the king about us, to deliver us from death]. KJV Esther 6:13: “thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him” Hebrew: כִּֽי־נָפֹ֥ול תִּפֹּ֖ול לְפָנָֽיו [but falling thou shalt fall before him], the last words of the verse. Greek: καὶ οὐ μὴ δύνῃ αὐτὸν ἀμύνασθαι, ὅτι Θεὸς ζῶν μετʼ αὐτοῦ. [and thou shalt not be able to withstand him, because a living God is with him]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/6/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/4/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG06.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG02.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG04.htm.
reasoning: In the Hebrew and the KJV of these verses no one names God: the king cannot sleep, and Haman’s fall is foretold without any mention of God. The Greek states in each place that God is acting or is to be obeyed or called upon. That is a statement the KJV does not make in these passages.
scope: G applies at the four verses listed. The search is a word search of the ten chapters of the packaged KJV for “God”, “gods” and “Lord” in any letter case; it found nothing. It is not a claim about what the book implies. The Greek also names God many times in its lettered passages, which are not counted here because the KJV has no matching verses. title: In Shushan “on the spoil laid they not their hand” — the Greek has “and they plundered”
summary: The KJV, with the Hebrew, says three times that the Jews did not take spoil. Brenton’s Greek agrees the second and third time, but at 9:10, of the first day in Shushan, it says without a negative that they plundered.
text: KJV Esther 9:10: “slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand” Hebrew (WLC) 9:10: וּבַ֨בִּזָּ֔ה לֹ֥א שָׁלְח֖וּ אֶת־יָדָֽם [and on the spoil they did not put forth their hand]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek), the end of 9:10 and the start of 9:11: τοῦ ἐχθροῦ τῶν Ἰουδαίων, καὶ διήρπασαν ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ· [the enemy of the Jews, and they plundered on that same day]. KJV Esther 9:15: “but on the prey they laid not their hand” Greek 9:15: καὶ οὐδὲν διήρπασαν [and they plundered nothing]. KJV Esther 9:16: “but they laid not their hands on the prey” Greek 9:16: καὶ οὐδὲν διήρπασαν. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/9/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG09.htm.
reasoning: At 9:10 the Greek uses the same verb as at 9:15 and 9:16 but without “nothing”, so that it affirms what the Hebrew and the KJV deny. On the first day in Shushan the Jews take no spoil in the KJV and take spoil in the Greek.
scope: G applies at 9:10. At 9:15 and 9:16 the three texts agree. The Greek of 9:10 prints no object for the verb, so it does not say what was plundered or from whom. title: “In the days of Ahasuerus” — the Greek of Esther calls the king Artaxerxes
summary: The KJV, with the Hebrew, calls the king of the book of Esther Ahasuerus. Brenton’s Greek calls him Artaxerxes. In Ezra 4:6–7 the KJV prints both names, Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes, in consecutive verses.
text: KJV Esther 1:1: “Now it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus, (this is Ahasuerus which reigned, from India even unto Ethiopia” Hebrew (WLC) 1:1: וַיְהִ֖י בִּימֵ֣י אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹ֑ושׁ ה֣וּא אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹ֗ושׁ [and it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus, that is Ahasuerus]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek), the verse labelled 1:1s, which follows a passage the KJV does not have: Καὶ ἐγένετο μετὰ τοὺς λόγους τούτους ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις Ἀρταξέρξου· οὗτος ὁ Ἀρταξέρξης ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰνδικῆς ἑκατὸν εἰκοσιεπτὰ χωρῶν ἐκράτησεν [and it came to pass after these things in the days of Artaxerxes; this Artaxerxes held a hundred and twenty-seven regions from India]. KJV Esther 1:2: “when the king Ahasuerus sat on the throne of his kingdom” Greek 1:2: ὅτε ἐθρονίσθη βασιλεὺς Ἀρταξέρξης. KJV 3:1: “After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman” Greek 3:1: ἐδόξασεν ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἀρταξέρξης Ἀμὰν. KJV 10:3: “For Mordecai the Jew was next unto king Ahasuerus” Greek 10:3: Ὁ δὲ Μαρδοχαῖος διεδέχετο τὸν βασιλέα Ἀρταξέρξην. KJV Ezra 4:6: “And in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign” KJV Ezra 4:7: “And in the days of Artaxerxes wrote Bishlam” Brenton’s Greek of those two verses has other forms: 4:6 ἐν βασιλείᾳ Ἀσσουήρου, 4:7 ἐν ἡμέραις Ἀρθασασθὰ. reasoning: Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes are both names the KJV prints, in consecutive verses of Ezra 4, and Brenton’s Greek of Ezra keeps them apart as well. A reader of the Greek Esther is told the story happened under a king Artaxerxes; a reader of the KJV, under Ahasuerus.

title: “Who had been carried away from Jerusalem … with Jeconiah” — Mordecai, or his forefather Kish?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The KJV names Mordecai “the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish” and goes on, “Who had been carried away from Jerusalem” with king Jeconiah. The verse does not say whether “who” is Mordecai or the last man named, Kish. The answer decides whether Mordecai himself came from Jerusalem, and so how long before the king’s seventh and twelfth years that carrying away lay.
text: KJV Esther 2:5: “Now in Shushan the palace there was a certain Jew, whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite;” KJV Esther 2:6: “Who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity which had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away.” KJV 2 Kings 24:15: “And he carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon” KJV Jeremiah 24:1: “after that Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah” KJV Esther 2:16: “in the seventh year of his reign” KJV Esther 3:7: “in the twelfth year of king Ahasuerus” Hebrew (WLC) 2:5: וּשְׁמֹ֣ו מָרְדֳּכַ֗י בֶּ֣ן יָאִ֧יר בֶּן־שִׁמְעִ֛י בֶּן־קִ֖ישׁ אִ֥ישׁ יְמִינִֽי [and his name Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjamite]; 2:6: אֲשֶׁ֤ר הָגְלָה֙ מִיר֣וּשָׁלַ֔יִם עִם־הַגֹּלָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָגְלְתָ֔ה עִ֖ם יְכָנְיָ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֑ה [who was carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity that was carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2:6: ὃς ἦν αἰχμάλωτος ἐξ Ἱερουσαλὴμ, ἣν ᾐχμαλώτευσε Ναβουχοδονόσορ βασιλεὺς Βαβυλῶνος. [who was a captive from Jerusalem, which Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon took captive]. In a passage the KJV does not have, the verse labelled 1:1c says of Mardochaeus: Ἦν δὲ ἐκ τῆς αἰχμαλωσίας, ἦς ᾐχμαλώτευσε Ναβουχοδονόσορ βασιλεὺς Βαβυλῶνος ἐξ Ἰερουσαλὴμ, μετὰ Ἰεχονίου τοῦ βασιλέως τῆς Ἰουδαίας. [and he was of the captivity which Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon took captive from Jerusalem, with Jechonias the king of Judaea]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG02.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG01.htm.
reasoning: The clause opens with a relative word that follows three forefathers’ names. Read of Mordecai, it makes him a man who was himself taken from Jerusalem in Jeconiah’s day and who is still active in the twelfth year of Ahasuerus. Read of Kish, it dates the family’s removal and says nothing of Mordecai’s age. The verses quoted do not say how many years lie between Jeconiah’s captivity and the reign of Ahasuerus, so the weight of the question depends on which king is meant as well.
scope: Readings, none stated in the two KJV verses: that “who” is Mordecai; that “who” is Kish, the nearest name; or that it speaks of the family as a whole. The Hebrew relative word and the Greek of 2:6 leave the same choice open. The Greek’s added verse 1:1c does state one reading, that Mordecai himself was of that captivity; the KJV and the Hebrew edition have no such verse. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV finds “Jeconiah” at 1 Chronicles 3:16 and 3:17, Esther 2:6 and Jeremiah 24:1, 27:20, 28:4 and 29:2; none of those verses names Mordecai or Kish. That is a word search, not a reading of every passage about the captivity. Which king Ahasuerus is has been asked in another record and is not settled here. This is not presented as a contradiction. title: “But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence” — why not?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The king commands that all bow to Haman, and Mordecai does not. He is asked why and no answer of his is reported; the passage says only that “he had told them that he was a Jew”. Haman’s plan to destroy all the Jews follows from this refusal, and the KJV does not state its reason.
text: KJV Esther 3:2: “And all the king's servants, that were in the king's gate, bowed, and reverenced Haman: for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence.” KJV Esther 3:3: “Why transgressest thou the king's commandment?” KJV Esther 3:4: “when they spake daily unto him, and he hearkened not unto them, that they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai's matters would stand: for he had told them that he was a Jew” KJV Esther 3:5: “when Haman saw that Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence, then was Haman full of wrath” KJV Esther 3:6: “wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus” Bowing to men elsewhere in the KJV: Genesis 23:7 “And Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land”; 1 Samuel 24:8 “David stooped with his face to the earth, and bowed himself” Hebrew (WLC) 3:2: וּמָ֨רְדֳּכַ֔י לֹ֥א יִכְרַ֖ע וְלֹ֥א יִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶֽה [but Mordecai would not kneel and would not bow down]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 3:2: ὁ δὲ Μαρδοχαῖος οὐ προσεκύνει αὐτῷ. [but Mardochaeus did not do him obeisance]. In a prayer of Mardochaeus that the KJV does not have, the verses labelled 4:17d and 4:17e give a reason: ὅτι οὐκ ἐν ὕβρει, οὐδὲ ἐν ὑπερηφανείᾳ, οὐδὲ ἐν φιλοδοξίᾳ ἐποίησα τοῦτο, τὸ μὴ προσκυνεῖν τὸν ὑπερήφανον Ἀμάν. [that not in insolence, nor in pride, nor in love of glory did I do this, not to do obeisance to the proud Aman] Ἀλλʼ ἐποίησα τοῦτο, ἵνα μὴ θῶ δόξαν ἀνθρώπου ὑπεράνω δόξης Θεοῦ [but I did this that I might not set the glory of a man above the glory of God]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/3/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG03.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG04.htm.
reasoning: Everything that follows in the book turns on this refusal, yet the KJV reports the question put to Mordecai and not his reply. The one clue, that he had told them he was a Jew, is given as the reason the servants informed Haman; it is not said to be the reason he would not bow. In the two other verses quoted, Abraham and David bow to men and the verses record no blame.
scope: Readings, none stated in the KJV verses quoted: that he held bowing to Haman to be forbidden to a Jew; that the refusal was aimed at Haman in particular, for his descent or his person; or that it was a matter between the two men which the book does not tell. The Greek’s added prayer states one reason, that he would not set a man’s glory above God’s; the KJV and the Hebrew edition have no such passage. Genesis 23:7 and 1 Samuel 24:8 were chosen as examples of bowing to men; other passages on bowing were not collected, and the kind of bowing Haman was to receive is not described. This is not presented as a contradiction or as a fault in the passage. title: “Enlargement and deliverance … from another place” — from where, and why would Esther’s house still be destroyed?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Mordecai tells Esther that if she keeps silent, deliverance will come to the Jews “from another place”, but she and her father’s house will be destroyed. He does not say what the other place is, on what he rests his certainty, or by whom her house would be destroyed if the Jews are delivered.
text: KJV Esther 4:13: “Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king's house, more than all the Jews” KJV Esther 4:14: “For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” KJV Esther 4:16: “fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day” Hebrew (WLC) 4:14: רֶ֣וַח וְהַצָּלָ֞ה יַעֲמֹ֤וד לַיְּהוּדִים֙ מִמָּקֹ֣ום אַחֵ֔ר וְאַ֥תְּ וּבֵית־אָבִ֖יךְ תֹּאבֵ֑דוּ [relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place, and thou and thy father’s house will perish]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 4:14: ἄλλοθεν βοήθεια καὶ σκέπη ἔσται τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις· σὺ δὲ καὶ ὁ οἶκος τοῦ πατρός σου ἀπολεῖσθε [from elsewhere help and shelter will be for the Jews; but thou and thy father’s house will perish]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/4/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG04.htm.
reasoning: The sentence is the turning point of Esther’s decision, and it rests on an assurance whose ground is not given. If “another place” means God, the verse does not say so; if it means some other human helper, none is named. The second half is as open: the verse does not say whether Esther’s house would fall amid violence from which other Jews were delivered, or by a judgment on her silence. The promise of deliverance does not itself specify that every threatened person survives.
scope: Readings, none stated in the verses quoted: that “another place” is a guarded way of speaking of God; that it means another person or power at court; or that Mordecai speaks from confidence in earlier promises to his people, which he does not cite. The Hebrew and the Greek are as general as the KJV here. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV of Esther finds neither “God” nor “Lord” in the book; the Greek names the Lord at 4:8, in words the KJV does not have, and that difference is set out in another record. The fast of 4:16 names no one to whom it is addressed. This is not presented as a contradiction or as a fault in the passage. title: Job’s wife: one sentence in the KJV, a speech of six lines in the Greek
summary: In the KJV, with the Hebrew, Job’s wife says one sentence. Brenton’s Greek says that much time had passed and gives her a longer speech about her dead children, Job sitting in the open air among worms, and her own life as a wandering servant.
text: KJV Job 2:9: “Then said his wife unto him, Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die.” Hebrew (WLC) 2:9: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר לֹו֙ אִשְׁתֹּ֔ו עֹדְךָ֖ מַחֲזִ֣יק בְּתֻמָּתֶ֑ךָ בָּרֵ֥ךְ אֱלֹהִ֖ים וָמֻֽת. Septuagint (Brenton Greek), printed under the labels 9 and 9a to 9e. 9: Χρόνου δὲ πολλοῦ προβεβηκότος, εἶπεν αὐτῷ ἡ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ, μέχρι τίνος καρτερήσεις, λέγων, [and when much time had gone by, his wife said to him, How long wilt thou hold out, saying,] 9a: ἰδοὺ ἀναμένω χρόνον ἔτι μικρὸν, προσδεχόμενος τὴν ἐλπίδα τῆς σωτηρίας μου; [Behold, I wait yet a little time, looking for the hope of my deliverance?] 9b: ἰδοὺ γὰρ ἠφάνισταί σου τὸ μνημόσυνον ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς· υἱοὶ καὶ θυγατέρες, ἐμῆς κοιλίας ὠδῖνες καὶ πόνοι, οὓς εἰς τὸ κενὸν ἐκοπίασα μετὰ μόχθων· [for behold, thy memorial is blotted out from the earth: sons and daughters, the pangs and pains of my womb, for whom I laboured in vain with toils;] 9c: σύ τε αὐτὸς ἐν σαπρίᾳ σκωλήκων κάθησαι διανυκτερεύων αἴθριος, [and thou thyself sittest in the rottenness of worms, passing the night in the open air,] 9d: κᾀγὼ πλανωμένη καὶ λάτρις τόπον ἐκ τόπου καὶ οἰκίαν ἐξ οἰκίας, προσδεχομένη τὸν ἥλιον πότε δύσεται, ἵνα ἀναπαύσωμαι τῶν μόχθων μου καὶ τῶν ὀδυνῶν αἵ με νῦν συνέχουσιν· [and I a wanderer and a hired servant from place to place and from house to house, waiting for when the sun will set, that I may rest from my toils and from the pains that now hold me;] 9e: ἀλλὰ εἶπόν τι ῥῆμα εἰς Κύριον, καὶ τελεύτα. [but say some word unto the Lord, and die.] The KJV verses on either side: 2:7 “smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown”; 2:8 “And he took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal; and he sat down among the ashes.”; 2:10 “Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh” Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/2/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB02.htm.

The KJV’s question, “Dost thou still retain thine integrity?”, is not in the Greek speech as quoted; the Greek opens with “How long wilt thou hold out”.

title: Satan “came also among them” — is he one of the sons of God, and by what standing does he come before the Lord?
summary: Twice Satan comes before the Lord with the sons of God, is questioned, and is given power over Job within limits. The passage does not say whether he is one of the sons of God, what his office is, or why he is admitted.

title: “There was a man in the land of Uz” — where was Uz, and when did Job live?
summary: The book opens with a man in the land of Uz, the greatest of the men of the east. The opening names no king, no year, no father and no people for him. Brenton’s Greek adds a passage at the end of the book that gives a place, a line of descent and another name; the Hebrew and the KJV have no such passage.
text: KJV Job 1:1: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil.” Hebrew (WLC) 1:1: אִ֛ישׁ הָיָ֥ה בְאֶֽרֶץ־ע֖וּץ אִיֹּ֣וב שְׁמֹ֑ו. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:1: ἌΝΘΡΩΠΟΣ τις ἦν ἐν χώρᾳ τῇ Αὐσίτιδι, ᾧ ὄνομα Ἰὼβ. KJV 1:3: “so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east” The name Uz elsewhere in the KJV. Genesis 10:23: “And the children of Aram; Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash.” Genesis 36:28: “The children of Dishan are these; Uz, and Aran.” Jeremiah 25:20: “and all the kings of the land of Uz” Lamentations 4:21: “O daughter of Edom, that dwellest in the land of Uz” Job named elsewhere. Ezekiel 14:14: “Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it” James 5:11: “Ye have heard of the patience of Job” The end of the book. KJV Job 42:17: “So Job died, being old and full of days.” Brenton’s Greek prints 42:17 and then five lettered verses, 17a to 17e, which the Hebrew edition and the KJV do not have. 17b: Οὗτος ἑρμηνεύεται ἐκ τῆς Συριακῆς βίβλου, ἐν μὲν γῇ κατοικῶν τῇ Αὐσίτιδι, ἐπὶ τοῖς ὁρίοις τῆς Ἰδουμαίας καὶ Ἀραβίας· προϋπῆρχε δὲ αὐτῷ ὄνομα Ἰωβάβ· [This man is interpreted out of the Syriac book as dwelling in the land of Ausitis, on the borders of Idumaea and Arabia; and his name before was Jobab]. 17c, in part: ὥστε εἶναι αὐτὸν πέμπτον ἀπὸ Ἁβραάμ· [so that he was the fifth from Abraam]. KJV Genesis 36:33 has a Jobab among the kings of Edom: “Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his stead” Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB01.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB42.htm.
reasoning: In the KJV and the Hebrew the opening places Job by one name of a land and by the phrase “the men of the east”, and gives no reign, generation or kindred by which to date him. The other KJV verses that have the name Uz use it of a son of Aram, of a son of Dishan, of a land with kings (Jeremiah), and of a land where the daughter of Edom dwells (Lamentations); none of them mentions Job. Where and when Job lived bears on how his sacrifices, his knowledge of God and the book’s relation to Israel are read.

title: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever” — who is the king of Psalm 45, and who is called “God”?

title: “The waters stood above the mountains” — which event does Psalm 104:6–9 describe?
summary: Psalm 104:6–9 says the earth was covered with the deep, the waters stood above the mountains, they fled at God’s rebuke, and a bound was set so that they “turn not again to cover the earth”. The verses do not say whether the setting is the gathering of the waters at creation or the flood.
text: KJV Psalms 104:5: “Who laid the foundations of the earth, that it should not be removed for ever.” KJV 104:6: “Thou coveredst it with the deep as with a garment: the waters stood above the mountains.” KJV 104:7: “At thy rebuke they fled; at the voice of thy thunder they hasted away.” KJV 104:8: “They go up by the mountains; they go down by the valleys unto the place which thou hast founded for them.” KJV 104:9: “Thou hast set a bound that they may not pass over; that they turn not again to cover the earth.” KJV Genesis 1:9: “Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear”. KJV Genesis 7:19: “all the high hills, that were under the whole heaven, were covered”. KJV Genesis 9:11: “neither shall there any more be a flood to destroy the earth”. Hebrew (WLC) 104:6: תְּ֭הֹום כַּלְּב֣וּשׁ כִּסִּיתֹ֑ו. Hebrew (WLC) 104:7: מִן־גַּעֲרָ֣תְךָ֣. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/104/.
reasoning: The psalm describes the deep covering the earth, the waters above the mountains, their flight at God’s rebuke, and a boundary they may not pass or return over “to cover the earth”. It does not name a day, a person or an event. Genesis tells of two occasions on which waters covered land or were removed from it, and the psalm’s verses could be set beside either; the answer bears on whether the psalm speaks of the origin of the dry land or of the flood and its end.

title: Who speaks the curses of Psalm 109:6–19: is it the psalmist’s own prayer, or words he reports from his adversaries?
summary: Psalm 109 first speaks of adversaries in the plural (“they”), then of a single man (“him”, “he”) in a series of curses, then of “mine adversaries” again. The verses quoted do not say whether the curses are the psalmist’s own words or words he reports from his adversaries.
text: KJV Psalms 109:2: “For the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of the deceitful are opened against me: they have spoken against me with a lying tongue.” KJV Psalms 109:4–5: “For my love they are my adversaries: but I give myself unto prayer.” “And they have rewarded me evil for good, and hatred for my love.” KJV Psalms 109:6–8: “Set thou a wicked man over him: and let Satan stand at his right hand.” “When he shall be judged, let him be condemned: and let his prayer become sin.” “Let his days be few; and let another take his office.” KJV Psalms 109:16–19: “Because that he remembered not to shew mercy, but persecuted the poor and needy man, that he might even slay the broken in heart.” “As he loved cursing, so let it come unto him: as he delighted not in blessing, so let it be far from him.” “As he clothed himself with cursing like as with his garment, so let it come into his bowels like water, and like oil into his bones.” “Let it be unto him as the garment which covereth him, and for a girdle wherewith he is girded continually.” KJV Psalms 109:20–21: “Let this be the reward of mine adversaries from the Lord, and of them that speak evil against my soul.” “But do thou for me, O God the Lord, for thy name's sake: because thy mercy is good, deliver thou me.”
reasoning: In the verses quoted, 109:2–5 speak of what “they” have done to the speaker. From 109:6 the verbs and pronouns of the verses quoted are about a single person, “him” and “he”, and the verses quoted from 109:6 to 109:19 are wishes for harm to that person or statements of why it is wished. At 109:20 the speaker refers to “mine adversaries” and to “them that speak evil against my soul”, and at 109:21 turns to ask the Lord to do something for him. The verses quoted do not mark where the curses begin or end as someone’s reported speech, and do not say who the single man of 109:6–19 is. Possible readings: (1) the curses are the psalmist’s own prayer against one adversary among those named in the plural; (2) the curses are the words the adversaries spoke against the psalmist, which he reports before 109:20 answers them; (3) the plural adversaries and the single man are the same people spoken of in two numbers. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. This question is about the verses quoted in this record; it does not say what the rest of the psalm, its title or other books say. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, and does not claim that the psalm is a contradiction.

title: “The Lord said unto my Lord” — who is “my Lord” in Psalm 110:1?
summary: Psalm 110:1 reports one speech by “the Lord” to “my Lord”. The psalm’s own verses quoted do not name the one addressed, and two New Testament passages quote the verse and give an application of their own.
text: KJV Psalms 110:1–2: “The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.” “The Lord shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies.” KJV Psalms 110:4: “The Lord hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.” KJV Matthew 22:43–45: “He saith unto them, How then doth David in spirit call him Lord, saying,” “The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool?” “If David then call him Lord, how is he his son?” KJV Acts 2:34–36: “For David is not ascended into the heavens: but he saith himself, The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand,” “Until I make thy foes thy footstool.” “Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made the same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ.”
reasoning: Psalm 110:1 has two persons, “the Lord” who speaks and “my Lord” who is told to sit at his right hand. In the psalm verses quoted (110:1, 2 and 4) the one addressed is told to sit at the right hand, to “rule thou in the midst of thine enemies”, and is called “a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek”, but no verse quoted gives his name or says whether he is a person then living, a later person, or a role. In Matthew 22:43–45 the question asked is how David calls him Lord, and the passage as quoted does not answer it. In Acts 2:34–36 the verse is applied to Jesus. The record does not say whether those applications settle who the one addressed was in the psalm’s own setting. Possible interpretations of the quoted passages: a person David addressed as lord; a person later than David; the one the New Testament passages apply it to.

text: KJV Proverbs 8:1: “Doth not wisdom cry? and understanding put forth her voice?” KJV Proverbs 8:12: “I wisdom dwell with prudence, and find out knowledge of witty inventions.” KJV Proverbs 8:22–23: “The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old.” “I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was.” KJV Proverbs 8:29–30: “When he gave to the sea his decree, that the waters should not pass his commandment: when he appointed the foundations of the earth:” “Then I was by him, as one brought up with him: and I was daily his delight, rejoicing always before him;” KJV Proverbs 9:1: “Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars:”
reasoning: The speaker is named as “wisdom” in 8:1 and 8:12. In the quoted verses of 8:22–30 she says that the Lord possessed her “in the beginning of his way”, that she was “set up from everlasting”, that she was “by him” when he laid the foundations of the earth, and that she was his delight. In 9:1 “Wisdom hath builded her house”. The verses quoted do not say whether the speaker is a figure of speech for a quality of the Lord, a quality of the creation, a being distinct from the Lord, or a personification used only to teach. Possible readings: (1) a poetic personification of the Lord’s wisdom, as a literary reading of the quoted personification; (2) a personification of the order the Lord put into the creation; (3) a being that the passage speaks of as distinct from the Lord. The record does not decide between them.

title: “Since the days of Jeshua the son of Nun unto that day had not the children of Israel done so” — yet the feast of tabernacles is reported kept before
summary: Nehemiah 8 says that when the returned congregation made booths and sat under them, the children of Israel had not done so since the days of Joshua. Ezra 3 says the first to return “kept also the feast of tabernacles, as it is written”, and 2 Chronicles 8 counts that feast among Solomon’s yearly offerings. The law quoted makes dwelling in booths part of the feast.
text: KJV Nehemiah 8:14: “And they found written in the law which the Lord had commanded by Moses, that the children of Israel should dwell in booths in the feast of the seventh month:” KJV Nehemiah 8:17: “And all the congregation of them that were come again out of the captivity made booths, and sat under the booths: for since the days of Jeshua the son of Nun unto that day had not the children of Israel done so. And there was very great gladness.” KJV Ezra 3:4: “They kept also the feast of tabernacles, as it is written” KJV Leviticus 23:42: “Ye shall dwell in booths seven days; all that are Israelites born shall dwell in booths:” KJV 2 Chronicles 8:13: “three times in the year, even in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles” Hebrew (WLC) Nehemiah 8:17: כִּ֣י לֹֽא־עָשׂ֡וּ מִימֵי֩ יֵשׁ֨וּעַ בִּן־נ֥וּן כֵּן֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל עַ֖ד הַיֹּ֣ום הַה֑וּא [for the children of Israel had not done so from the days of Jeshua the son of Nun until that day]; Ezra 3:4: וַֽיַּעֲשׂ֛וּ אֶת־חַ֥ג הַסֻּכֹּ֖ות כַּכָּת֑וּב [and they kept the feast of booths as it is written]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Nehemiah 8:17: ὅτι οὐκ ἐποίησαν ἀπὸ ἡμερῶν Ἰησοῦ υἱοῦ Ναυῆ οὕτως οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραὴλ ἕως τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης; Ezra 3:4: Καὶ ἐποίησαν τὴν ἑορτὴν τῶν σκηνῶν κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/16/8/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/15/3/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EZR18.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EZR03.htm.
reasoning: If “done so” means keeping the feast with booths at all, Nehemiah 8:17 says it had not happened from Joshua’s time to that day, while Ezra 3:4 reports the feast kept “as it is written” at an earlier time by those who had returned, and the written law quoted requires booths. The name of the feast in the Hebrew of Ezra 3:4 is itself “the feast of booths”.
scope: No tag is proposed: the KJV follows the Hebrew in both books and the Greek agrees with both. The two statements can stand together if “done so” points to something narrower than keeping the feast — the making of booths by all the congregation, the manner or the gladness described in Nehemiah 8:16–17 — or if the feast of Ezra 3:4 was kept without booths; neither book says which, and Ezra 3:4 does not mention booths. The record therefore rests on one reading of “done so”. 2 Chronicles 8:13 speaks of offerings at the feast, not of booths. Other mentions of the feast between Joshua and Nehemiah were not collected. title: “A virgin shall conceive, and bear a son” — which child does Isaiah 7:14 mean?
summary: Isaiah 7:14 gives Ahaz a sign: “a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel”. The verses quoted do not say who the woman is, when the child is born, or whether he is the child of 8:3–4.
text: KJV Isaiah 7:10–14: “Moreover the Lord spake again unto Ahaz, saying,” “Ask thee a sign of the Lord thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above.” “But Ahaz said, I will not ask, neither will I tempt the Lord.” “And he said, Hear ye now, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also?” “Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.” KJV Isaiah 7:15–16: “Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good.” “For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings.” KJV Isaiah 8:3–4: “And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the Lord to me, Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz.” “For before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria.” KJV Isaiah 8:8: “And he shall pass through Judah; he shall overflow and go over, he shall reach even to the neck; and the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel.” KJV Isaiah 8:10: “Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for God is with us.” KJV Isaiah 8:18: “Behold, I and the children whom the Lord hath given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel from the Lord of hosts, which dwelleth in mount Zion.” A search of the packaged KJV text of Isaiah 1–27 for “virgin” finds 7:14, 23:4 and 23:12 (23:4 and 23:12 are not about this sign); for “Immanuel” it finds 7:14 and 8:8.
reasoning: The sign is given to “you”, the house of David (7:13–14); verse 16 says that before “the child” knows to refuse the evil “the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings”. The verses name no mother and no father, and give no year. In chapter 8 the prophet goes to “the prophetess”, who conceives and bears a son named Mahershalalhashbaz, and verse 4 gives a similar timing (“before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother”); verse 8 addresses “O Immanuel”, and verse 18 says the prophet and “the children whom the Lord hath given me” are signs. text: KJV Isaiah 49:3–6: “And said unto me, Thou art my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified.” “Then I said, I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought, and in vain: yet surely my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God.” “And now, saith the Lord that formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob again to him, Though Israel be not gathered, yet shall I be glorious in the eyes of the Lord, and my God shall be my strength.” “And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.”
reasoning: Verse 3 names the servant “Israel”. Verse 5 says the servant was formed from the womb “to bring Jacob again to him”, with “Israel” named as not yet gathered, and verse 6 says it is “a light thing” that he should “raise up the tribes of Jacob” and “restore the preserved of Israel”. The same name is used for the servant and for those he is sent to. The verses do not say whether “Israel” in verse 3 is the whole people, a faithful part of it, or a single person who bears the name. Possible readings: the nation; a faithful remnant; an individual figure. The record does not decide between them.

title: “the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim … came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon” or “the fourth year of Jehoiakim … the first year of Nebuchadrezzar”?
summary: Daniel 1:1 has Nebuchadnezzar, “king of Babylon”, come against Jerusalem “in the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim”. Jeremiah 25:1 says the fourth year of Jehoiakim “was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon”. Jeremiah 46:2 puts his smiting of Pharaohnecho in that fourth year.
text: KJV Daniel 1:1: “In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon unto Jerusalem”. KJV Jeremiah 25:1: “in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, that was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon”. KJV Jeremiah 46:2: “Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim”.
reasoning: Daniel 1:1 names Nebuchadnezzar “king of Babylon” in the third year of Jehoiakim. Jeremiah 25:1 gives the fourth year of Jehoiakim as the first year of Nebuchadrezzar, and 46:2 gives that fourth year for the battle at Carchemish. Read as worded, the king is called king of Babylon one year before his first year. The two statements could both stand if the two books count the years of a reign by different methods, or if the title in Daniel 1:1 is the title used of him when the event is told; neither passage says how the years are counted.
scope: No tag is proposed: the record compares the wording of the KJV only, and does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek. It does not say that either book is mistaken, and it does not say that the siege of Daniel 1:1 and the battle of Jeremiah 46:2 are the same event. The spellings Nebuchadnezzar and Nebuchadrezzar are the KJV’s two spellings of the name and are not the point.

title: “Darius the Median took the kingdom” — who is Darius, and how does his reign stand to the reign of Cyrus?
summary: Daniel 5:31 has “Darius the Median” take the kingdom, 9:1 calls him “the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes”, and 6:28 speaks of “the reign of Darius, and … the reign of Cyrus the Persian”. Daniel 1:21 and 10:1 count years of Cyrus. The verses do not say how the two reigns relate.
text: KJV Daniel 5:31: “And Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old.” KJV Daniel 9:1: “In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans”. KJV Daniel 6:28: “So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.” KJV Daniel 1:21: “And Daniel continued even unto the first year of king Cyrus.” KJV Daniel 10:1: “In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia”.
reasoning: Darius is given a people (Median or of the seed of the Medes), a father’s name and an age, and 9:1 says he “was made king”, which does not say by whom. Cyrus is given the title “king of Persia” at 10:1 and “the Persian” at 6:28. Chapter 6:28 can be read as two reigns, one after another, or as one person’s reign told under two names or titles with “and” between them. The verses quoted do not say which, and they do not say whether the years of Cyrus in 1:21 and 10:1 count from the same point as the reign of Darius. Possible readings, named only as readings: two successive kings; one person under two names; Darius as a ruler under Cyrus. The record does not decide between them.

title: “Beat your plowshares into swords” or “they shall beat their swords into plowshares”?
summary: Joel 3:10 has the nations told “Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruninghooks into spears”. Micah 4:3 and Isaiah 2:4 have the same two pairs of tools in the opposite direction: swords into plowshares and spears into pruninghooks.
text: KJV Joel 3:10: “Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruninghooks into spears”. KJV Micah 4:3: “they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks”. KJV Isaiah 2:4: “they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks”.
reasoning: The same two pairs of things, plowshares with swords and pruninghooks with spears, are changed in one direction in Joel and in the other in Micah and Isaiah. Read as worded, the verses describe opposite transformations of the same tools in different settings; Joel gives a command, while Micah and Isaiah describe future conduct. The verses could both stand: Joel 3:9–10 is spoken to the nations as a call to prepare war, and Micah 4:3 and Isaiah 2:4 describe the nations’ conduct when the Lord has judged among them; neither passage refers to the other.
scope: No tag is proposed: the record compares the wording of the KJV only, and does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek. It does not say that either passage is mistaken, does not say that the passages are one saying or two, and does not say which of the writers had the other’s words in view. Isaiah 2:4 is given as the third verse of the same wording; the pair at issue is Joel 3:10 against Micah 4:3.

title: Fowl brought forth by the waters, or formed from the ground? The Hebrew of Genesis 1:20 does not say the waters bring them forth
summary: The KJV of Genesis 1:20 and Brenton’s Greek have the waters bring forth fowl, while Genesis 2:19 forms the fowl from the ground. The Hebrew of 1:20 has the waters swarm with living creatures and the fowl fly, as a separate clause.
text: KJV Genesis 1:20: “Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth” KJV Genesis 1:21: “which the waters brought forth abundantly” KJV Genesis 2:19: “out of the ground the Lord God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air”. Hebrew (WLC) 1:20: יִשְׁרְצ֣וּ הַמַּ֔יִם שֶׁ֖רֶץ נֶ֣פֶשׁ חַיָּ֑ה [the waters swarm with a swarm of living creatures]; וְעֹוף֙ יְעֹופֵ֣ף עַל־הָאָ֔רֶץ [and fowl fly above the earth]. Hebrew (WLC) 2:19: מִן־הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה כָּל־חַיַּ֤ת הַשָּׂדֶה֙ וְאֵת֙ כָּל־עֹ֣וף הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם [out of the ground, every beast of the field and every fowl of the heavens]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:20: ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν, καὶ πετεινὰ πετόμενα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [let the waters bring forth creeping things having life, and flying birds above the earth]. Brenton Greek 2:19: ἔπλασεν ὁ Θεὸς ἔτι ἐκ τῆς γῆς πάντα τὰ θηρία τοῦ ἀγροῦ, καὶ πάντα τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ [God formed further, out of the earth, all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the heaven]. NETS renders the Greek with the waters bringing forth creeping things and birds. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/1/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN01.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN02.htm and https://ccat.sas.upenn.edu/nets/edition/01-gen-nets.pdf.
reasoning: Read in the KJV, the waters bring forth the moving creature and the fowl in chapter 1, while chapter 2 forms the fowl from the ground. Brenton’s Greek of 1:20 has one verb, “let the waters bring forth”, governing both the creeping creatures and the flying birds, so the Greek reads as the KJV does. The Hebrew has a verb for the waters (they swarm) whose object is the swarm of living creatures, and then a separate clause in which the fowl themselves fly. On the Hebrew wording, chapter 1 does not say what the fowl came from, and 2:19 says they were formed from the ground. The conflict therefore exists in the KJV and the Greek, and is not clearly present in the Hebrew.
scope: This is a demonstrated difference in clause structure, not a difference between synonymous English words. It does not show that the Hebrew has no tension with chapter 2: it says the fowl fly above the earth, and 1:22 has the fowl multiply “in the earth”, and some readers take the fowl to be among the creatures the waters produce. Genesis 1:24 has the earth bring forth the land animals, which is consistent with 2:19 for the beasts. title: Birds before land animals?
summary: Read as the first physical appearance of these groups, Genesis places birds before land animals. The scientific account places the terrestrial dinosaur ancestors of birds before birds.
text: KJV Genesis 1:21: “and every winged fowl after his kind”. KJV Genesis 1:23: “And the evening and the morning were the fifth day.” KJV Genesis 1:24: “Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind”. KJV Genesis 1:25: “And God made the beast of the earth after his kind”. KJV Genesis 1:31: “And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.” OpenStax Biology 2e describes birds as evolving within theropod dinosaurs; this places their terrestrial ancestors before birds.
reasoning: If day five introduces birds and day six introduces all land animals for the first time, the sequence puts birds before the terrestrial animals from which the scientific account derives them. The comparison concerns relative order, not a calculation of the length of a day. It does not require every modern land-animal species to predate every bird species.
scope: A literary or theological arrangement, a later appearance of already-existing creatures, or miraculous creation changes the claim being evaluated; none is established by the science source. The KJV categories are ordinary descriptions, not modern taxonomic ranks: the conditional comparison assumes the day-six land animals include terrestrial ancestors of birds. No Hebrew or Greek lexical finding is claimed. Science models natural processes and cannot independently test an unspecified miracle. This does not reconstruct events, assign a date or give a verdict on the whole passage.

title: Sarah’s late pregnancy and reproductive aging
summary: Sarah is described as old, with the usual female cycle ceased, before her later conception. The narrative attributes the birth to God’s promise and gives no physiological mechanism.
text: KJV Genesis 17:17: “and shall Sarah, that is ninety years old, bear?” KJV Genesis 18:11: “it ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women”. KJV Genesis 18:14: “Is any thing too hard for the Lord?” KJV Genesis 21:1: “And the Lord visited Sarah as he had said”. KJV Genesis 21:2: “For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age”. MedlinePlus describes menopause as the end of menstrual periods and natural fertility, recognized after twelve months without a period. The narrative supplies no menstrual timeline sufficient for that clinical comparison or an ordinary explanation of the subsequent conception.
reasoning: If the description in Genesis 18:11 refers to the end of menstruation, it supplies reproductive-aging context for why the promised birth is presented as exceptional. Modern information about menopause does not by itself diagnose Sarah, establish a natural conception mechanism in this account or test the divine action it attributes. Context preserves that distinction rather than treating an unspecified miracle as a scientifically disproved event.
scope: The comparison depends on reading the KJV’s manner-of-women wording as menstruation; no original-language lexical finding is claimed. A literary or theological account and miraculous intervention remain possible readings, not scientifically established explanations. The passage is not a clinical case history, and age alone is not used here to diagnose menopause or calculate fertility. No historical event or treatment is reconstructed, and the record gives no verdict on the whole passage.

title: A recent flood covering every mountain?
summary: A recent, mountain-covering global flood and destruction of terrestrial humanity conflict with evidence from sediment records, ice cores, tree rings, genetics and archaeology. Regional floods are a different claim.
text: KJV Genesis 7:19: “And the waters prevailed exceedingly upon the earth; and all the high hills, that were under the whole heaven, were covered.” KJV Genesis 7:20: “Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail; and the mountains were covered.” KJV Genesis 7:23: “And every living substance was destroyed which was upon the face of the ground, both man, and cattle, and the creeping things, and the fowl of the heaven; and they were destroyed from the earth: and Noah only remained alive, and they that were with him in the ark.” KJV Genesis 8:13: “And it came to pass in the six hundredth and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried up from off the earth: and Noah removed the covering of the ark, and looked, and, behold, the face of the ground was dry.” Svensson and colleagues reconstruct a continuous Greenland ice-core chronology extending 60,000 years, using annual layers and comparisons with independently dated records. This is evidence of a long preserved environmental sequence, not a date assigned to Genesis. Other independent records include Lake Suigetsu sediments (Nakagawa et al.), overlapping European tree-ring sequences (Friedrich et al.) and the long archaeological sequence at Madjedbebe (Hayes et al.). The field comparisons below identify what each record contributes and what it does not establish. KJV Genesis 7:22: “All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died.”
reasoning: The global reading predicts worldwide inundation and the elimination of land-dwelling, air-breathing humanity outside the ark, followed by repopulation. Instead, separately observed environmental and biological sequences support long regional histories. Their agreement is stronger than absence of a single flood deposit. No individual ancient artefact, old tree fragment or deep genetic lineage alone proves that a later flood did not occur. The conflict is with the combined recent global-inundation-and-reset reconstruction under ordinary processes; the studies cited are not all direct tests of Genesis.
scope: Disagrees applies to a recent, globe-covering physical event, not to every flood in every geological period. Genesis supplies no absolute calendar date here; no flood year, mountain height or water volume is calculated. A regional, literary or theological reading changes the claim. Science does not independently test an unspecified miracle or a proposal that evidence was supernaturally restored. Genesis 7:21–23 concerns land-dwelling, air-breathing life outside the ark; this record does not claim that the narrative says every aquatic organism or microorganism died. The archaeological sequence is not an annual census, and the tree chronology is assembled from overlapping trees, not one tree that lived for twelve millennia.

title: Did all humanity recently descend exclusively from one family?
summary: A recent replacement of all humanity by Noah’s household conflicts with the deep population history inferred from genomes. Shared ancestry is different from an exclusive population bottleneck.
text: KJV Genesis 9:19: “These are the three sons of Noah: and of them was the whole earth overspread.” KJV Genesis 7:23: “And every living substance was destroyed which was upon the face of the ground, both man, and cattle, and the creeping things, and the fowl of the heaven; and they were destroyed from the earth: and Noah only remained alive, and they that were with him in the ark.” KJV Genesis 6:18: “But with thee will I establish my covenant; and thou shalt come into the ark, thou, and thy sons, and thy wife, and thy sons' wives with thee.” KJV Genesis 2:7: “And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.” KJV Genesis 2:22: “And the rib, which the Lord God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man.” The Simons Genome Diversity Project examined 300 genomes from 142 populations and inferred that some ancestral populations were already substantially separated about 100,000 years ago. Hawks and colleagues compare bottleneck expectations with genetic and anthropological data and argue against a recent severe population-size bottleneck, while stressing limits of demographic inference.
reasoning: The scientific comparison concerns the recent, exclusive-family interpretation of the passage under ordinary inheritance. The genomic evidence supports a much older, structured ancestry; additional bottleneck analyses compare expected reductions in variation with multiple genetic systems. The paper is not a direct simulation of an eight-person flood bottleneck; the comparison draws on both its reconstructed history and the separately cited bottleneck analysis. The Adam-and-Eve references provide related context for an exclusive recent founding-couple reading.
scope: No minimum census population, precise bottleneck date or universally excluded ancestral couple is inferred. Effective population size is not a literal headcount. A couple or family being genealogical ancestors within a larger population is a different claim, as are regional survival and literary or theological readings. The cited study does not test miraculous creation or restoration of genetic diversity.

title: Creation chronology and the age of Earth
summary: A young Earth inferred from six ordinary creation days and an unbroken genealogy conflicts with scientific dating. Genesis does not explicitly state a creation date or Earth’s present age.
text: KJV Genesis 1:31: “And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.” KJV Genesis 2:2: “And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.” KJV Genesis 5:5: “And all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years: and he died.” KJV Genesis 11:10: “These are the generations of Shem: Shem was an hundred years old, and begat Arphaxad two years after the flood:” NASA describes Earth forming about 4.5 billion years ago. Richter and colleagues report an age of 315 ± 34 thousand years for heated flints directly associated with early Homo sapiens remains at Jebel Irhoud.
reasoning: These independent scientific timescales are incompatible with fitting all Earth and human history into only several thousand years. That short chronology is an interpretation combining creation days, genealogies and later dating assumptions; the quoted verses do not themselves state it. Existing vegetation/Sun and bird/land-animal records address different sequence questions.

title: Could viewing striped rods determine offspring coat patterns?
summary: If viewing striped rods is the proposed cause of inherited coat patterns, it conflicts with the demonstrated genetic basis of sheep pigmentation. Selective breeding and the narrative’s divine explanation are separate possibilities.
text: KJV Genesis 30:39: “And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted.” KJV Genesis 30:37: “And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods.” KJV Genesis 30:41: “And it came to pass, whensoever the stronger cattle did conceive, that Jacob laid the rods before the eyes of the cattle in the gutters, that they might conceive among the rods.” KJV Genesis 30:42: “But when the cattle were feeble, he put them not in: so the feebler were Laban's, and the stronger Jacob's.” KJV Genesis 31:9: “Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me.” KJV Genesis 31:12: “And he said, Lift up now thine eyes, and see, all the rams which leap upon the cattle are ringstraked, speckled, and grisled: for I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee.” Zhang and colleagues altered the sheep ASIP gene with CRISPR/Cas9 and observed changes in coat pigmentation and patterns. Their experiment demonstrates a genetic contribution; it did not test Jacob’s rods.
reasoning: The passage places patterned offspring alongside visual exposure to peeled rods, while also describing selective treatment of stronger animals. Demonstrated genetic mechanisms do not support transferring the appearance of an object into offspring through the parents seeing it. Genesis 31 attributes the outcome to God, so an exclusively natural rods mechanism is not the only reading.
scope: Disagrees is conditional on treating the visual stimulus itself as a heritable-pattern mechanism. The cited sheep experiment is not a reconstruction of ancient flocks, does not explain every coat trait or species, and does not rule out selection of existing variation. No original-language botanical or zoological identification is claimed. Miracle and literary interpretations are not experimentally disproved.

title: Is Joseph’s seven-year famine independently established?

title: Joseph’s land purchases and Egypt’s fifth-part levy
summary: The nationwide land purchase and continuing fifth-part levy are not independently established by the Egyptian parallels. Royal land rights and priestly privileges varied, so resemblance alone cannot date or verify Joseph’s policy.

Evidence of royal estates or temple privileges can illuminate those features without confirming that one official introduced them in a famine. Conversely, evidence of private management alone does not refute theoretical royal ownership. Guérin considers later Egyptian settings as possible contexts for the narrative.
scope: No land-tenure system is treated as constant across Egyptian history, and the narrative’s unto-this-day claim is not extended indefinitely beyond its narrator. The comparison does not identify a pharaoh, date the transaction or establish that Joseph never existed.
